questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient has cyanosis in the lower extremities, but examination reveals that the upper extremities are pink and well oxygenated. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Large Patent Ductus Arteriosus

Differential cyanosis (cyanosis of the lower extremities with pink upper extremities) is a classic finding in large Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) with Eisenmenger syndrome. Progressive pulmonary hypertension causes reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) across the PDA, allowing deoxygenated blood to enter the descending aorta distal to the origin of the subclavian arteries, thereby affecting the lower limbs while sparing the upper limbs.

• In a large PDA with Eisenmenger physiology:

• Initial shunt: Left → Right
• With pulmonary hypertension: Right → Left
• Deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta distal to the branches supplying the upper limbs.
• Upper extremities remain pink, while the lower extremities become cyanotic (differential cyanosis).

Why not the other options?

• A. Severe peripheral vascular disease: Causes ischemia but does not produce differential cyanosis.
• C. Atrioventricular septal defect: Eisenmenger syndrome causes central cyanosis, not differential cyanosis.
• D. Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome: Causes hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with recurrent epistaxis and AVMs, not differential cyanosis.
questions.learning: Large Patent Ductus Arteriosus Differential cyanosis (cyanosis of the lower extremities with pink upper extremities) is a classic finding in large Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) with Eisenmenger syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about retrosternal goitre?
options: Operated in all patients regardless of symptoms
Sternal incision is always required to operate
It receives blood supply from the thoracodorsal artery
Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision

Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach).

Retrosternal goitre is defined as having >50% of the goiter below the suprasternal notch. It can be either primary or secondary.

• Primary: rare and arises from ectopic thyroid tissue in the mediastinum; receives blood supply from intrathoracic blood vessels. It is not related to thyroid tissue in the neck.
• Secondary: they are the most common type; an extension of enlarged thyroid from the neck, usually arising from the lower pole of nodular goitre. It receives its blood supply from superior and inferior thyroid vessels.

The majority of patients are asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms. If the gland enlarges within the thoracic inlet, the pressure may lead to dysphagia, tracheal compression, and eventually airway symptoms. Pemberton sign can be positive (facial flushing and dilatation of cervical veins upon raising the arms above the head).

CECT neck and thorax is the investigation of choice.

Over 95% of retrosternal goiters can be removed via a transcervical incision since they are an extension from thyroid tissue in the neck.

Other options:

Option A: Surgical removal of the retrosternal goiter is indicated in patients with significant airway compression, and in young patients who have symptoms such as dyspnoea or dysphagia.

Option B: Median sternotomy approach is indicated in:

• Primary mediastinal goiter
• Malignant retrosternal goitre
• Very large retrosternal goiter
• Recurrence in the mediastinum

For a primary mediastinal goiter whose boundaries are completely within the chest, resection is often achieved through median sternotomy or thoracotomy to ensure that the vessels supplying the tumor are properly ligated. Removing the tumor through a cervical approach can result in uncontrolled bleeding and is generally avoided.

Option C: Blood supply to the retrosternal goiter is from the thyroid vessels (secondary retrosternal goiter).
questions.learning: Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In biomedical waste management, which category of waste is disposed of in a yellow- colored bag?
questions.explanation: According to the Biomedical Waste Management Rules in India, the yellow bag is used for highly infectious, non-plastic waste. This includes anatomical waste, soiled cotton, plaster casts, and blood bags. Waste in yellow bags is typically disposed of through incineration. Gloves (Option B) and recyclable contaminated plastic waste are placed in red bags. Sharps (Option C), such as needles and blades, are placed in white, translucent, puncture-proof containers. Urine bags (Option D), if emptied and treated, are generally considered recyclable plastic waste belonging in red bags. Proper segregation at the source is vital to prevent environmental contamination and healthcare-associated infections. Therefore, because blood bags are considered highly hazardous infectious waste that requires high-temperature destruction, they must be discarded in the yellow bag
questions.learning: According to the Biomedical Waste Management Rules in India, the yellow bag is used for highly infectious, non-plastic waste. This includes anatomical waste, soiled cotton, plaster casts, and blood bags.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The loading dose of MgSO4 in pre-eclampsia is?
options: 4 ml Mgso4 (50% w/v) in 16 ml NS
8 ml MgSo4 (50% w/v) in 12 ml NS
12 ml MgSo4 (50% w/v) in 8 ml NS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8 ml MgSo4 (50% w/v) in 12 ml NS

The loading dose of MgSO4 is 8ml MgSO4 (50% w/v) in 12ml NS. For loading dose IV infusion of 4g of 20% solution is needed.

One 2mL vial has 1g MgSO4. Therefore, to make a 20% solution containing 4g of MgSO4, we would need to take 8 mL of 50% magnesium sulfate, and dilute it with 12 mL NS. Therefore the final 20mL solution (8+12) would have 4g of MgSO4, making it a 20% solution.

MgSO4 is used as an anticonvulsant in the management of eclampsia and as prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia. The therapeutic level of magnesium in eclampsia is 4–7 mEq/L. Measurement of serum magnesium levels is indicated to monitor magnesium toxicity if serum creatinine >1.0 mg/dL.

MgSO4 regimens for management of eclampsia and severe preeclampsia:

Regimen

Loading Dose

Maintenance Dose

Intramuscular (Pritchard)

4 g (20% solution) IV over 3-5 minute

followed by 10 g (5O%), deep IM

(5 gm in each buttock)

5 g (5O%) IM 4 hourly in the alternate buttock

Intravenous (Zuspan or Sibai)

4g IV slow over 15-20 minute

1-2 g/h IV infusion

Repeat injections of magnesium sulfate are continued only if the patellar reflex is present, respiratory rate is >12, and urine output is >30 mL/h. Magnesium sulfate is discontinued either 24 hours after delivery or 24 hours after the onset of convulsions (whichever is later).

Loss of patellar reflex is the first sign of MgSO4 toxicity and occurs when the plasma magnesium level reaches 10 mEq/L. Elevated magnesium levels above 10 mEq/L weaken breathing, while 12 mEq/L or higher levels can lead to respiratory paralysis and arrest.
questions.learning: 8 ml MgSo4 (50% w/v) in 12 ml NS The loading dose of MgSO4 is 8ml MgSO4 (50% w/v) in 12ml NS. For loading dose IV infusion of 4g of 20% solution is needed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 60-year-old man post-MI had the following lab values. Which of the following must be his treatment plan?

• LDL - 125mg/dl
• HDL - 33 mg/dl
• TGL - 270mg/dl
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atorvastatin 80 mg

In this 60 yr old patient with post-myocardial infarction (Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease patient), high-intensity statins should be given irrespective of cholesterol levels. So atorvastatin 80mg is the treatment plan in the given case scenario.

Examples of high-intensity statins include high-dose atorvastatin 40–80 mg/day and rosuvastatin 20–40 mg/day.

Note: Fenofibrate is not advocated unless TG is more than 500 mg/dl. It can be administered along with a moderate-intensity statin.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child with a history of intubation presented to the OPD with shortness of breath while playing, approximately six weeks later. X-ray finding is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute laryngotracheobronchitis

The diagnosis in this child with a history of intubation and shortness of breath with X-ray showing the 'steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing is acute laryngotracheobronchitis.

Acute laryngotracheobronchitis is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The age of presentation of laryngotracheobronchitis ranges from 6 months to 6 years. The clinical features include barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and low-grade fever.

Management:

* Racemic epinephrine nebulization rapidly improves upper airway obstruction. Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway oedema.

* Dexamethasone is administered by the least invasive route (Oral > IV > IM ) for all grades of croup.

* Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %).

Antibiotics are not indicated in acute laryngotracheobronchitis.

Other options:

Option A: Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency presenting in children with a rapidly progressive course of fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and respiratory obstruction, followed by a toxic appearance and drooling. The neck is hyperextended and stridor is a late finding. Radiography shows a classic thumb sign as given in the image below.

Option C: In children with acute bronchitis, chest radiographs typically show minimal to non-specific findings. The most common radiological features include hyperinflation of lung fields, indicating air trapping and bronchial wall thickening.

Option D: Laryngomalacia is a congenital laryngeal anomaly presenting in children with low-pitched inspiratory stridor exacerbated by exertion. The laryngoscopy image showing omega-shaped epiglottis is given below.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

Diphtheria
Cervical lymph nodes (bull neck), dirty grey/ white membrane, and un-immunized

Foreign body aspiration
Choking, decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 3-year-old has acute onset barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and low-grade fever. He appears well and is not drooling. X-ray is shown below. He has moderate stridor with mild retractions. Most appropriate management is:
options: IV ceftriaxone for H. influenzae type B
Oral/IM dexamethasone + racemic epinephrine nebulisation for moderate-severe croup
Rigid laryngoscopy to visualise the epiglottis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral/IM dexamethasone + racemic epinephrine nebulisation for moderate-severe croup

The child has viral croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis), suggested by a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever, non-toxic appearance, and the classic steeple sign on the AP neck radiograph, indicating subglottic narrowing. The commonest causative organism is Parainfluenza virus type 1. As the child has moderate croup (stridor at rest with mild chest retractions), the recommended treatment is a single dose of dexamethasone (oral, IM, or IV) plus nebulized racemic epinephrine, which rapidly reduces airway edema. Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure. IV ceftriaxone and laryngoscopy are indicated for acute epiglottitis, which typically presents with high fever, toxic appearance, drooling, tripod position, muffled voice, and the thumbprint sign on lateral neck radiography.

| ----- | ------------

| Barking cough, hoarseness | Drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice

| Steeple sign | Thumbprint sign

| Parainfluenza virus | Haemophilus influenzae type b

| Dexamethasone ± nebulized epinephrine | Secure airway + IV ceftriaxone

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with complaints of greenish-frothy vaginal discharge for 1 month. On examination vulvovaginal erythema is noticed. On saline microscopy, motile organisms are seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trichomoniasis

The clinical vignette and microscopic findings are suggestive of trichomoniasis.

The clinical features include vaginal discharge which is profuse, thin, slightly green in color, and frothy. It may be associated with vaginal irritation, dysuria, and increased frequency. Cervical inflammation with punctate hemorrhagic spots known as the strawberry cervix is typically seen in trichomoniasis, caused by Trichomonas vaginalis. It is a sexually transmitted infection. Motile trichomonads are seen on wet mount examination.

The below image shows the strawberry cervix seen in trichomoniasis.

Other options:

Option B: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by an alteration in the normal vaginal flora and presents a malodorous grey-white discharge. It is diagnosed using Amsel's criteria, where at least three of the four following criteria should be present to confirm the diagnosis:

* Homogenous vaginal discharge

* Vaginal pH > 4.5

* Amine-like odor on adding KOH (Whiff test positive)

* Clue cells (>20% of cells)

Option C: Chlamydial cervicitis may present with severe abdominal pain with high fever, dyspareunia, prolonged menstrual cycles, and intermenstrual bleeding can be elicited. On examination, cervicitis with a yellow, cloudy, mucoid discharge can be seen from the os. The cervix tends to bleed easily when scraped.

Option D: Candidiasis is caused by infection with Candida albicans and presents with pruritus, burning, and dysuria with vulvar erythema, edema, and excoriations. A curdy white discharge will be present.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which radiographic view is considered best for optimal visualization of the maxillary sinus?
questions.explanation: The "Water’s view" (occipitomental projection) is the standard radiographic projection used for the "optimal visualization of the maxillary sinuses". By tilting the patient’s head back, the dense petrous ridges are projected below the maxillary antra, providing a clear view of any air-fluid levels or mucosal thickening. Towne’s view (Option B) is used primarily for the occipital bone and the foramen magnum. Law’s view (Option C) and Stenvers view (Option D) are specialized projections used for imaging the "mastoid air cells" and the "petrous temporal bone" (internal auditory canal), respectively. While CT scans have largely replaced plain films for detailed sinus evaluation, Water’s view remains a useful, cost-effective initial screening tool for acute sinusitis. Radiologists look for opacification of the normally air-filled sinuses to confirm the presence of inflammatory disease. Accurate positioning is essential to ensure the sinuses are not obscured by the skull base

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presented with colicky pain. Following type of crystals were found on urine examination. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystinuria

The presence of hexagonal crystals in urine is pathognomonic of cystinuria, a genetic disorder affecting amino acid transport. Defective renal tubular reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids (COLA: cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine)

• Cystine is poorly soluble in urine → precipitates to form hexagonal crystals and stones
• Leads to recurrent renal colic and kidney stones

Clinical features:

• Recurrent kidney stones at a young age
• Colicky abdominal pain
• May have family history (autosomal recessive)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Calcium oxalate stones: Envelope-shaped crystals
• ADPKD: Cystic kidneys, not crystal-related
• Glomerulonephritis: Hematuria, proteinuria (no characteristic crystals)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with O negative and husband B positive delivered a baby. Has received anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks. In which of the following conditions will you give anti-D post-delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Baby +ve, DCT -ve

Rh Isoimmunization occurs when:

• Rh-negative mother
• Rh-positive fetus

Fetal red blood cells entering maternal circulation stimulate production of anti-D antibodies, which can attack fetal RBCs in future pregnancies.

Rh-positive fetal RBCs enter maternal circulation

↓

Mother forms anti-D antibodies

↓

Antibodies cross placenta in next pregnancy

↓

Fetal hemolysis

↓

Hemolytic disease of the newborn

Anti‑D Immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitization by destroying fetal Rh-positive cells before the immune system reacts.

Anti-D is given within 72 hours after delivery if:

• Mother is Rh-negative
• Baby is Rh-positive
• Mother is not already sensitized

Thus:

| Baby Rh status | DCT | Anti-D required

| -------------- | --- | ---------------

| Rh negative | Any | ❌ Not required

| Rh positive | DCT negative | ✅ Give Anti-D

| Rh positive | DCT positive | Usually sensitization already present

DCT detects antibodies bound to fetal RBCs.

| DCT result | Meaning

| ---------- | -------

| Negative | No antibodies attached

| Positive | Hemolysis due to antibodies

Doses of Anti-D-

| Situation | Dose

| --------- | ----

| Routine antenatal prophylaxis | 300 µg at 28 weeks

| Post-delivery prophylaxis | 300 µg within 72 hours

| Early pregnancy events | 50–100 µg

questions.text: Identify the maternal condition that can lead to the findings in the baby as shown below: (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pre-gestational diabetes

The image depicts caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis), a congenital malformation strongly associated with maternal pregestational diabetes mellitus.

• Partial or complete absence of sacrum/lumbar vertebrae
• Lower limb deformities
• Abnormal pelvic development
• Neurogenic bladder and bowel dysfunction

Important association:

• Maternal pregestational diabetes markedly increases the risk
• Risk is much higher with poorly controlled glucose during organogenesis

Gestational diabetes usually develops after organogenesis. Therefore, it is less associated with major congenital malformations.

Other important diabetic embryopathies:

• Neural tube defects
• Congenital heart disease
• Renal anomalies

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident with thoracic and abdominal injuries and is found to be in hypovolemic shock. What is the most likely cause of the decreased cardiac output in this scenario?
options: Decrease in contractility of the heart
questions.explanation: In the context of a road traffic accident with significant internal injuries, the primary cause of shock is acute hemorrhage, leading to hypovolemic shock. Hypovolemia causes a severe reduction in the total circulating blood volume, which directly results in a decrease in preload (venous return to the heart). According to the Frank-Starling mechanism, a lower end-diastolic volume (preload) leads to a reduced stroke volume and, subsequently, a decreased cardiac output. Decrease in contractility (Option B) is characteristic of cardiogenic shock, often seen in myocardial infarction rather than trauma. Increase in preload (Option C) would occur in congestive heart failure, not hemorrhage. Increase in afterload (Option D) is a compensatory response to shock (vasoconstriction) to maintain blood pressure, but it is not the cause of the decreased output. Therefore, the fundamental hemodynamics of trauma-induced hypovolemic shock centers on the loss of blood volume leading to critically low cardiac filling or preload
questions.learning: In the context of a road traffic accident with significant internal injuries, the primary cause of shock is acute hemorrhage, leading to hypovolemic shock.

Plasma contains various components like ions, inorganic and organic molecules which help in the transport of substances across various parts of the body. Albumin, globulin, and fibrinogen fractions are important plasma proteins. Some of the plasma proteins act as antibodies and are also concerned with blood clotting. Where some others are non-specific carriers of hormones, drugs, and other solutes. Majority of plasma proteins are synthesized in the liver. The above table shows some of the proteins synthesized by the liver and the molecules they carry.

Thyroxine is carried by thyroid-binding pre-albumin which is also known as transthyretin.

Hemopexin binds with heme, particularly for heme recycling.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a neck swelling that moves with deglutition and undergoes surgical excision. Postoperatively, she is unable to raise the pitch of her voice. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. External laryngeal nerve

The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (external laryngeal nerve) is closely related to the superior thyroid artery and is therefore at risk during thyroid surgery. It supplies the cricothyroid muscle, the only tensor of the vocal cords. Injury to this nerve results in inability to tense and elongate the vocal cords, causing difficulty producing high-pitched sounds, voice fatigue, and reduced vocal projection, while normal speech may remain relatively preserved.

Why not the other options?

• A. Internal laryngeal nerve: Provides sensory innervation above the vocal cords. Injury causes loss of supraglottic sensation and an increased risk of aspiration but does not affect pitch.
• C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. Injury causes hoarseness, weak/breathy voice, and vocal cord paralysis; bilateral injury may lead to airway obstruction and stridor.
• D. Glossopharyngeal nerve: Supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle, sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue, and afferent limb of the gag reflex; it is not responsible for pitch control.
questions.learning: External laryngeal nerve — The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (external laryngeal nerve) is closely related to the superior thyroid artery and is therefore at risk during thyroid surgery.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following methods is specifically used for plasma sterilization?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma is a modern, low-temperature sterilization method specifically used for heat- and moisture-sensitive medical equipment. The process involves using radiofrequency or microwave energy to excite hydrogen peroxide vapor into a plasma state. In this state, highly reactive free radicals are generated that rapidly destroy all microorganisms, including bacterial spores. Ethylene oxide (Option A) is another low-temperature gas used for sterilization, but it is not a "plasma" method and is associated with significant toxicity and aeration requirements. Gamma rays (Option B) are a form of ionizing radiation used for industrial-scale sterilization of disposable items. UV rays (Option D) have low penetrative power and are used primarily for surface and air disinfection rather than definitive sterilization of complex instruments. Hydrogen peroxide plasma is favored in hospitals for its speed (cycles often under an hour) and safety, as the only byproducts are oxygen and water, leaving no toxic residue on the instruments

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of leg swelling accompanied by diarrhea. Several family members report experiencing similar symptoms, and mustard oil is commonly used in their household diet. Based on this history, what is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of multiple family members developing acute edema (leg swelling) and gastrointestinal symptoms (loose stools) after consuming mustard oil is pathognomonic for Epidemic Dropsy. This condition is caused by the contamination of mustard oil with argemone oil, which contains the toxic alkaloid Sanguinarine. Sanguinarine causes widespread capillary leakage and heart failure, leading to the characteristic edema. Clavine alkaloids (Option A) are associated with ergotism. BOAA (-oxalyl-amino-alanine) (Option C) is the toxin in Lathyrus sativus (Kesari dal) that causes neurolathyrism (spastic paraplegia). Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (Option D) are found in Crotalaria seeds and cause hepatic veno-occlusive disease. Because the family’s symptoms of swelling and diarrhea are directly linked to mustard oil ingestion, Sanguinarine toxicity from argemone contamination is the definitive cause
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of multiple family members developing acute edema (leg swelling) and gastrointestinal symptoms (loose stools) after consuming mustard oil is pathognomonic for Epidemic Dropsy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Post-exposure Measles vaccine should be given ?
questions.explanation: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection. For susceptible individuals who have been exposed to the virus, the measles vaccine can prevent or modify the disease if administered promptly. The recommended window for post-exposure vaccination is within 72 hours (3 days) of exposure. Administration within this timeframe provides active immunity that can overtake the natural infection's incubation period. If the 3-day window has passed, immunoglobulin (IG) can be given up to 6 days after exposure to provide passive immunity. Options A, C, and D do not match the clinically established "golden period" for post-exposure prophylaxis with the vaccine. This intervention is crucial during outbreaks to protect unimmunized contacts. Therefore, the 3-day rule is the standard epidemiological practice for post-exposure measles control
questions.learning: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection. For susceptible individuals who have been exposed to the virus, the measles vaccine can prevent or modify the disease if administered promptly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A neonate shows hypoplasia of the mandible and zygomatic bones, malformed external ears, and downward-slanting palpebral fissures. Abnormal development of which pharyngeal arch most likely accounts for these anomalies?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation described is characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome, which results from the abnormal development of the first pharyngeal arch. The first pharyngeal arch, also known as the mandibular arch, is responsible for forming the mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bones, and certain structures of the external and middle ear. Specifically, the maxillary process forms the zygomatic bone and maxilla, while the mandibular process forms the mandible through Meckel’s cartilage. Defects in the second pharyngeal arch (Option B) would primarily affect the stapes, styloid process, and muscles of facial expression. The third arch (Option C) contributes to the greater horn of the hyoid and stylopharyngeus muscle. The fourth arch (Option D) is involved in forming laryngeal cartilages and pharyngeal constrictors. Therefore, because the zygomatic and mandibular bones are the primary structures affected, the first pharyngeal arch is the definitive site of abnormal embryological development
questions.learning: The clinical presentation described is characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome, which results from the abnormal development of the first pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A baby is being evaluated for delayed developmental milestones. On examination, the child has hepatosplenomegaly. A microscopic image of the bone marrow evaluation is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gaucher disease

The microscopic image of the bone marrow biopsy shows Gaucher cells and the diagnosis is Gaucher disease.

Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disease with autosomal recessive inheritance. The condition results due to the deficiency of acid β-glucosidase. This results in the accumulation of glucosylceramide (a glycolipid substrate) in the reticuloendothelial cells. There is progressive infiltration of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

There are three clinical types:

• Type 1: Adult (non-neuronopathic form)
• Type 2: Infantile (acute neuronopathic form)
• Type 3: Juvenile (subacute neuronopathic form)

Type 1 is the most common. It presents with a myriad of symptoms, such as bruising secondary to thrombocytopenia, fatigue due to anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone pain. Lytic lesions and osteosclerosis of the femur, ribs, and pelvis may also be seen. A few patients may have pulmonary involvement. Growth retardation may be observed in cases presenting in the first decade.

Type 2 is rare, and presents with hypertonia, strabismus, and organomegaly. Neurodegeneration is the characteristic feature. Stridor and failure to thrive can also be the presenting features. Ultimately, death can occur due to respiratory arrest.

Type 3 presents with intermediate symptoms, as seen in the other two types. By the age of 10-15 years, the child succumbs to death.

Gaucher cells  are reticuloendothelial cells with glucosylceramide, and have a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic substrate inclusions. These cells stain strongly with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain. This is characteristic of Gaucher's disease.

Other options:

Option B - Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency results in Niemann-Pick disease types A and B. Both are autosomal recessive conditions. Type A has a neurodegenerative course, while type B is non-neuronopathic. The former presents with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and psychomotor retardation. Type B is associated with hepatosplenomegaly and mild pulmonary involvement.

Option-C - Hunter disease is an X-linked inherited disorder due to a deficiency of the enzyme iduronate sulfatase. It leads to the accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate. Clinical features involve coarse facies, cardiovascular involvement, and distinctive skin lesions.

Option-D - Hurler/Scheie disease is a mucopolysaccharidosis that has childhood and adult onset. It presents with cognitive degeneration.
questions.learning: Gaucher disease — The microscopic image of the bone marrow biopsy shows Gaucher cells and the diagnosis is Gaucher disease. Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disease with autosomal recessive inheritance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: False statement regarding the condition shown below in the image?
options: Staph aureus is the causative organism
questions.explanation: The image depicts Fournier's gangrene, a necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and scrotum. It is a surgical emergency characterized by rapid tissue destruction. The false statement among the options is that Staph. aureus is the primary causative organism. In reality, Fournier's gangrene is typically "polymicrobial," caused by a synergistic mixture of aerobes and anaerobes (including E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, and Bacteroides). It is indeed very common in diabetic patients (Option B), as hyperglycemia impairs immunity and wound healing. It carries a high mortality rate (Option C), often due to sepsis, if not treated aggressively with broad-spectrum antibiotics and extensive surgical debridement. Interestingly, the testes themselves usually remain unaffected (Option D) because they have a separate, independent blood supply from the internal spermatic (testicular) artery, which originates directly from the abdominal aorta, sparing them from the local subcutaneous vascular thrombosis. Therefore, while Staph. aureus may be present, the condition is fundamentally polymicrobial
questions.learning: The image depicts Fournier's gangrene, a necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and scrotum. It is a surgical emergency characterized by rapid tissue destruction.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a gunshot injury where autopsy findings show an entry wound with inverted margins and surrounding tattooing, but no blackening or singeing of hair, what is the most probable range from which the firearm was discharged?
questions.explanation: Forensic determination of the firing range is based on artifacts found on the skin. Tattooing (peppering) is caused by unburnt gunpowder particles embedding in the skin and is the hallmark of a Close shot (typically within a range of 1 to 3 feet for handguns). In this case, the absence of blackening (smoke deposit) and singeing of hair suggests the weapon was far enough away that the heat and smoke didn't reach the skin, but close enough for gunpowder particles to leave their mark. A Contact shot (Option A) would show a muzzle mark, "star-shaped" tearing, and internal soot. A Near shot (Option B) would definitely include blackening and singeing. A Distant shot (Option D) would show only the entry hole (abrasion collar) without any tattooing, blackening, or singeing. Therefore, the combination of tattooing without smoke deposits is the classic forensic indicator for a "Close range" gunshot
questions.learning: Forensic determination of the firing range is based on artifacts found on the skin. Tattooing (peppering) is caused by unburnt gunpowder particles embedding in the skin and is the hallmark of a Close shot (typically within a range of 1 to 3 feet for handguns).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A vegetable vendor with no prior criminal history went missing and was found dead a week later in an advanced state of decomposition. What methods can be used to identify the body in such a situation?
questions.explanation: In cases of advanced decomposition, many traditional methods of identification become unreliable. General recognition (Option A) is impossible as the facial features are destroyed. Fingerprints (Option D) are often lost due to skin "gloving" or putrefaction. While dental records (Option C) are a highly effective and standard method, they require a pre-existing dental chart for comparison, which a person like a "vegetable vendor with no history" may not have. DNA profiling is currently the most definitive and robust method for identifying decomposed remains. DNA can be extracted from stable tissues like the teeth or long bones (the femur) even a week or more after death. The profile can then be compared to a reference sample from the missing person's belongings or, more commonly, to DNA from living first-degree relatives. DNA profiling provides a scientific certainty of identification that is essential for legal and closure purposes in missing person cases
questions.learning: In cases of advanced decomposition, many traditional methods of identification become unreliable. General recognition (Option A) is impossible as the facial features are destroyed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Dohlman’s procedure is for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zenker’s diverticulum

Dohlman’s  procedure is done for Zenker’s diverticulum.

A transoral endoscopic approach (Dohlman's procedure) -using staplers, laser, or coagulation through an endoscope that ablate the septum between the diverticulum and the cervical esophagus, can be used for diverticula between 2 and 5 cm in size.

The treatment is either endoscopic or open surgery.For diverticula 3 cm or smaller in size, surgical repair is superior and thus preferred to endoscopic repair.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Utilizing the provided X-ray, identify the type of fracture using the Salter-Harris classification?
questions.explanation: The Salter-Harris classification system is used to describe fractures involving the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) in children. A Type 2 fracture, the most common type, occurs when the fracture line passes through the growth plate (physis) and then extends upwards through the metaphysis. The X-ray shows the characteristic "Thurston Holland fragment," which is the triangular piece of metaphysis that remains attached to the epiphysis. Type 1 (Option A) involves the growth plate only. Type 3 (Option C) passes through the growth plate and extends through the epiphysis into the joint space. Type 5 (Option D) is a crush injury of the growth plate, which is often difficult to see on initial X-rays. Type 2 fractures generally have a good prognosis because the germinal layer of the growth plate remains intact. Management usually involves closed reduction and immobilization, as the fracture does not enter the joint surface
questions.learning: The Salter-Harris classification system is used to describe fractures involving the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) in children. A Type 2 fracture, the most common type, occurs when the fracture line passes through the growth plate (physis) and then…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anti-tubercular drugs is associated with visual disturbances?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol is a key component of the standard four-drug regimen for tuberculosis. Its most significant and characteristic side effect is optic neuritis, which leads to visual disturbances. This typically manifests as a decrease in visual acuity and an inability to distinguish between red and green (red-green color blindness). This toxicity is dose-dependent and usually reversible if the drug is stopped early. Rifampicin (Option A) famously causes an orange-red discoloration of body fluids. Streptomycin (Option B) is an aminoglycoside associated with ototoxicity (hearing loss) and nephrotoxicity. Pyrazinamide (Option C) can cause hyperuricemia and gout. Because of the risk of optic nerve damage, patients starting ethambutol should have a baseline visual acuity and color vision test and should be counseled to immediately report any changes in their vision. It is generally avoided in children who are too young to accurately report such visual changes
questions.learning: Ethambutol is a key component of the standard four-drug regimen for tuberculosis. Its most significant and characteristic side effect is optic neuritis, which leads to visual disturbances.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is not a risk factor for the acquisition of chronic hepatitis C?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sharing food

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is primarily transmitted through blood-to-blood exposure. Sharing food does not transmit HCV.

Why the other options are risk factors?

• A. Intravenous drug abuse: Correct risk factor

• Sharing contaminated needles or injection equipment is a major route of HCV transmission.

• B. Unscreened infected blood transfusion: Correct risk factor

• Transfusion of HCV-contaminated blood can transmit infection, particularly in settings where blood screening is inadequate.

• C. Vertical transmission: Correct risk factor

• HCV can be transmitted from an infected mother to her infant, although the risk is relatively low.

• D. Sharing food: Not a risk factor

• HCV is not spread through food, water, coughing, sneezing, or casual contact.
questions.learning: Sharing food Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is primarily transmitted through blood-to-blood exposure. Sharing food does not transmit HCV.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman who recently underwent emergency laparotomy for perforation peritonitis now develops features suggestive of wound dehiscence. Which clinical sign is the most reliable indicator of impending or established wound failure?
questions.explanation: The most classic and reliable early clinical sign of impending or actual deep wound dehiscence (failure of the fascial layer) after a laparotomy is the sudden appearance of copious, serosanguinous (pinkish, watery) discharge from the surgical incision. This is often described as "salmon-colored" fluid and represents peritoneal fluid leaking through the failing fascial closure. This sign often precedes the visible protrusion of viscera (evisceration). Rebound tenderness (Option B) indicates peritoneal irritation, which is expected post-laparotomy for peritonitis but does not specifically point to wound failure. While acute hemorrhage (Option C) can occur, it is usually a sign of a vascular complication rather than general wound failure. Hypotension (Option D) is a systemic sign of shock or sepsis but lacks the specificity of the local wound findings. Recognizing the specific "sero-sanguinous" leak allows for urgent intervention, such as binding the wound and planning a surgical re-closure of the fascia
questions.learning: The most classic and reliable early clinical sign of impending or actual deep wound dehiscence (failure of the fascial layer) after a laparotomy is the sudden appearance of copious, serosanguinous (pinkish, watery) discharge from the surgical incision.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: World Health Organisation (WHO) considers blindness as a major public health problem. As per WHO, what is the definition of blindness?
options: Visual acuity <6/60 after correction in better eye
Visual acuity <3/60 after correction in better eye
Visual acuity <6/60 without correction in better eye
Visual acuity <3/60 without correction in better eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Visual acuity <3/60 after correction in better eye

As per WHO definition, blindness is defined as best corrected visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye, or a corresponding visual field loss.

WHO Classification

• Normal vision: ≥ 6/18
• Visual impairment: < 6/18 to ≥ 3/60
• Severe visual impairment: < 6/60 to ≥ 3/60
• Blindness: < 3/60

(All based on best-corrected visual acuity in the better eye)

India runs the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI) to reduce avoidable blindness.
questions.learning: Visual acuity <3/60 after correction in better eye As per WHO definition, blindness is defined as best corrected visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye, or a corresponding visual field loss.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male patient presents with a bulky scrotal swelling. On evaluation, malignancy is suspected. Orchidectomy is done and the gross section is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

The given cut section of testicular mass is homogenous, grey-white, and does not show haemorrhage or necrosis suggesting a diagnosis of seminoma.

Seminoma is the most common testicular tumour. In about 15% of cases, serum HCG levels are raised as these seminomas contain syncytiotrophoblasts. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels are also measured to assess tumour burden. They are bulky, homogenous, pale, and well-circumscribed masses that do not show any haemorrhage or necrosis, as shown in the image below.

Microscopically, sheets of uniform tumour cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by fibrous septa are seen. Each cell is large, and round, and has a distinct cell membrane, abundant clear cytoplasm, and a large central nucleus with a few nucleoli.

Therapy depends on the stage of the tumour. Seminoma has the best prognosis. Most cases of seminoma stages I and II can be cured by orchidectomy with or without chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option B, C: Yolk sac tumour and endodermal sinus tumour  will not present with a homogenous appearance on gross examination.

Option D: Teratoma has origins from ectodermal, mesodermal and endodermal germ cell layers. The gross cut section will have tissues from this origin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A lady presents with vascular injury to the inferior frontal gyrus. Which functional area is likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Motor speech area

Broca's motor speech area is likely to be affected in the vascular injury of the inferior frontal gyrus

A lesion in this region leads to motor/Broca's aphasia. Speech is non-fluent and interrupted by many word-finding pauses. The speech is impoverished in function words that contribute to the syntax but is enriched in meaningful nouns and verbs. However, comprehension of speech is intact and the patient knows what he wants to say.

For example, a patient with Broca's aphasia may say "walk dog" instead of "I want to take the dog for a walk".
questions.learning: Motor speech area Broca's motor speech area is likely to be affected in the vascular injury of the inferior frontal gyrus A lesion in this region leads to motor/Broca's aphasia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child weighing 40 kg presents with intellectual disability. On examination, the upper segment–to–lower segment (US:LS) ratio is 1.1 : 1. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In a healthy 10-year-old, the normal US:LS ratio is approximately 0.9:1, reflecting the fact that the lower segment (legs) has grown longer than the upper segment. A ratio of 1.1:1 indicates a disproportionate shortening of the lower segment relative to the upper body. This is commonly seen in childhood rickets, where defective bone mineralization leads to limb deformities and stunted long-bone growth. Cretinism (Option A) and Hypothyroidism (Option D) typically cause proportionate short stature rather than a specific US:LS disparity. Achondroplasia (Option C) results in a much more extreme ratio (often ~1.5:1) present from birth. Thus, the specific finding of moderate limb shortening in a healthy 10-year-old identifies rickets as the most likely underlying cause
questions.learning: In a healthy 10-year-old, the normal US:LS ratio is approximately 0.9:1, reflecting the fact that the lower segment (legs) has grown longer than the upper segment.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not involved in renal auto-regulation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal sympathetic system fibres

Renal sympathetic system fibres is not involved in the autoregulation of renal blood flow, because a denervated kidney also maintains the auto regulation of renal blood flow as that of a normal kidney.

Tubulo glomerular feedback, myogenic reflex, and renin-angiotensin system are all involved in the autoregulation of renal blood flow.

Tubulo glomerular feedback:

• When the renal artery pressure increases, the renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) increases
• This increased GFR results in increased delivery of solute and water to the early distal tubule, particularly the macula densa
• The macula dense, then secretes a vasoactive substance that constricts afferent arteriole via a paracrine mechanism
• This vasoconstriction then reduces renal blood flow and GFR back to normal

Myogenic reflex:

• The increase in renal arterial pressure stretches the walls of the afferent arterioles, which then contracts
• This contraction increases the afferent arteriolar resistance
• This increase in resistance then compensates for the increase in blood pressure, thereby keeping the renal blood flow constant.

Renin-angiotensin system:

• Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor of both afferent and efferent arterioles
• However efferent arterioles are more sensitive to angiotensin II than afferent arteriole
• Thus low levels of angiotensin II produce an increase in GFR by constricting efferent arterioles
• High levels of angiotensin II decreases GFR by constricting afferent and efferent arterioles, thereby decreasing the renal blood flow
questions.learning: Renal sympathetic system fibres Renal sympathetic system fibres is not involved in the autoregulation of renal blood flow, because a denervated kidney also maintains the auto regulation of renal blood flow as that of a normal kidney.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presented with weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, purple striae, and easy bruising. What is the likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypercortisolism

Correct answer is A because weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, purple striae, and easy bruising are classic features of Cushing syndrome due to excess cortisol.

Hypercortisolism causes protein catabolism, skin thinning, and central fat redistribution.

| Mechanism | Clinical Effect

| --------- | ---------------

| ↑ Protein breakdown | Muscle weakness

| ↓ Collagen synthesis | Thin skin → easy bruising

| Fat redistribution | Central obesity

| Skin thinning | Purple striae

Causes of Hypercortisolism

| Type | Cause

| ---- | -----

| Exogenous | Steroid therapy (most common)

| ACTH-dependent | Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease)

| | Ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer)

| ACTH-independent | Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma

Thyroid, parathyroid, or aldosterone excess do not produce this characteristic constellation of findings.
questions.learning: Hypercortisolism Correct answer is — A because weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, purple striae, and easy bruising are classic features of Cushing syndrome due to excess cortisol.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions would have the highest levels of ACTH and cortisol?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cushing's disease

Among the given conditions, the levels of ACTH and cortisol will be highest in Cushing's disease.

Cushing’s disease is caused by an ACTH secreting pituitary adenoma. The increased ACTH causes increased cortisol production.

Note: In normal physiologic state, ACTH levels are higher in the early morning but not as high as in Cushing's disease.
questions.learning: Cushing's disease Among the given conditions, the levels of ACTH and cortisol will be highest in Cushing's disease. Cushing’s disease is caused by an ACTH secreting pituitary adenoma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following techniques is based on behavioral sciences?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Management by objective

Management by objective is based on behavioral sciences.

Management methods used in health programmes are either quantitative or based on behavioral sciences.

Methods based on behavioral sciences include:

• Organizational design
• Personnel management
• Communication
• Information systems
• Management by objectives (MBO)

Quantitative methods include:

• Cost-benefit analysis
• Cost-effective analysis
• Cost–accounting
• Input-output analysis
• Model
• Systems analysis
• Network analysis - includes programme evaluation and review technique (PERT) and critical path method (CPM)
• Planning–programming–budgeting system (PPBS)
• Work sampling
• Decision making

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The flipped LDH ratio implies _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LDH 1 > LDH 2

The flipped lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio is LDH 1 > LDH 2.

Under normal conditions, LDH 2 is predominantly present in the blood and LDH 1 is predominantly present in the heart. When cardiac tissue is damaged LDH 1 is released into the bloodstream.

LDH 1 > LDH 2 (flipped pattern) in the blood is suggestive of myocardial infarction.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the doctor testing for in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior cruciate ligament

The test done in the image is the anterior drawer test. This is done to detect injuries to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Procedure:

* The patient is made to lie supine on the examining table. The hip is flexed to 45° and the knee is flexed to 90° with the foot flat on the table.

* The upper end of the tibia is held in both hands and tibia is gently pushed anteriorly. Increased displacement compared to the normal knee indicates injury to ACL.

Lachman test is also done to detect injuries to the anterior cruciate ligament. Here the leg is in slight external rotation and the knee is in the position between flexion and extension. One hand is placed to stabilise femur and another hand applies the anterior force to the proximal tibia.

questions.text: Ligation of common hepatic artery will impair blood supply in:

Right gastric and left gastric artery

Correct answer: A. Right gastric and right gastroepiploic artery

Ligation of the common hepatic artery will cause impairment in the blood supply through its branches i.e right gastric artery and right gastroepiploic artery.

Blood supply of the stomach:

The arterial supply of the stomach is contributed exclusively by the branches of the celiac trunk. They are:

• Splenic artery- This further divides into:

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A farmer presented with loose stools and rashes over the sun-exposed areas. Careful diet history reveals a diet rich in maize. Which of the following deficiencies would you suspect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

History of a maize-rich diet along with loose stools and rashes over the sun-exposed areas is suggestive of niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which is low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds- nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes NAD ( nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and NADP (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency

Other options:

Option B: Dietary pyridoxine deficiency (vitamin B6) is rare but has been observed in alcoholics, newborn infants formulas low in vitamin B6, and women taking oral contraceptives. Isoniazid, an anti-TB drug, leads to pyridoxine deficiency resulting in peripheral neuropathy. Hence pyridoxine supplementation is included in ATT regimens.

Option C: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) can manifest as wet beriberi (CVS features like heart failure and edema) or Shoshin beriberi, an acute and fulminant form of wet beriberi, dry beriberi (peripheral neuritis), or as Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis (in alcoholics). Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis.

Option D: Dietary biotin deficiency is unknown but rarely, dermatitis, glossitis, loss of appetite, and nausea may occur after consumption of large amounts of uncooked egg white, which contains the protein avidin. It binds biotin and makes it unavailable for absorption.

Note: A similar image-based question on vitamin B3 deficiency was previously asked in NEET PG 2020. Vitamin deficiencies are a high-yield topic and are repeatedly tested every year.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An elderly man presents with an ulcerative lesion near the inner canthus of the eye, characterized by pearly margins. Histopathological examination reveals a palisading arrangement of cells. What is the most likely diagnosis of this lesion?
questions.explanation: The combination of an ulcerative lesion with "pearly margins" and microscopic "peripheral palisading" of cells is pathognomonic for basal cell carcinoma (BCC). BCC, also known as a "rodent ulcer," is a slow-growing, locally invasive tumor that rarely metastasizes. It commonly appears on sun-exposed areas like the face, nose, and around the eyes. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A) typically presents with "keratin pearls" and is more aggressive. Keratoacanthoma (Option C) is a dome-shaped lesion with a central keratin plug that often resolves spontaneously. Melanocytic melanoma (Option D) is characterized by atypical melanocytes and is usually pigmented. Histologically, BCC tumor cells line up in a row at the periphery, mimicking the basal layer of the epidermis. Treatment options include surgical excision (Mohs surgery) or topical agents like Imiquimod
questions.learning: The combination of an ulcerative lesion with "pearly margins" and microscopic "peripheral palisading" of cells is pathognomonic for basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The transplacental transmission of the organism given in the image which causes microcephaly is-
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zika virus

The image shows transplacental transmission of a virus, leading to microcephaly, with the Aedes mosquito as its vector. Among the given options, Zika virus has the above features.

Zika virus is a mosquito-borne Flavivirus mainly transmitted through Aedes aegypti. Zika virus infection presents with mild symptoms of fever, rash, conjunctivitis, malaise, headache and muscle and joint pain. These symptoms usually last for 2-7 days. Maternal infection during pregnancy leads to congenital Zika syndrome or microcephaly.

The complications of Zika virus infection include Guillain-Barré syndrome, neuropathy, and myelitis.

Note: NCDC Delhi and the National Institute of Virology Pune are the only institutes that have the capacity to provide the diagnosis in an acute febrile stage. RT-PCR is the standard test available for the diagnosis of Zika virus infection.

questions.text: Which of the following is a synthetic PGF2 alpha derivative used as an abortifacient?
questions.explanation:

Carboprost is a 15-methyl synthetic derivative of PGF2 alpha. It is used as an abortifacient and in refractory PPH.

Option B:  Dinoprostone is natural PGE2 preparation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a derivative of neural crest cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinal pigment epithelium

Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells.

Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm. The RPE develops from the outer layer of the optic cup, a structure that arises from the neural tube (neuroectodermal origin), not from neural crest cells.

Neural crest cells are a group of cells that migrate during embryonic development and give rise to various structures, including parts of the nervous system, face, and heart.

Neural crest cells (NCC) are present adjacent to the neural tube and are sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer. It contributes to the formation of many organs and tissues:

In the trunk region, they form:

• Melanocytes (Option D)
• Sensory ganglia
• Sympathetic and enteric neurons
• Schwann cells
• Adrenal medulla cells

In the cranial region, they contribute to the:

• Craniofacial skeleton
• Neurons for cranial ganglia-Ciliary ganglion  (Option C)
• Ciliary muscles  (Option A)
• Satellite glial cells
• Melanocytes

Some of the other neural crest derivatives are:

• C cells of the thyroid gland
• Conotruncal septum in the heart
• Odontoblasts
• Smooth muscle cells to blood vessels to the face and forebrain.
questions.learning: Retinal pigment epithelium Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A disease has an incubation period of 3-14 days. It has a median incubation of 10 days. A person had to travel abroad and he was not vaccinated. As the disease is of international significance, how long will he have to be quarantined?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 14 days

A person who is not vaccinated and has been exposed to a disease of international significance (like COVID) with an incubation period of 3-14 days should be quarantined for 14 days(longest incubation period).

Quarantine is defined as the limitation of freedom of movement of well-persons or animals, exposed to a communicable disease for a period of time not longer than the longest usual incubation period, to prevent contact with those not exposed. This is done to prevent the potential spread of the disease during its incubation period, which is the time between exposure and the onset of symptoms.

The quarantined person:

• Should stay in a well-ventilated single room and stay away from high-risk individuals
• Should not attend any religious or social gatherings
• Must wash hands often
• Their surroundings must be disinfected with 1% sodium hypochlorite solution

In case the person being quarantined becomes symptomatic, all his contacts should be home quarantined for 14 days and followed up for another 14 days or till the report turns out negative on lab testing.

Note: The median incubation period refers to the time between exposure to a pathogen and the onset of symptoms in 50% of cases. And isolation is the separation and restriction of movements or activities of persons who are sick, to prevent the transmission of disease.
questions.learning: 14 days A person who is not vaccinated and has been exposed to a disease of international significance (like COVID) with an incubation period of 3-14 days should be quarantined for 14 days(longest incubation period).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient has a history of three miscarriages. Identify the investigation that was done from the image shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hysterosalpingography

The investigation shown in the given image is hysterosalpingography. The given hysterosalpingogram shows a unicornuate uterus.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is an imaging modality in which radiopaque contrast is injected through the cervical canal to assess the endometrial cavity, the fallopian tubes, and the endocervical canal.

HSG should be done between days 5 and 10 of the menstrual cycle, in the preovulatory phase, as an outpatient procedure. Leech Wilkinson cannula, Rubin's cannula, or Foley's catheter no.14 is introduced into the endometrial cavity through the cervical os, and the contrast is injected. The uterine cavity and fallopian tubes are then visualized and X-rays are obtained.

HSG can be used for the following:

• To assess tubal patency in infertility
• To detect uterine anomalies, synechiae, and polyps
• To detect incompetence of the cervical os

Contraindications to HSG:

• Acute pelvic infection
• Active uterine bleeding
• Pregnancy/ suspected pregnancy
• Contrast allergy
• Premenstrual phase

HSG is a safe procedure, however, complications such as ascending spread of infection, chemical peritonitis, allergic reaction to the dye, or pelvic endometriosis may occur.

Other options:

Option A: Hysteroscopy is an operative procedure in which the uterine cavity can be visualized by passing a fiberoptic telescope via the cervix. It can be diagnostic or therapeutic. A hysteroscopic image of a uterus with carcinoma is shown below.

Option B: Saline infusion sonography is a procedure where normal saline is injected into the uterine cavity and the uterus is imaged with transvaginal sonography. It is shown in the image below.

Option D: Transvaginal ultrasonography is a noninvasive imaging technique using the transvaginal approach. It provides a more detailed evaluation of the pelvic organs as compared to the transabdominal approach.
questions.learning: Hysterosalpingography — The investigation shown in the given image is hysterosalpingography. The given hysterosalpingogram shows a unicornuate uterus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not characteristic of the clinical condition given below?
options: Abnormal activity of p53 is seen in the pterygium tissue.
Decreased activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases is seen.
Destruction of Bowman's layer occurs when the pterygium invades the cornea.
Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.

Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the conjunctival connective tissue occurs in pinguecula (and not pterygium).

In pterygium, there is elastotic degeneration of collagen with fibrovascular proliferation.

It is important to distinguish a pterygium from a pinguecula. A pterygium, while histologically similar to a pinguecula, is distinguished by fibrovascular tissue that grows onto the cornea. Pingueculae do not have vascularized tissue and do not cross the limbus.

Pterygium is a subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue and is never inflammatory. It occurs due to exposure to UV-B radiation and the most common site is the nasal.

It is made up of three parts-a "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body.

Clinical features:

* Astigmatism with the rule - most common finding

* Stocker's line - deposition of iron on the advancing edge

* Fuchs islets - small, discrete, whitish flecks consisting of clusters of pterygial epithelial cells, often present at the advancing edge.

The differential diagnosis is pseudo pterygium.

Pterygium
Pseudo-pterygium

Degenerative process
Inflammatory process

Occurs in elderly
Can occur at any age

Situated at the palpebral aperture
Can occur at any site

Either progressive, regressive, or stationary
Always stationary

A probe cannot be passed underneath
A probe can be passed under the neck

The treatment for pterygium is usually excision. To prevent a recurrence, mitomycin C or 5 fluorouracil is used. Other methods:

* Auto-grafting- Conjunctival limbal autograft (CLAG) from the superior limbal conjunctiva is the best method.

* Bare sclera technique- high recurrence rate of 30 to 80%.

* PERFECT surgery- zero rates of recurrence. (PERFECT stands for Pterygium Extended Removal Followed by Extended Conjunctival Transplant)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is deficient in the mucopolysaccharidosis associated with Natowicz disease?
questions.explanation: Natowicz Disease, also classified as Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IX (MPS IX), is an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hyaluronidase. This enzyme is responsible for the degradation of hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan); its deficiency leads to the abnormal accumulation of hyaluronic acid in various tissues. Clinical features are relatively mild compared to other MPS types and include soft tissue masses and joint stiffness. In contrast, dermatan and heparan sulfate (Options A and B) accumulate in MPS I (Hurler) and MPS II (Hunter) syndromes due to different enzyme defects. Keratan sulfate (Option C) accumulates in MPS IV (Morquio syndrome). Because Natowicz disease is specifically the "hyaluronan-accumulation" disorder, the absence of hyaluronidase makes hyaluronic acid the deficiently processed glycosaminoglycan (GAG)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy has swelling of knee joints and non-blanching rashes as seen in the picture. Urine exam reveals haematuria +++ and proteinuria +. Platelet levels are normal. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP)

The given clinical scenario showing swelling of knee joints (arthritis), non-blanching rash in the lower limbs (palpable purpura), along with hematuria and proteinuria (renal involvement) in a child is suggestive of Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP).

HSP (IgA vasculitis) is a small vessel vasculitis most commonly seen in the age group of 3-8 years. It generally follows an upper respiratory tract infection and there is a history of atopy in one-third of the cases.

The pathology of HSP involves leukocytoclastic vasculitis and the deposition of IgA in the affected blood vessels. IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distribution similar to that of IgA nephropathy.

Clinical manifestations include palpable purpura, the hallmark feature of HSP, which characteristically involves the extensor surfaces of arms and legs. Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthritis and arthralgia are common. Gastrointestinal symptoms can include abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding. Renal involvement may lead to gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic syndrome, or nephrotic syndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in adults. A rapidly progressive form of glomerulonephritis is seen in some cases. Nephritis usually follows the appearance of the rash.

Diagnosis of HSP is primarily based on clinical findings, including the palpable purpura, along with the presence of other symptoms. Laboratory tests are not specific to HSP but may show nonspecific markers of inflammation and sometimes elevated levels of IgA. Imaging studies and biopsies of affected tissues can provide additional diagnostic information

Treatment of HSP is generally supportive, focusing on hydration, pain relief, and nutrition. Corticosteroids may be used in severe cases or for significant gastrointestinal involvement. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) and plasma exchange are occasionally employed for severe disease. Nephritis due to IgA vasculitis should be treated with immunosuppressants like prednisolone and azathioprine. Complications of HSP can include serious gastrointestinal problems, kidney disease, and recurrences, but overall, the prognosis for childhood HSP is favorable. Regular monitoring of blood pressure and urine is recommended to detect and manage potential complications.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During a modified radical neck dissection, which of the following anatomical structures is not preserved?
questions.explanation: Neck dissections are performed to remove lymph nodes involved in head and neck cancers. A modified radical neck dissection (MRND) is defined by the removal of all lymph node levels (I-V) while preserving one or more of the non-lymphatic structures typically removed in a "radical" dissection. These structures include the Sternocleidomastoid muscle (Option A), the Internal jugular vein (Option B), and the Spinal accessory nerve (Option C). However, the submandibular gland (found in Level Ib) is routinely excised during MRND because it is intimately associated with the Level I lymph nodes, and its preservation would compromise the oncological thoroughness of the procedure. Preserving the spinal accessory nerve is particularly crucial to avoid "shoulder syndrome," characterized by pain and limited abduction. MRND aims to achieve a balance between effective cancer control and minimizing functional morbidity. Distinguishing between radical, modified radical, and selective neck dissections is a core requirement for surgical oncology and ENT clinical practice

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The true statement about screening tests for genetic diseases is:
options: Screening test has better accuracy than diagnostic test
It defines risk of transmission of disease to the child
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It defines risk of transmission of disease to the child

The true statement about screening tests for genetic diseases is it defines the risk of transmission of disease to the child.

A screening test is an initial examination done in apparently healthy individuals while diagnostic tests are done on individuals with positive test results for further workup and treatment.

The aim of performing a screening test is to favorably change the natural history of the disease by an early diagnosis and treatment in individuals who are positive for the particular screening test. They are less invasive and less accurate than diagnostic tests.

Genetic screening is a type of public health program done in high-risk asymptomatic individuals in which tests are used to detect an inherited predisposition to disease, risk of transmitting the disease, prevention of the disease, early treatment, or family planning. For example, prenatal screening during pregnancy.

Genetic mapping is a tool used to identify new genes and their functions. It also may give information on which chromosome contains the defective gene and where the gene is present on that chromosome. Gene maps have been used to pinpoint the gene responsible for rare single-gene inherited disorders. Screening does not require genetic mapping.
questions.learning: It defines risk of transmission of disease to the child The true statement about screening tests for genetic diseases is it defines the risk of transmission of disease to the child.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The CSF findings in bacterial meningitis would include which of the following?
options: Elevated WBC count with normal glucose
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis is characterized by distinct cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) abnormalities: elevated protein levels (>100 mg/dL) due to blood-brain barrier disruption and decreased glucose (<40% of blood glucose) because of utilization by bacteria and neutrophils. It also features a high white blood cell count, predominantly polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). Options B and D are incorrect because the glucose level is almost always low in bacterial infections. Option C is the opposite of the typical finding. In contrast, viral meningitis (Option D-like) usually has normal glucose and a lymphocyte predominance. Fungal or tubercular meningitis also has low glucose but typically features lymphocyte predominance rather than the high PMNs seen in bacterial causes. Therefore, the combination of high protein and low glucose is the classic biochemical hallmark of bacterial meningitis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old patient was brought to the casualty ward with high fever and pain abdomen. He had a history of bloody diarrhea for several months. His past history was negative for long-term medications and previous surgeries. The abdominal X-ray image obtained is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Toxic megacolon

The clinical scenario and the radiograph are suggestive of toxic megacolon.

Toxic megacolon may present with fever, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension. Abdominal radiography shows transverse or right colonic dilation of >6 cm and loss of haustrations. It is usually associated with ulcerative colitis as indicated by history of chronic bloody diarrhoea.

It can be triggered by electrolyte imbalance and narcotics which interfere with gut motility. Features of secondary bacterial infecton and sepsis may be present. It can be complicated by intestinal perforation.

It usually resolves with supportive treatment (correcting electrolyte imbalance, fluids, and bowel rest) and medical therapy which includes glucocorticoids, anti-inflammatory drugs, and antibiotics. However, an urgent colectomy is indicated in patients who do not show signs of improvement.

Indications for urgent surgery include:

• Frank intraperitoneal peritonitis, secondary to perforation
• Life-threatening hemorrhage or increasing transfusion requirements
• Worsening systemic toxicity
• Worsening colonic dilatation

Other options:

Option B: Volvulus occurs when the air-filled segment of the colon twists around the mesentery. The sigmoid colon is the most commonly involved part of the large intestine (90%). The patient can present with abdominal distension, nausea and vomiting. X-ray abdomen shows a bent inner tube or coffee bean appearance.

Option C: Ogilvie syndrome, also known as colonic pseudo-obstruction is a functional disorder with colonic dilatation without mechanical obstruction. It occurs commonly in hospitalized patients and is associated with narcotics, bed rest and comorbid disease. X-ray shows dilatation of the colon (predominantly transverse colon) with absent mechanical obstruction.

Option D: Pneumatosis intestinalis is the presence of gas within the bowel wall seen in any part of the GI tract but most commonly in the jejunum. It is a pathognomic feature of necrotizing enterocolitis. X-ray of the abdomen will show intramural gas in the bowel.
questions.learning: Toxic megacolon — The clinical scenario and the radiograph are suggestive of toxic megacolon. Toxic megacolon may present with fever, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man presented with a history of stab injury over the arm. On examination, there was a hematoma present, and radial and ulnar pulses were not felt. A 3.5cm longitudinal tear is noted in the brachial artery. Which among the following is the best treatment option?
options: Primary repair with end to end anastomosis
Repair with great saphenous vein graft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Repair with great saphenous vein graft

In this patient, who has sustained a long tear to the brachial artery due to a stab injury, the best treatment option is to repair it with a great saphenous vein interposition graft harvested from the patient's uninjured leg.

The most desirable graft used is the great saphenous vein . A native vein graft is preferable to a prosthetic graft because:

• Its elastic properties are comparable to that of an artery and enable pulsatile flow
• The diameter is similar to that of an extremity artery
• It is not thrombogenic and has long term patency

Other grafts that can be used are cephalic vein, lesser saphenous vein, and prosthetic conduits. Cephalic vein is not the first choice because it is less muscular than greater saphenous vein, and might also compromise the upper limb venous access in the already injured patient. Both the cephalic and the lesser saphenous veins present problems while harvesting in a trauma patient.

Other options:

Option A: Primary arterial repair with end-to-end anastomosis can be done only if the repair is tension-free. If the length of the injured area is long, vessel injuries cannot be repaired by primary end-to-end anastomoses and instead require an interposition graft.

Option C: Prosthetic grafts are only preferred when there has been a trauma to the native saphenous vein or when there is a size mis-match. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) graft is commonly used.

Option D: Saphenous vein patch is used in the closure of the arteriotomy site during carotid endarterectomies.
