questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the first step in the management of an 18-month-old child with both eyes deviated medially:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Refractive error testing

In children, who present with a convergent squint, the first step is to check the visual acuity and estimate the error of refraction.

Convergent squint also known as Esotrpia is commonly seen in children with hyperopia (also known as hypermetropia) of which the accomdative type of esotropia is more common in the age group below 3 years.

The first line of management in the treatment of esotropia includes refractive error correction with glasses.

If a child with accomdative issues, is unable to use spectacles (such as a child ≤ 2 years) or is non compliant with wearing glasses we can eliminate accommodation by temporarily treating him with miotic drugs such as echothiophate.

Further treatment may include orthoptic training with specific exercises or surgical correction when the angle of squint is 10° or more with correcting lenses and when orthoptic training doesnt help in reasonable correction of the squint.

Mnemonic:

The algorithm for the management of accommodative esotropia is as follows:

• R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics
• O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: for amblyopia
• O: Operative correction: for non-accommodative component
• P: Prism correction: for remaining error

Classification of Accomdative esotropia:

Type
Criteria

Refractive

• Associated with high hypermetropia (+4 to +7 D)
• Typically esotropia is for both near and distance.
• Fully correctable by spectacles

Non-refractive

• Occurs independent of refractive errors
• Abnormal accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio
• Typically esotropia is greater for near than for distance
• Fully corrected by bifocal glasses

The below image shows accomdative esotropia before and after correction.

Option A: Forced Duction Test (FDT) is performed to differentiate between the paralytic and restrictive type of inconcomitant squint.

FDT is positive in restrictive squint where a resistance is encountered during passive rotation.

Correct answer: C. Terminal bronchus

This histological image shows a section of lung tissue displaying various components of the respiratory pathway. The marked structure represents a terminal bronchiole (terminal bronchus), which is characterized by its relatively thick muscular wall compared to the surrounding structures.

The respiratory pathway follows a hierarchical organization: primary bronchus → secondary bronchus → tertiary bronchus (supplying bronchopulmonary segments) → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A lady who is 38 weeks pregnant comes to the OPD for a routine checkup. She has a history of normal twin delivery at term 4 years ago. What is her gravida and para score? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. G2P1

• The obstetric score is used to summarize the past obstetric history as follows:

o   G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one

o   P - Parity, denoting the total number of pregnancies crossing the period of viability

o   This includes both live births and stillbirths

o   The current pregnancy is not included

o   A - Abortus or the number of pregnancies that were lost for any reason, including induced abortions or miscarriages

o   L - Living children.
• The GTPAL system includes the following:

o   Gravida

o   Term (>37 weeks)

o   Preterm (20w - 36w 6d)

o   Abortions (<20 weeks)

o   Number of living children

Obstetric Score

• Gravidity: G2 (Second pregnancy)
• Parity: P1 (One previous pregnancy reaching viability, twins count as one para)

So, the correct obstetric score for this lady is G2P1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient was provisionally diagnosed with intestinal obstruction. An emergency laparotomy was done, and the following specimen was removed. Identify the following specimen.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trichobezoar

The given specimen is that of a trichobezoar. This is a type of bezoar that forms in the stomach due to the accumulation of hair.

Trichophagia is the compulsive eating of hair associated with trichotillomania. Trichotillomania is a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder that is associated with hair pulling. In trichophagia, people also ingest the hair that they pull.

Complications of trichotillomania include

* Trichobezoars

* Malnutrition

* Intestinal obstruction

The modalities currently used in the management of trichotillomania are cognitive behavioral therapy and habit reversal training.

Other options:

* A phytobezoar forms when undigested plant material, such as fibers from fruits and vegetables, clump together in the stomach and create a mass that can lead to gastrointestinal symptoms.

* Lactatobezoar is a rare type of bezoar that forms in newborns' stomachs due to the accumulation of undigested milk or formula.

* Gangrene of the stomach can occur as a complication of conditions like gastric volvulus (twisting of the stomach), which leads to compromised blood flow to the stomach tissues.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant came with vomiting, jaundice, and hypoglycemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Galactosemia

Galactosemia is an inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, leading to accumulation of toxic metabolites after milk ingestion.

• Presents in neonates/infants after starting milk feeds
• Features include vomiting, jaundice, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive
• Can also cause cataracts and risk of E. coli sepsis
• Early diagnosis is crucial
• Management requires immediate elimination of galactose/lactose from diet

Contrast:

• Phenylketonuria: intellectual disability, musty odor, no jaundice/hypoglycemia
• Wilson disease: presents later with liver and neurological features
• Menkes disease: copper metabolism disorder with kinky hair and neurodegeneration

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure primarily facilitates the pronation and supination movements of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Supination and pronation are the unique rotational movements of the forearm where the radius rotates around the ulna. These movements occur specifically at the superior and inferior radioulnar joints, which are classified as pivot (trochoid) joints. In a pivot joint, a rounded bone rotates within a ring formed by another bone and a ligament. A saddle joint (Option B), such as the first carpometacarpal joint, allows for flexion, extension, and opposition but not rotation. An ellipsoid joint (Option C), like the wrist joint, allows for biaxial movement but lacks independent rotation. A ball and socket joint (Option D), such as the shoulder or hip, is multiaxial but is not the specific joint type responsible for the distinct forearm rotation between the radius and ulna. Thus, the anatomical design of the pivot joint at the radioulnar articulation is the primary structure enabling pronation and supination
questions.learning: Supination and pronation are the unique rotational movements of the forearm where the radius rotates around the ulna. These movements occur specifically at the superior and inferior radioulnar joints, which are classified as pivot (trochoid) joints.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of fever for the past 4 days and new onset of breathlessness was admitted to ICU as he was deteriorating. He was unresponsive to the incremental flow rate of oxygen and his oxygen saturation was progressively decreasing. A Chest X-ray was ordered and the findings are shown in the image below and his PaO2/FiO2 was 204 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ARDS

The history of fever for less than 1 week, refractory hypoxia, chest x-ray showing bilateral infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 <300 mmHg is diagnostic of ARDS.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome is characterized by rapid onset dyspnea, hypoxemia, and diffuse lung infiltrates resulting in respiratory failure. ARDS is caused by diffuse lung injury due to varied causes like inhalation injury, pneumonia, gastric aspiration, pulmonary contusion, burns, pancreatitis, and sepsis.

In patients with ARDS, there is an inflammatory response in the lungs leading to high levels of neutrophils and their secretory products in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. This is characteristic of non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

An early chest x-ray typically reveals diffuse opacities due to consolidation. Later these opacities progress to more extensive and asymmetrical consolidation. The CT scan of the lungs shows heterogeneous involvement and predominantly affects gravity-dependent areas.

The affected airspaces are filled with fluid and cannot contribute to ventilation, leading to hypoxemia (due to increased pulmonary shunt) and hypercapnia (due to inadequate ventilation in some areas of the lung); resulting in, ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

The hypoxemia in ARDS is refractory to the increasing concentration of inhaled oxygen that occurs due to increased intrapulmonary shunting of blood.

The most common cause of death is sepsis in ARDS. Due to improvement in ventilator support systems, respiratory failure causes mortality in less than 20% of cases.

Diagnostic criteria in ARDS—Berlin definition: The Berlin definition requires each of the following criteria be present to diagnose ARDS:

* Onset- Acute: Respiratory symptoms must have begun within one week of a known clinical insult

* Bilateral alveolar or interstitial infiltrates: must be present on a chest X-ray image or CT scan

* Respiratory failure must not be fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Objective assessment e.g Echo should be done in cases of no known cause.

* Impairment of oxygenation must be present: The severity of hypoxemia defines the severity of ARDS

Severity

PaO2/FiO2

On ventilator settings that

include PEEP ≥5 cm H2O.

Mild

> 200 mmHg but ≤ 300 mmHg

Moderate

> 100 mmHg but ≤ 200 mmHg

Severe
≤ 100 mmHg

Clinical disorders commonly associated with ARDS:

* Direct lung injury:

* Pneumonia

* Aspiration of gastric contents

* Pulmonary contusion

* Near-drowning

* Toxic inhalation injury

* Indirect lung injury:

* Sepsis

* Severe trauma- multiple fractures, flail chest, head trauma, burns

* Multiple transfusions

* Drug overdose

* Pancreatitis

* Post-cardiopulmonary bypass

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following features differentiates the exocrine pancreas from the parotid gland?
options: Basal lamina lining the serous acini
Presence of serous acini with acidophilic tip
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absence of striated duct

Absence of striated duct in exocrine pancreas differentiates it from the parotid gland.

The exocrine pancreas is comprised entirely of serous acini. Hence, its general structure is similar to that of the parotid gland, but the two are easily distinguished by:

• The parotid gland has striated and intercalated intralobular ducts, whereas the pancreas has only the intercalated type.
• The excretory ducts of the parotid gland are striated columnar, whereas the excretory duct of the pancreas is a simple columnar.
questions.learning: Absence of striated duct Absence of striated duct in exocrine pancreas differentiates it from the parotid gland. The exocrine pancreas is comprised entirely of serous acini.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A urine sample from a 4-year-old child appeared normal at first but gradually darkened on standing, with the discoloration becoming more intense over time, as seen by the laboratory technician. This finding suggests deficiency of which enzyme as the underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The phenomenon where clear urine turns dark or black upon standing is the classic presentation of alkaptonuria. This rare autosomal recessive disorder is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme homogentisic acid oxidase (Option D) in the phenylalanine-tyrosine metabolic pathway. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of homogentisic acid, which is excreted in the urine and oxidizes into a black pigment (alkapton) when exposed to air. Beta-carotene (Option A) is a precursor to Vitamin A and does not cause urine darkening. Tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency (Option B) leads to Tyrosinemia Type II, characterized by eye and skin lesions but not black urine. L-ascorbic acid (Option C) is Vitamin C, which is sometimes used as a treatment adjunct but is not the cause of the disease. Therefore, based on the pathognomonic finding of urine darkening upon oxidation, the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase is the causative enzyme defect

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a normal curve, what is the percentage of the distribution that falls within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 68%

According to the empirical rule of normal distributions, 68% of the distribution falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean.

In a normal curve, the area on either side of the mean will include :

Approximately 68% of the distribution falls within ±1 standard deviations of the mean.

Approximately 95% of the distribution falls within ±2 standard deviations of the mean.

Approximately 99.7% of the distribution falls within ±3 standard deviations of the mean.

Pearl PF0301: Normal Distribution

* Normal distribution is the most widely used continuous distribution.

* It is also called bell curve (bell shaped) or Gaussian distribution after a mathematician named Karl Friedrich Gauss.

* The following is an image of three different types of normal distributions.

* Normal distributions are defined by two parameters: the mean and the standard deviation.

* The mean, median and mode are all equal in a normal distribution.

* All normal distributions are symmetric and have bell-shaped density curves with a single peak.

* Exactly half of the values are to the left of the centre and the other half to the right.

* The total area under the curve is 1.

* The density of a normal distribution is more around the centre and less around the tails.

* There is no skew in the curve.

* Looking at the figure below, we can understand the empirical rule of a normal distribution which states that:

* Approximately 68% of the distribution falls within one standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 1 SD).

* Approximately 95% of the distribution falls within two standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 2 SD).

* Approximately 99.7% of the distribution falls within three standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 3 SD).

* Many data like blood pressure, heights, IQ scores, etc. form a normal distribution.

* A standard normal distribution is a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following cataract surgery prefers suturing with nylon 10-0?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Extracapsular cataract extraction

Suturing with nylon 10-0 is preferred in extracapsular cataract extraction.

In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydro dissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.

The newer techniques of cataract surgery like phacoemulsification, MICS and FLACS doesn't require a suturing either because they use self sealing incisions or doesn't require a long incision.,

Pearl PF1395: Different extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) techniques

Conventional ECCE

* Incision: 10 to 2 o'clock

* Anterior capsulotomy

* Can opener’s technique

* Envelope technique

* Continuous circular capsulorrhexis

Manual SICS

* Incision: 4-6 mm

* A self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel incision is made.

Phacoemulsification

* Incision:1.5–2.4 mm

* Phacoprobe and foldable IOL is used

* Sutureless surgery is possible with self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel or clear corneal incision.
questions.learning: Extracapsular cataract extraction Suturing with nylon 10-0 is preferred in extracapsular cataract extraction. In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28 year old female is started on Oral Contraceptive Pills. She presents after 2 weeks with a history of missing 4 tablets on different days in the first 2 weeks of the cycle. What will you advise her? (NEET PG 2021)
options: Discontinue the packet and start an alternate method of contraception
Take 4 tablets the next day, continue the remaining packet, use additional contraception (condom) and give Emergency Pill if h/o intercourse in the last 72 h
Take the next pill as soon as possible, continue the remaining packet, use additional contraception (condom) and give Emergency Pill if h/o intercourse in the last 72 h
Take the next pill as soon as possible and continue the remaining tablets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Take the next pill as soon as possible, continue the remaining packet, use additional contraception (condom) and give Emergency Pill if h/o intercourse in the last 72 h

When ≥2 active oral contraceptive pills are missed during the first 2 weeks of the cycle, contraceptive protection decreases significantly.

Recommended management:

• Take the next active pill as soon as possible
• Continue the remaining pills as scheduled
• Use backup contraception (eg, condoms) for the next 7 days
• Give emergency contraception if unprotected intercourse occurred within the previous 72 hours

Multiple missed pills early in the cycle increase the risk of ovulation and unintended pregnancy

Patients should not:

• Stop the entire packet unnecessarily
• Take multiple missed pills together after several missed doses

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-week USG of a pregnant shows marginal placenta. Reassessment by USG is done at?
questions.explanation: When a marginal placenta (Type II placenta previa) is detected at 22 weeks, the recommended approach is follow-up with repeat ultrasonography at 28 weeks. This is because most low-lying placentas resolve by 28–32 weeks due to placental migration as the uterus expands and the lower segment develops. Early reassessment at 28 weeks helps determine whether the placenta has moved away from the internal os or if it persists, in which case another scan at around 32–36 weeks (or near term) is planned for delivery decision. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 32 weeks: Useful for later confirmation, but first reassessment is done earlier at 28 weeks. (B) 38 weeks: Too late; management decisions must be made well before term. (D) 30 weeks: Not a standard recommended interval; 28 weeks is the accepted first follow-up timing
questions.learning: When a marginal placenta (Type II placenta previa) is detected at 22 weeks, the recommended approach is follow-up with repeat ultrasonography at 28 weeks.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a 15-year history of smoking one pack per day presents with hemoptysis. Chest X-ray reveals a 3 cm mass in the upper lobe near the lung apex. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: For a peripheral lung mass, specifically one located in the upper lobe near the apex (Pancoast tumor region or peripheral nodule), a CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy is the most appropriate next step to obtain a tissue diagnosis. This method provides high diagnostic yield for peripheral lesions that are difficult to reach via internal airways. Bronchoscopy (Option A) is better suited for central masses that are visible within the larger bronchial trees; peripheral masses are often beyond the reach of standard fiberoptic bronchoscopes. Sputum cytology (Option C) has a low sensitivity for diagnosing lung cancer and is rarely the definitive next step for a 3 cm mass. Sputum for Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) (Option D) is used to rule out tuberculosis (TB); while TB is a differential for a lung mass, the smoking history and mass characteristics strongly mandate ruling out malignancy first via biopsy. Therefore, CT-guided biopsy provides the necessary pathology to guide subsequent cancer staging and treatment
questions.learning: For a peripheral lung mass, specifically one located in the upper lobe near the apex (Pancoast tumor region or peripheral nodule), a CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy is the most appropriate next step to obtain a tissue diagnosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with joint pain, swelling, and difficulty in movement. Examination reveals a tender, swollen knee, and the history is notable for a recent sore throat. Laboratory investigations show elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers, while renal biopsy findings are consistent with post- streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Considering the association with both acute rheumatic fever and PSGN, which streptococcal species is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of migratory arthritis (joint discomfort/swelling) followed by symptoms of glomerular disease (PSGN) after a recent throat infection is diagnostic for the sequelae of Streptococcus pyogenes infection. Streptococcus pyogenes, also known as Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GABHS), is the only organism responsible for both acute rheumatic fever and PSGN. High ASO titers confirm the immune response to a recent GABHS pharyngeal infection. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) causes pneumonia and meningitis. Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B) (Option C) is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis. Streptococcus mutans (Option D) is associated with dental caries and subacute endocarditis. While PSGN can follow either a throat or skin infection, acute rheumatic fever characteristically follows only a pharyngeal infection with GABHS. Understanding this shared etiology is fundamental in pediatric medicine for emphasizing the need for prompt treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of migratory arthritis (joint discomfort/swelling) followed by symptoms of glomerular disease (PSGN) after a recent throat infection is diagnostic for the sequelae of Streptococcus pyogenes infection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as Medical Eligibility Criteria 1( MEC-1) for the use of oral contraceptive pills(OCPs)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HIV

According to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC), HIV falls under category 1, meaning OCPs can be used in any circumstance.

Combined oral contraceptives contain estrogen (ethinylestradiol/mestranol) and progestins (levonorgestrel, norethisterone, desogestrel). Their primary mode of action is inhibition of ovulation: estrogen suppresses FSH to prevent follicular growth, while progestins suppress LH to block ovulation. This negative feedback on the hypothalamo-pituitary axis prevents the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge.

Additionally, they act by producing a non-receptive endometrium, thickening cervical mucus to block sperm penetration, and possibly altering tubal motility to prevent fertilization. Progestins also counteract estrogen’s proliferative effect on the endometrium, reducing the risk of hyperplasia and controlling withdrawal bleeding.

WHO category 1- Indication of OCPs

* Age: Menarche to 40 years

* Postabortion

* Anemia (iron deficiency, malaria)

* HIV or AIDS (additional to condom use)

* GTN following normal hCG level

* History of ectopic pregnancy

* Endometriosis, uterine fibroid, ovarian or endometrial cancer

* Dysmenorrhea, DUB

* Pelvic inflammatory disease

* Epilepsy

* Thyroid disease

* Varicose veins

* Tuberculosis

* Benign breast disease

Contraindications of OCPs :

A. WHO Category–2 (advantages outweigh

the risks)

• Age ≥ 40 years
• Smoker < 35 years
• History of jaundice
• Mild hypertension
• Gallbladder disease
• Diabetes
• Sickle cell disease
• Headache
• Cancer cervix

Absolute (WHO category 4)

A. Circulatory diseases (past or present)

• Arterial or venous thrombosis
• Severe hypertension
• History of stroke
• Heart disease: Valvular, ischemic
• Diabetes with vascular complications
• Migraine with focal neurologic symptoms

B. WHO Category–3 (risks outweigh advantages)

• Unexplained vaginal bleeding
• Hyperlipidemia
• Liver tumors (benign)
• Breastfeeding (postpartum 6 weeks to 6 months)
• Heavy smoker (> 20 cigarettes/day)

B. Diseases of the liver

• Active liver disease, jaundice
• Liver adenoma, carcinoma

C. Others

• Pregnancy
• Breastfeeding (postpartum 6 weeks)
• Major surgery
questions.learning: HIV According to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC), HIV falls under category 1, meaning OCPs can be used in any circumstance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Conducting a village-based session on wound care after a dog bite by demonstrating it through enactment represents which method of health communication?
questions.explanation: In health communication and community education, Demonstration is a highly effective method involving the physical enacting or showing of a specific skill or procedure. By acting out the steps of wound care after a dog bite (e.g., washing with soap and water for 15 minutes), the health worker provides a visual and practical model that is easier for villagers to understand and replicate than verbal instructions alone. A Lecture (Option A) is a one-way verbal communication of information. A Group discussion (Option B) is a multi-way exchange of ideas among a small group. Flash cards (Option C) are a visual aid used to support a presentation but are not the primary mode of enacting a skill. Demonstration is based on the principle of "learning by seeing and doing." It is particularly useful in rural public health for teaching life-saving skills like ORS preparation, hand-washing techniques, or immediate first aid for common injuries, significantly improving the community's health literacy and emergency response
questions.learning: In health communication and community education, Demonstration is a highly effective method involving the physical enacting or showing of a specific skill or procedure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most commonly seen tumor in the retroperitoneal space?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liposarcoma

Liposarcoma is the most commonly seen tumor in retroperitoneal space.

Retroperitoneal tumors can be benign or malignant. Malignant retroperitoneal tumors may be mesodermal (75%), neuroectodermal (24%), or embryonic remnant (1%) in origin. Rarely it can be urologic or metastatic also. The order of frequency of primary retroperitoneal malignancy is as follows:

• Liposarcoma
• Leiomyosarcoma
• Rhabdomyosarcoma
• Fibrosarcoma
• Malignant nerve sheath tumors

Liposarcoma is composed of three histologic varieties (listed in order of decreasing frequency):

• Well-differentiated and undifferentiated liposarcoma
• Pleomorphic liposarcoma
• Myxoid/round cell liposarcoma

Among the three subtypes, pleomorphic liposarcoma is the most malignant and often metastasizes, while the well-differentiated is the least malignant. Myxoid liposarcoma has intermediate malignant behavior.

Diagnosis is confirmed by contrast-enhanced CT with CT of the chest to look for metastases.

Surgery is the main modality of treatment. Wide excision with complete en bloc dissection is done. Post-operative radiotherapy and chemotherapy are used as adjuvant methods. Radiotherapy is given at a dose of 5000 cGY, it can be external beam or intra-operative radiotherapy. Chemotherapeutic agents used are mesna, adriamycin, ifosfamide and dacarbazine (MAID regimen).
questions.learning: Liposarcoma Liposarcoma is the most commonly seen tumor in retroperitoneal space. Retroperitoneal tumors can be benign or malignant.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following cataracts is seen in blunt trauma?
questions.explanation: A rosette cataract is the characteristic type of lens opacification that develops following blunt trauma to the eyeball. The concussion force causes the lens fibers to separate or opacify along their natural suture lines, creating a flower-shaped or "rosette" appearance, usually at the posterior capsule. This may appear immediately after injury or can be delayed. Blunt trauma can also cause a "Vossius ring" (pigment on the anterior lens). Toxic cataracts (Option B) result from exposure to certain drugs (like steroids or chlorpromazine). Metabolic cataracts (Option C) are associated with systemic diseases like diabetes ("snowflake" cataract) or galactosemia ("oil-drop"). Nuclear cataract (Option D) is a common form of age-related (senile) cataract characterized by hardening and yellowing of the lens nucleus. Recognizing the rosette pattern is critical for establishing a history of ocular trauma. Traumatic cataracts often require surgical intervention if they significantly impair vision or are associated with other injuries like lens subluxation or glaucoma

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 20-day-old infant presents with prolonged jaundice, umbilical hernia, and macroglossia. Feeding is normal and there is no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital hypothyroidism

Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability and should be suspected in any neonate with prolonged jaundice, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, constipation, poor activity, and feeding difficulties. Early diagnosis through newborn screening and prompt levothyroxine therapy are essential to prevent irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment.

Why not the other options?

• A. Neonatal sepsis: Typically presents with fever or hypothermia, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory distress, and systemic illness, which are absent here.
• B. Down syndrome: May have macroglossia and hypotonia but prolonged jaundice with umbilical hernia is more characteristic of congenital hypothyroidism. Down syndrome should also be evaluated for associated hypothyroidism.
• D. Galactosemia: Presents with jaundice, vomiting, poor feeding, hepatomegaly, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis after milk feeding, not macroglossia and umbilical hernia.

questions.text: What does phase III represent in the below image?

Correct answer: D. Alveolar plateau

Phase III of the capnography waveform represents the alveolar plateau, where exhaled gas is predominantly alveolar. CO₂ concentration rises gradually until the end of this phase, giving the EtCO₂ value. It reflects alveolar ventilation, V/Q matching & quality of ventilation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common side effect she is likely to experience following the insertion?
questions.explanation: The Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD) is a highly effective, long-acting reversible contraceptive. However, users frequently experience specific side effects. The most common side effect leading to the removal of the device is abnormal vaginal bleeding (Option D), which can manifest as heavier or longer menstrual periods (menorrhagia) or intermenstrual spotting. Pain (Option C), such as pelvic cramps, is the second most common side effect . While pelvic infection (Option B) (PID) and ectopic pregnancy (Option A) are serious potential complications, their overall incidence is significantly lower than the occurrence of bleeding. Most bleeding issues are mild and resolve within the first few months after insertion, but they remain the primary reason for patient dissatisfaction. Clinicians should counsel patients about these expected changes to improve compliance. Therefore, increased menstrual bleeding is the most frequent adverse outcome of IUCD use
questions.learning: The Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD) is a highly effective, long-acting reversible contraceptive. However, users frequently experience specific side effects.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is the best indicator of chronic malnutrition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Height for age

Height for age is the best indicator of chronic malnutrition.

Nutritional status is often assessed in terms of anthropometry:

* Low height for age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

* Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.

* High weight-for-height indicates overweight.

* Low weight for the age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent parameter used for the screening of wasting in children.

questions.text: A male was brought with the following injury in a gunshot incident. What is the possible range from which the weapon inflicted injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Contact shot

In the given scenario, based on the stellate-shaped wound seen, it seems to be a contact shot entry wound.

A contact shot entry wound on the skull typically has a stellate shape due to high-energy impact.

* Firearm wounds are fundamental of two main types: wounds of entry and wounds of exit. The wound of entry is the wound through which the bullet or pellets enter the body, and the wound of exit is the wound through which the bullet emerges out of the body.

* To determine the range of firing, the following parameters are used:

* The entry wound size and shape

* Blast effect: Muzzle end imprint and edge eversion

* Blackening, tattooing, singeing of hair, abrasion collar, and grease collar

* Hair should be preserved to determine the range of firing which can be examined for carbonization/desiccation at close range, and also from lead deposition around the wound to assess the range of firing.

Pearl PF2153: Types of bullets:

1. Ricochet bullet: Bullet first strikes an intermediate object and then after being reflected strikes the target. It produces a key hole entry wound .

2. Yawning bullet: Travels in an irregular fashion.

3. Tandem (Piggy Back) Bullet Effect: Two bullets are ejected one after the other; first bullet failed to leave the barrel and is ejected by subsequently fired bullet. This occurs due to defect in the weapon or due to faulty ammunition or with loaded firearms unused for several years. Tandem cartridge (also called duplex cartridge) is a single cartridge containing two bullets.

4. Frangible bullet: Fragments on hitting the target.

5. Dum Dum bullet: Tip is chiseled out, fragments extensively on impact.

6. Tumbling bullet:  Rotates end on end during its motion. This produces an atypical entry wound .

7. Souvenir bullet:  Bullet left in the body for a long time and covered with dense fibrous connective tissue.

8. Tracer bullet: This type of bullet leaves a visible mark or trace while in flight so that the gunner can observe the strike of shot. Rear portion of bullet is filled with mixture of barium nitrate, strontium nitrate and powdered magnesium which is ignited by the burning powder. Mixture burns and sheds red sparks which makes the projectile visible to naked eye which enables shooter to make aiming corrections.

9. Incendiary bullet: It is filled with white phosphorous and ignites the target.

From left to right : Blank with frangible wooden bullet, ball, tracer and incendiary bullets

Smudging/blackening:

* It is due to the deposition of smoke particles, lead or metal of which the missile is made of.

Tattooing/peppering

* It is due to deposition of fine or coarse gunpowder particles, which become truly impregnated into and mark the skin, and cannot be washed or scrubbed off.

Medicolegal importance

* Smudging and tattooing effects can help to assess the range of firing, as below

* If both are present, the range of firing is close or near shot.

* If both are absent, the range of firing is a distant shot.

* If both are found deeper, i.e. on the inner aspect of the wound, the range is contact shot.

* If only tattooing is present, the range is near shot.

* Thus as the range increases, blackening fades first, followed by tattooing, the reason being their causative agents cannot travel beyond a fixed distance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year old alcoholic and a chronic smoker presented with bouts of vomiting and stabbing pain in the epigastrium. He was binge drinking shortly before the symptoms started. He is febrile and tachycardic. The given findings were seen on bedside radiological imaging. Which among the following is a likely cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peptic ulcer perforation

In the given case scenario, the supine abdominal x-ray shows air beneath the diaphragm along with Rigler's double-wall sign indicating pneumoperitoneum. The likely cause for this would be peptic ulcer perforation. Consumption of alcohol and chronic tobacco smoking are high-risk factors for developing peptic ulcers. Fever and tachycardia suggest peritonitis from the perforated ulcer.

Gastric ulcers are more prone to perforate than bleed. Thus, these perforations lead to pneumoperitoneum which is an emergency and warrants immediate surgical intervention.

Other options:

A. Tension pneumothorax - presents with a rapid hemodynamic compromise with absent breath sounds. Pneumoperitoneum rarely is caused by pneumothorax, and downward displacement of air is more likely seen in retroperitoneal spaces.

C. Boerhaave syndrome or spontaneous esophageal rupture - occurs in alcoholics after binge drinking, due to forced vomiting from the closed glottis.  Pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema are seen here.

D. Mallory Weis tear - longitudinal mucosal tear resulting in upper GI bleeding. It is commonly seen in alcoholics.
questions.learning: Peptic ulcer perforation — In the given case scenario, the supine abdominal x-ray shows air beneath the diaphragm along with Rigler's double-wall sign indicating pneumoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A respiratory illness outbreak is reported in a paediatric ward, primarily affecting infants under the age of 12 months. The majority of patients present with fever, cough, and tachypnea, as well as wheezing and signs of respiratory distress. Hyperinflation is frequently seen on chest radiographs. What is the most likely cause of the outbreak?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory syncytial virus

The given clinical features with a radiograph showing hyperinflated lungs and respiratory distress in patients aged 12 months or younger suggest bronchiolitis, which is most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease in children younger than 2 years. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases. Bronchiolitis occurs due to viral lower respiratory tract infection, most commonly by the RSV (respiratory syncytial virus). It is common in children less than 12 months of age.

Acute bronchiolitis refers to airway inflammation and obstruction of the lower respiratory tract. Commonly, symptoms of bronchiolitis begin with rhinitis or congestion and cough and may progress to signs of increasing respiratory distress (tachypnoea, wheezing, and accessory muscle use).

Clinical features of bronchiolitis include fever, cough, fine inspiratory crackles, expiratory wheezes, and breathing difficulty. Cyanosis may be seen in severe cases. Radiographs may be normal in some patients. In the majority of them, there will be interstitial infiltrates, hyperexpansion of the chest, and peribronchial thickening. It is more common in boys, in those who have not been breastfed, and in those who live in crowded conditions. The risk is higher for infants with young mothers or mothers who smoked during pregnancy.

Management is mainly conservative. Hypoxemic children should receive cool, humidified oxygen. Rarely, a child might develop respiratory failure and require hospitalisation and invasive ventilation.

Other options:

Option A: Influenza belongs to the Orthomyxovirus family. It presents with fever, myalgia, and respiratory symptoms.

Option B: The most common causative organism for croup is the parainfluenza virus.

Option C: Rotavirus is the most common identifiable viral cause of diarrhoea in children below the age of 5 years and is most frequent between 6 and 24 months of age

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
If the contractility of the heart is decreased, which of the following is seen

ESV: End-systolic volume

EDV: End-diastolic volume
options: End diastolic volume and pressure curve shifts to left without change in slope
Slope changes in ESV pressure curve
End systolic volume and pressure curve shifts to left without change in slope
Slope changes in EDV and pressure curve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Slope changes in ESV pressure curve

If the contractility of the heart is decreased, slope changes in the ESV pressure curve are seen.

To answer this question, we will first understand the volume-pressure diagram and the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) during cardiac cycle.

Volume-pressure diagram during the cardiac cycle

The volume pressure diagram plots the changes in the pressure and volume in the left ventricle that occurs during the cardiac cycle. The x-axis shows the changes in ventricular volume, while the y-axis shows the changes in ventricular pressure.

It has the following phases.

Phase I- This phase is called the period of filling and extends between points A and B. Point A is at the end of systole when the ventricular volume is about 50 mL. This volume is called end-systolic volume. The pressure at this point is about 2 to 3 mm Hg. These volume and pressure go on increasing as the blood from the atrium flows to the ventricle during diastole. At the end of diastole, marked by point B, the ventricle will have a volume of around 120 mL. This volume is called end-diastolic volume. The pressure is slightly raised to 5-7mm Hg.

Phase II- It is the phase of isovolumetric contraction, and extends between points B and C. At the end of diastole (point B), a slight increase in the ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve, and contraction starts. The ventricle contracts while both mitral and aortic valves are closed. Therefore, the pressure within the ventricle slowly rises without any changes in the volume.

Phase III- It is the phase of ejection and extends between point C and point D. Point C is the place where the aortic valve opens. The pressure within the left ventricle rises slowly during isovolumetric contraction until it is sufficient to open the aortic valve. Once the aortic valve opens, blood within the left ventricle is ejected into the aorta. This decreases the volume of the left ventricle, while increasing the pressure within the ventricle.

Phase IV- It is the period of isovolumetric relaxation. It extends between points D and A. At the end of the ejection (Point D), the aortic valve closes. However, the ventricular relaxation continues despite closed aortic and mitral valves. Therefore, the ventricular pressure continues to fall while the volume remains the same. The ventricle returns to its starting point, with about 50 ml of blood left in the ventricle and pressure of about 2 to 3 mm Hg

End-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR)

ESPVR is the maximum pressure that can be developed by the ventricle at the end-systolic volume. It is determined by the line intersecting the upper left corners of the loops. This line can be extended down to the x-axis. The slope of this line is called as ESPVR slope.

Now coming to the question, when the contractility of the heart is decreased, the force of ejection decreases leading to decreased stroke volume, and increased end-systolic volume. Therefore, the volume-pressure diagram shifts to the right. If the diagram shifts to the right, then ESPVR also changes, leading to a change in the slope of the ESPVR curve.

Other options:

Options A and D- End diastolic volume and pressure curve (EDPVR) mainly assesses the compliance of the ventricle, rather than contractility. The slope of this curve increases when the compliance decreases, and vice versa.

Option C- ESPVR shifts to right with change in slope.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following parasites directly invade the skin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schistosoma mansoni

The parasite that directly invades the skin is Schistosoma mansoni.

Adult worms of S. mansoni live in the inferior mesenteric vein and their infective form is fork-tailed cercaria. Following skin penetration by cercariae, a pruritic rash termed cercarial dermatitis or swimmers itch develops locally which is self-limiting.

After 4- 8 weeks of the cercarial invasion, high worm load, and egg antigen stimuli lead to the formation of immune complexes which result in a serum sickness-like illness termed Katayama fever. They present with high-grade fever, rash, arthralgia, and hepatosplenomegaly.

When eggs get deposited in the small intestine, patients develop abdominal pain and blood dysentery for a long time called intestinal bilharziasis. The drug of choice is praziquantel 40mg/kg single oral dose. Oxamniquine 15mg/kg single oral dose is also an effective dose.

A yellowish-brown egg with a lateral spine near the rounded posterior end is suggestive of Schistosoma mansoni. In Schistosoma hematobium, the egg has a terminal spine. In Schistosoma japonicum, the egg has no spine but shows a lateral small rudimentary knob.

The life cycle of schistosomes is represented below:

Other options:

Option B: Dracunculiasis/Guinea worm disease is a vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Dracunculus medinenesis. Transmission occurs by consumption of water containing cyclops harboring infective stages of the parasite. This disease is totally a water-based disease and has no alternate way of transmission.

Option C: Wuchereria bancrofti causes filariasis. The adult worms block the lymphatic vessels leading to inflammation and granuloma formation. This causes hard pitting or brawny edema. It can present as lymphadenitis, lymphedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis. The disease spreads from person to person through mosquito bites.

Option D: Onchocerca volvulus is a tissue nematode. The life cycle of Onchocerca volvulus is completed partly in humans, the definitive host, and partly in female blackflies, the intermediate host. During a blood meal, the female blackfly ingests the microfilariae from the skin and lymphatics of an infected person. Within the vector, the microfilariae develop into the infective stage. When the infected black fly bites another person, it introduces third-stage filarial larvae into the skin of the human host.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: For assessing the viral load in a test sample, which test utilizes the provided graph?
questions.explanation: The graph depicted is an "amplification curve" characteristic of Real-time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR). This technique measures the increase in fluorescence (representing DNA amplification) during each cycle of the PCR process. The " value" (cycle threshold) is the point where the fluorescence crosses the background noise; a lower value indicates a higher initial "viral load" in the sample. Antigen tests (Option A) are rapid immunoassays that do not involve cycles or DNA amplification. While CBNAAT (Option C) and TruNat (Option D) are also molecular tests that use similar technology, "Real-time RT-PCR" is the broader, fundamental category that this specific type of cycle-fluorescence graph represents. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this graph became the global standard for identifying infected individuals and assessing how infectious they might be based on the value
questions.learning: The graph depicted is an "amplification curve" characteristic of Real-time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR). This technique measures the increase in fluorescence (representing DNA amplification) during each cycle of the PCR process.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive limb weakness over the past year. Examination reveals muscle fasciculations and increased muscle tone, with preserved sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the simultaneous involvement of both upper motor neurons (UMN) and lower motor neurons (LMN). The presence of hypertonia (a UMN sign) and muscle fasciculations (an LMN sign) in the same limb, while the sensory system remains intact, is pathognomonic for ALS. Spinal Muscular Atrophy (Option B) is a pure LMN disease and would not present with UMN signs like hypertonia. Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (Option C) typically presents with pure LMN weakness that is often asymmetric and lacks UMN features. Becker Muscular Dystrophy (Option D) is a genetic myopathy that causes proximal muscle weakness but does not involve motor neurons, meaning it lacks fasciculations and UMN signs. Because ALS relentlessly destroys both sets of motor neurons in the motor cortex and spinal cord while sparing sensory pathways, it is the only viable diagnosis for this clinical picture
questions.learning: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the simultaneous involvement of both upper motor neurons (UMN) and lower motor neurons (LMN).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Criterion that differentiates exudative from transudative pleural effusion?
questions.explanation: Differentiating between transudative and exudative effusions is the first step in diagnosing pleural disease. This is achieved using Light's Criteria. An exudative effusion (caused by inflammation or malignancy) is characterized by increased capillary permeability, leading to a high protein content in the pleural fluid. Specifically, Light's criteria define an exudate if the pleural fluid/serum protein ratio is , or the pleural fluid/serum LDH ratio is . A transudative effusion (caused by hydrostatic pressure, like heart failure) has low protein (Option A). Sugar (glucose) levels (Options C and D) are not primary differentiators in Light's criteria, although low glucose level in an exudate can suggest specific pathologies like tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis, or parapneumonic effusions. Distinguishing these two is vital; transudates are treated by managing the underlying systemic condition, while exudates require a search for local pleural pathology, infections, or pulmonary emboli
questions.learning: Differentiating between transudative and exudative effusions is the first step in diagnosing pleural disease. This is achieved using Light's Criteria.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of dapsone, considering that it is used in the treatment of leprosy, fungal infections and, also for immunomodulatory actions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Folic acid synthesis inhibitor

The mechanism of action of dapsone is inhibition of folic acid synthesis.

Dapsone [4,4‐diaminodiphenylsulphone (DDS)] is a structural analog of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) and a competitive inhibitor of dihydropteroate synthase in the folate pathway. It is weakly bactericidal and can cause mild hemolysis, and rarely anemia or psychosis.

DDS syndrome is a rare side effect of dapsone therapy in leprosy patients which starts after 5-6 weeks of starting dapsone and leads to exfoliative dermatitis, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, fever and hepatitis and may be fatal. It is also called 'five-week dermatitis'.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: An ICU patient who was already on endotracheal intubation now requires a tracheostomy. Which type of tube will you use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cuffed tracheostomy tube

A cuffed tracheostomy tube is used in this patient for tracheostomy.

Cuffed tracheostomy is preferred in unconscious patients or patients on ventilators for a long time. When the cuff is inflated, it not only prevents the aspiration of pharyngeal secretions into the trachea but also prevents the leakage of air. The cuff should be deflated every 2 hours for 5 minutes to prevent pressure necrosis of the cartilage and trachea.

Metallic tubes(Option C) and uncuffed tracheostomy(Option A) tubes are not used too commonly because of the risk of displacement and aspiration of secretions into the trachea.
questions.learning: Cuffed tracheostomy tube — A cuffed tracheostomy tube is used in this patient for tracheostomy. Cuffed tracheostomy is preferred in unconscious patients or patients on ventilators for a long time.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35 year old male presented to the clinic with complaints of episodic vertigo, sense of ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and a low-tone roaring tinnitus. What is the possible clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meniere's disease

The possible clinical diagnosis for a 35-year-old male presenting with episodic vertigo, ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and low-tone roaring tinnitus is Meniere's disease. It is also called endolymphatic hydrops.

The primary pathology in Ménière’s disease is the distension of the endolymphatic system due to an increased endolymph volume. This can result either from increased production of endolymph or its faulty absorption or both. Normally, endolymph secreted by stria vascularis fills the membranous labyrinth and is absorbed through the endolymphatic sac.

Meniere's disease is a chronic condition of the inner ear that affects balance and hearing. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, which are brief and intense episodes of spinning dizziness. Patients may also experience a sense of pressure or fullness in the affected ear, along with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus (ringing or buzzing in the ear). The tinnitus associated with Meniere's disease is typically low-tone roaring in nature.

Other options:

* Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is another common cause of vertigo, marked by brief episodes of dizziness or vertigo that are brought on by particular head movements. Common triggers include actions such as rolling over in bed or looking upwards. BPPV does not typically cause ear pressure, hearing loss, or low-tone roaring tinnitus.

* Labyrinthitis is an inflammation of the inner ear, usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection. It can cause vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus, but it is usually accompanied by other symptoms such as ear pain, fever, and a general feeling of illness.

* Syncope refers to a temporary loss of consciousness and muscle tone, often caused by a decrease in blood flow to the brain. It is not associated with the symptoms described in the scenario, such as vertigo, ear pressure, hearing loss, or tinnitus.
questions.learning: Meniere's disease — The possible clinical diagnosis for a 35-year-old male presenting with episodic vertigo, ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and low-tone roaring tinnitus is Meniere's disease.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 43-year-old person is brought to the emergency department by the police with a belief that his daughter plans to harm him. Investigations reveal that this claim is unfounded, and physical examination shows no abnormalities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient has a fixed, false belief that his daughter intends to harm him despite clear evidence to the contrary. This is a classic persecutory delusion. Since the belief is well-structured, persistent, and not accompanied by other major psychotic features or physical abnormalities, it fits delusional disorder. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Illusions : These are misinterpretations of real external stimuli (e.g., mistaking a rope for a snake), not fixed false beliefs. (C) Cotard syndrome : Involves nihilistic delusions (e.g., believing one is dead or organs are missing), not persecutory ideas. (D) Hallucinations : These are perceptions without external stimuli (e.g., hearing voices), not belief-based disturbances
questions.learning: The patient has a fixed, false belief that his daughter intends to harm him despite clear evidence to the contrary. This is a classic persecutory delusion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is false about von Willebrand disease?
options: Type I vWD presents with severe bleeding since birth
Type II vWD has reduced activity of von Willebrand factor
Type III vWD has very low levels of von Willebrand factor
Type III vWD presents clinically as a severe disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type I vWD presents with severe bleeding since birth

Correct answer is A because Type I von Willebrand disease is a partial quantitative deficiency and usually causes mild bleeding, often presenting later in life rather than severe bleeding since birth.

Type II vWD is a qualitative defect with reduced functional activity of vWF. Type III vWD has near absence of vWF and presents with severe bleeding resembling hemophilia.

| Type | Defect | Severity | Key Feature

| ---- | ------ | -------- | -----------

| Type I | Partial quantitative ↓ | ⭐ Mild | Most common

| Type II | Qualitative defect | Moderate | Dysfunctional vWF

| Type III | Severe deficiency | ⭐ Severe | Almost absent vWF

| Feature | vWD | Hemophilia

| ------- | --- | ----------

| Bleeding type | Mucosal | Deep (joints)

| Platelet function | Abnormal | Normal

| Bleeding time | ↑ | Normal

| aPTT | Mild ↑ | ↑
questions.learning: Type I vWD presents with severe bleeding since birth Correct answer is A because Type I von Willebrand disease is a partial quantitative deficiency and usually causes mild bleeding, often presenting later in life rather than severe bleeding since birth.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: If open cardiac massage were to be performed on a patient, what category would it come under?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Contaminated

Open cardiac massage is classified as a contaminated wound.

Contaminated wounds are class III surgical wounds. They include fresh open accidental wounds, surgeries with a major break in sterile technique, gross spillage of the gastrointestinal tract, or incision through an inflamed nonpurulent tissue. Examples include:

• Open cardiac massage
• Penetrating abdominal trauma

Surgical wounds are classified based on the expected amount of bacterial load at the time of surgery.

Open cardiac massage is performed when there is inadequate cardiac output, after emergency thoracotomy for penetrating chest trauma, during pericardial tamponade.

Class I surgical wounds are clean wounds (option A). They are noninfected surgical wounds without any inflammation. Examples include:

• Hernia repair
• Breast biopsy specimen

Class II surgical wounds are clean/contaminated wounds (option C). They are surgical wounds that include an entry hollow viscus such as the respiratory tract or gastrointestinal tract under controlled conditions without significant spillage. Examples include:

• Cholecystectomy
• Elective gastrointestinal surgery

Class IV surgical wounds are dirty wounds (option D). They are old traumatic wounds with the presence of necrotic tissue and perforated viscus with a heavy load of contamination. Examples include:

• Perforated diverticulitis
• Necrotizing soft tissue infection
questions.learning: Contaminated Open cardiac massage is classified as a contaminated wound. Contaminated wounds are class III surgical wounds.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following carcinomas is least likely to be seen in a patient on oral contraceptives?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial cancer

Oral contraceptive pills (OCP) protect against endometrial carcinomas. This effect is thought to be due to the opposition of estrogen induces proliferation by progestins in OCP. They also decrease the incidence of ovarian and colorectal cancers.

Other benefits of oral contraceptive pills:

* Regularisation of menstrual cycles results in relief of dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia

* Reduced incidence of fibrocystic breast disease and ovarian cysts

* Endometriosis and pelvic inflammatory disease are improved

On the other hand, OCP increase the incidence of hepatic adenomas , HCC and breast cancers.
questions.learning: Endometrial cancer Oral contraceptive pills (OCP) protect against endometrial carcinomas. This effect is thought to be due to the opposition of estrogen induces proliferation by progestins in OCP.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following CVS changes are not seen in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: A diastolic murmur is never considered a normal physiological finding in pregnancy and always warrants further investigation for underlying heart disease. In contrast, several other cardiovascular adaptations are common: a soft systolic murmur (Option A) is frequently heard due to increased blood flow and decreased viscosity. A third heart sound (S3) (Option C) often occurs because of rapid ventricular filling. Exaggerated splitting of the first heart sound (S1) (Option D) is also typically observed. Additionally, the apex beat shifts laterally, and systemic vascular resistance decreases due to the smooth muscle-relaxing effects of progesterone. While systolic, S3, and mammary murmurs are physiologic results of the hyperdynamic state, a diastolic murmur is always pathologic
questions.learning: A diastolic murmur is never considered a normal physiological finding in pregnancy and always warrants further investigation for underlying heart disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is included in co-testing for cervical cancer screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HPV DNA + Pap smear

Co-testing in cervical cancer screening refers to performing a pap smear and HPV DNA testing together.

Cervical cancer screening:

* Pap smear: Screening starts at 21 years and is repeated every 3 years until 29 years. From 30 to 65 years, cytology with HPV co-testing is recommended every 5 years. After 65 years of age, screening may be discontinued if there have been three consecutive negative cytology results or two consecutive negative co-tests within the past 10 years, with the most recent test done within the last 5 years.

* HPV DNA testing: If the result is positive for high-risk HPV, the next step is colposcopy followed by biopsy.
If the result is negative, the smear should be repeated after 5 years.

* Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA): In low-resource settings, a simple screening method is used in which, after exposing the cervix with a speculum, it is painted with 3.5% acetic acid. Any areas that turn white within one minute of application are considered suspicious and should be further evaluated with colposcopy or biopsy.

* Colposcopy: Colposcopy is the direct examination of the cervix using a microscope that provides low magnification, typically between 6 and 16 times. Indications include:

*

* Women whose cytology shows HSIL, ASC-H, or ASCUS with a positive HPV test

* Clinically abnormal cervix, even if cytology is normal

* Women with persistent high-risk HPV DNA positivity

* Abnormal cervical cytology accompanied by a positive HPV test

(HSIL: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, ASCUS: Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance, ASC-H: Atypical Squamous Cells – cannot exclude HSIL)

Incorporating HPV testing with pap smear improves its predictive value and reduces the number of colposcopic evaluations.

Pap smear:  The patient is put in a dorsal position and Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced. The squamocolumnar junction is identified and scraped with Ayre’s spatula. Endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush. Samples are spread separately on 2 different glass slides. The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol and stained with Pap stain.

The instruments used for pap smear are summarized in the image below:

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the appropriate treatment for cryptorchidism (undescended testis)?
options: Manually bringing the testis down to the bottom of the scrotum
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism is the most common congenital anomaly of the male genitalia. While surgical orchidopexy is the definitive gold standard for management (ideally performed by age 1), hormonal therapy is sometimes used as a preliminary or adjunctive measure. GnRH analogues (Option A) or human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) can be administered to stimulate endogenous testosterone production, which may encourage the descent of a "high scrotal" or "inguinal" testis. However, the success rate for hormonal therapy is generally low, around 10-20%. Testosterone (Option B) is not the primary hormonal treatment. Cold compressions (Option C) have no therapeutic role and may actually cause reflex retraction of the testis. "Manually bringing the testis down" (Option D) describes the diagnosis of a "retractile testis," which is a normal variant that does not require treatment, rather than a management strategy for true cryptorchidism. When hormonal therapy fails, surgical intervention is mandatory to preserve germ cell function and allow for cancer screening
questions.learning: Cryptorchidism is the most common congenital anomaly of the male genitalia. While surgical orchidopexy is the definitive gold standard for management (ideally performed by age 1), hormonal therapy is sometimes used as a preliminary or adjunctive measure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly woman presents with a sudden onset of severe ocular pain, redness, and decreased vision. On examination, she has a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure Glaucoma

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden obstruction of aqueous outflow, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure.

• Severe ocular pain + headache
• Red eye with hazy (edematous) cornea
• Fixed mid-dilated pupil
• Shallow anterior chamber
• Sudden decrease in vision ± halos

Pathophysiology: Closure of anterior chamber angle → blocked trabecular outflow → ↑ IOP

Why not others:

• Uveitis → constricted pupil, not mid-dilated
• Conjunctivitis → no vision loss or high IOP
• Open-angle glaucoma → painless, gradual
questions.learning: Acute angle closure Glaucoma Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden obstruction of aqueous outflow, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure. • Severe ocular pain + headache • Red eye with hazy (edematous)…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Modified biophysical profile includes:

NST - Nonstress test

AFI - Amniotic fluid index
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NST and AFI

The modified biophysical profile includes NST (nonstress test) and AFI (amniotic fluid index).

It is a modification of the biophysical profile (BPP) test, including only 2 parameters so that it can be performed more routinely (twice a week) for surveillance and takes less time (10 minutes). Modified BPP is considered nonreassuring when the NST is non-reactive and/ or the AFI is < 5.

The nonstress test is a screening test for fetal wellness. It describes fetal heart rate acceleration (measured by a Doppler) in response to fetal movements (perceived by mother). An acoustic stimulation nonstress test is a type of NST in which a loud external sound is used to startle the fetus and provoke heart rate accelerations.

• Reactive (Reassuring) NST - Two or more accelerations of 15 seconds duration, 15 beats per minute amplitude, in a 20-minute testing time.
• Non-reactive (Non-reassuring) NST - Absence of any fetal reactivity.

BPP is a multi-parametric, screening test to assess uteroplacental insufficiency. It consists of five components/ variables and the observations are made in a 30-minute time period.

Components of BPP:

(Mnemonic: BATMaN)

B - Breathing movements of the fetus

A - Amniotic fluid volume

T - Tone of the fetus

M - Movements of the fetus

N - Non-stress test (NST)

Parameters
Minimal Normal Criteria

Fetal breathing movements
≥ 1 episode lasting > 30 seconds

Amniotic fluid volume (AFV)
≥ 1 pocket measuring 2 cm in two perpendicular planes (2 ×2 cm pocket)

Fetal muscle tone
≥ 1 episode of active limb or trunk extension with the return of flexion; Eg. opening and closing of the hand, considered normal

Gross body movements
≥ 3 discrete body/limb movements

Non-stress Test (NST)
Reactive pattern

Each parameter has a maximum score of 2 and a minimum score of 0. So the total maximum score will be 10. A score of 4 or less indicates fetal acidemia.

Interpretation and management of BPP scores:

BPP score
Interpretation
Management

10
Normal, nonasphyxiated fetus
Repeat test weekly (or biweekly in diabetic mother or post-term pregnancy)

8 with normal AFV
Normal, nonasphyxiated fetus
Repeat test weekly (or biweekly in diabetic mother or post-term pregnancy)

8 with decreased AFV
Suspicion of chronic fetal asphyxia
Delivery

6
Possible fetal asphyxia

Deliver, if AFV is abnormal or >36weeks or if the repeat test score is ≤ 6. If the repeat score >6, observation and repeat test weekly

4
Probable fetal asphyxia

Repeat testing same day

If the repeat score ≤6, delivery

0-2
Almost certain fetal asphyxia
Delivery

BPP is directly related to fetal pH and fetal outcome. A lower BPP score is associated with a poor outcome (stillbirth, perinatal mortality) and lower APGAR scores at birth.

A score of <10 is associated with a pH of <7.2 and a score of 0 is associated with 100% fetal acidemia.

Note: The modified biophysical score has only 2 components i.e. NST and amniotic fluid index only. It is considered abnormal (nonreassuring) when the NST is non-reactive and/or the AFI is <5.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the provided pressure-volume loop, which point corresponds to the moment when the aortic valve opens during the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Point C

The pressure–volume (PV) loop depicts the changes in left ventricular pressure and volume during one cardiac cycle. The aortic valve opens at Point C, marking the transition from isovolumetric contraction to ventricular ejection. The valve opens only when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (≈80 mmHg).

Why not the other points?

• A. Point A: Mitral valve opens, initiating ventricular filling.
• B. Point B: Mitral valve closes, marking the beginning of isovolumetric contraction (S1).
• D. Point D: Aortic valve closes, marking the end of ventricular ejection and beginning of isovolumetric relaxation (S2).

Exam Pearls:

• A: Mitral valve opens → Ventricular filling begins
• B: Mitral valve closes → S1, start of isovolumetric contraction
• C: Aortic valve opens → Ventricular ejection begins
• D: Aortic valve closes → S2, start of isovolumetric relaxation
• Isovolumetric phases: Volume remains constant because all cardiac valves are closed.
• Ejection phase: Begins when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, causing the aortic valve to open.
questions.learning: Point C — The pressure–volume (PV) loop depicts the changes in left ventricular pressure and volume during one cardiac cycle. The aortic valve opens at Point C, marking the transition from isovolumetric contraction to ventricular ejection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida in her 10th week of gestation presents with spotting. On examination, the uterus corresponds to 12 weeks. Transvaginal ultrasound was done and it is given below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hydatidiform mole

The given clinical scenario of a primigravida with spotting and an ultrasound showing a characteristic snowstorm appearance (anechoic cystic spaces) is suggestive of a hydatidiform mole (complete mole). It refers to an echogenic uterine mass that has numerous anechoic cystic spaces.

Hydatiform mole belongs to the benign group of gestational trophoblastic diseases (GTD). It is an abnormality in chorionic villi making them partly proliferative and degenerative, thereby resulting in the formation of multiple small cysts. Based on the portion of the chorionic villi involved, they could be complete (diffused) or partial (focal)

The classical clinical features of a complete mole are:

• Abnormal vaginal bleeding -Most common (90%)
• Lower abdominal pain
• Hyperemesis gravidarum due to increased β-hCG
• Features of early-onset preeclampsia
• Uterus appears large for date
• Absent fetal parts and FHS
• Expulsion of vesicular tissues (grape-like vesicles)
• Theca lutein cyst of ovaries of more than 6 cm
• Hyperthyroidism (rare)
• Serum hCG > 100,000 mIU/ml
• USG - snowstorm appearance

The definitive management after diagnosis is suction and evacuation, after making the cervix favorable. Follow-up of the patients with serial hCG values is crucial.

Prophylactic chemotherapy can be started on high-risk women (WHO prognostic score > 7) with methotrexate 1mg/kg/day intramuscular/intravenous on days 1, 3, 5, and 7. Patients are also advised to not get pregnant for at least a year.

Other options:

Option A: Blighted ovum (silent miscarriage) occurs when a fertilized egg implants in the uterus but doesn't develop into an embryo. It is a sonographic diagnosis where there is an absence of a fetal pole in a gestational sac with a diameter of 3 cm or more.

Option B: Missed abortion is when the fetus is dead and retained inside the uterus for a variable period. USG shows an empty sac early in the pregnancy or the absence of fetal cardiac activity and fetal movements.

Option C: Ectopic pregnancy is one in which the fertilized ovum is implanted and develops outside the normal endometrial cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.
questions.learning: Hydatidiform mole — The given clinical scenario of a primigravida with spotting and an ultrasound showing a characteristic snowstorm appearance (anechoic cystic spaces) is suggestive of a hydatidiform mole (complete mole).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate has bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications. She also has hydrocephalus. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toxoplasma gondi

The presence of bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications and hydrocephalus in a neonate is suggestive of congenital toxoplasmosis.

The characteristic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications. Clinical manifestations apart from the triad include hydrops fetalis, intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity, peripheral retinal scars, persistent jaundice, and mild thrombocytopenia.

Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when a pregnant woman acquires the infection during gestation. The organism may cross to the fetus transplacentally or at the time of vaginal delivery. The severity of the disease in the neonate is greater if the woman gets infected early in her pregnancy. The causative agent is Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan.

The diagnosis is made by the detection of IgM anti-toxoplasma antibodies. IgG can cross the placenta is hence, cannot confirm infection in the infant. IgM immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) and IgA ELISA are the most useful diagnostic tests.

Spiramycin can be administered for cases of acute infection in early pregnancy to reduce vertical transmission. It does not cross the placenta and therefore cannot be used to treat an infected fetus. Pyrimethamine-sulfonamide (to be avoided in the first trimester) is used when a fetal infection is confirmed or in maternal infections after 18 weeks.

Other options:

Option A: Trypanosoma is a genus of protozoan parasites responsible for diseases like African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) and American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease). These diseases present with different clinical features, such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, and neurological symptoms in African trypanosomiasis, and fever, swelling at the infection site, and cardiomyopathy in Chagas disease.

Option C: Taenia solium is a parasitic tapeworm transmitted through undercooked pork, causing intestinal infection (taeniasis) or more severe cyst formation in tissues, including the brain (cysticercosis). It's prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and where pork is consumed.

Option D: Congenital cytomegalovirus presents with hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. Head neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss. Diagnosis is made by isolating the virus from the urine or blood by polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
questions.learning: Toxoplasma gondi — The presence of bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications and hydrocephalus in a neonate is suggestive of congenital toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle aged cement factory worker has developed mesothelioma. This is likely to be associated with
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asbestosis

Mesothelioma is classically associated with asbestos exposure, leading to asbestosis. Asbestos fibers cause chronic pleural inflammation and malignant transformation of mesothelial cells.

Inhalation of asbestos fibers

↓

Fibers lodge in pleura

↓

Chronic inflammation + ROS damage

↓

DNA damage

Malignant transformation

↓

Mesothelioma (pleural cancer)
