| ------ | -------- | ------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Silicosis | Silica dust | Fibrotic lung disease | Mining, sandblasting | ❌ No mesothelioma link | ↑ TB risk

| B. Asbestosis ✅ | Asbestos fibers | Mesothelioma + fibrosis | ✔ Classic association | ✔ Correct | Pleural plaques

| C. Anthracosis | Coal dust | Carbon deposition | Mild disease | ❌ No malignancy link | “Black lung”

| D. Byssinosis | Cotton dust | Occupational asthma | Textile workers | ❌ Not malignancy | “Monday disease”

Silicosis, anthracosis, and byssinosis are not linked to mesothelioma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to which nerve results in absent gag reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IX & X

The afferent limb of the gag reflex is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) from the posterior pharynx.

The efferent limb is carried by the vagus nerve (CN X) supplying the pharyngeal muscles.

Injury to either nerve can abolish the gag reflex.
questions.learning: IX & X — The afferent limb of the gag reflex is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) from the posterior pharynx. The efferent limb is carried by the vagus nerve (CN X) supplying the pharyngeal muscles.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the urinary crystal shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium oxalate

The given urinary crystal is the bipyramidal or envelope-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate dihydrate. Risk factors for calcium oxalate stones include higher urine calcium, urine oxalate, and lower urine citrate.

Oxalate-rich foods like spinach, rhubarb, almonds, and potatoes should be avoided. Avoiding high-dose vitamin C supplements reduces endogenous oxalate production.

Chlorthalidone can lower urine calcium excretion and can reduce the recurrence of calcium oxalate stones. Consumption of fruits and vegetables or supplemental alkali is advised to increase urine citrate, which is a natural inhibitor of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones.
questions.learning: Calcium oxalate — The given urinary crystal is the bipyramidal or envelope-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate dihydrate. Risk factors for calcium oxalate stones include higher urine calcium, urine oxalate, and lower urine citrate.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of fever for 3 days and general fatigue. On examination, splinter hemorrhages were seen. Echocardiography revealed vegetations on the valves and thus a blood culture was done. The organism in the culture was seen as cocci in chains that showed alpha hemolysis on blood agar and was resistant to optochin and bile. Which of the following bacteria is most commonly implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus sanguis

The clinical scenario of fever, splinter haemorrhages, and vegetations on echocardiography is suggestive of infective endocarditis. The bacteria seen as cocci with alpha hemolysis and resistant to optochin and bile are most suggestive of Streptococcus viridans and in the following options, Streptococcus sanguis is a type of viridans bacteria.

Streptococcus sanguis belong to the viridans group of streptococci and they cause subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Streptococci that show alpha hemolysis on blood agar are again classified on the basis of optochin sensitivity and bile solubility.

* Alpha hemolysis: Streptococcus pneumoniae is sensitive to optochin and is bile soluble. Viridians streptococci are resistant to optochin and are bile insoluble.

* Beta hemolysis: Group B is resistant to bacitracin and Group A is sensitive to it.

* Gamma hemolysis: Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl and non-enterococcus does not.

Viridans streptococci show alpha hemolysis on blood agar and are resistant to optochin. They contain:

* Streptococci sanguis causes subacute bacterial endocarditis

* Streptococci mitis

* Streptococci mutans

* Streptococci salvarius

Other options:

Option A- Streptococcus pyogenes are beta-hemolytic and bacitracin sensitive.

Option C- Enterococcus does not show hemolysis.

Option D- Streptococcus agalacticae shows beta hemolysis and is bacitracin resistant.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of revised trauma score (RTS)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pulse rate

Pulse rate is NOT a part of revised trauma score.

The Revised Trauma Score is made up of 3 categories: Glasgow Coma Scale, systolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate.

The score range is 0–12.

A patient with an RTS score of 12 is labelled delayed, 11 is urgent, and 3–10 is immediate. Those who have an RTS below 3 are declared dead.
questions.learning: Pulse rate Pulse rate is NOT a part of revised trauma score. The Revised Trauma Score is made up of 3 categories: Glasgow Coma Scale, systolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman with a history of multiple pregnancies presents with grade II/III uterine prolapse and cystocele. She reports involuntary urine leakage when coughing or sneezing. What type of urinary incontinence does she most likely have?
questions.explanation: The involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure—such as coughing or sneezing—is the defining symptom of Stress Incontinence . In this patient, the history of multiple pregnancies and the presence of a cystocele (bladder prolapse) and uterine prolapse indicate a significant weakening of the pelvic floor and the urethral support structures (hypermobility). Urge incontinence (Option B) involves a sudden, uncontrollable need to void and is caused by detrusor overactivity. Overflow incontinence (Option A) results from an overdistended bladder due to obstruction or nerve damage, leading to continuous dribbling. Neurogenic bladder (Option D) results from specific neurological lesions (e.g., spinal cord injury). Because the leakage is strictly associated with mechanical "stress" on the bladder in a patient with documented pelvic floor laxity, stress incontinence is the definitive diagnosis. Management often includes pelvic floor exercises or surgical "sling" procedures
questions.learning: The involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure—such as coughing or sneezing—is the defining symptom of Stress Incontinence .

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common route of the spread of retinoblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Direct invasion

Direct invasion is the most common mode of spread of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma arises from the neurosensory retina. It is a proliferation of neural cells that have failed to evolve normally. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children.  Tumours are composed of small basophilic cells (retinoblasts), with large hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm.

It is of 4 types:

1. Endophytic (into the vitreous)with seeding of tumor cells throughout the eye
2. Exophytic (into the subretinal space) leading to retinal detachment
3. Mixed type
4. Retinocytoma: retina may be diffusely infiltrated
questions.learning: Direct invasion Direct invasion is the most common mode of spread of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma arises from the neurosensory retina.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 24-year-old student presents with redness, watering, foreign body sensation, and mild photophobia for 3 days. It started in one eye and then involved the other eye. There is tender preauricular lymph node enlargement. Examination of the eye is as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis

Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is an adenoviral conjunctivitis characterized by acute follicular conjunctivitis, preauricular lymphadenopathy, and subsequent corneal involvement (keratitis). It is highly contagious and often begins in one eye before involving the other.

• Etiology: Adenovirus (serotypes 8, 19, 37 are common)
• Symptoms: Red eye, watering, irritation, photophobia, blurred vision
• Signs:

• Follicular conjunctivitis
• Tender preauricular lymphadenopathy
• Pseudomembranes (may occur)
• Subepithelial corneal infiltrates appear after 1–2 weeks and may reduce vision

• Transmission: Highly contagious by direct contact, contaminated instruments, swimming pools
• Treatment: Supportive—cold compresses, lubricants, hygiene measures. Topical steroids are reserved for severe corneal infiltrates under ophthalmologist supervision.

Differentiating from Other Options

• A. Allergic conjunctivitis: Severe itching, bilateral from onset, papillae, no preauricular lymphadenopathy.
• B. Bacterial conjunctivitis: Purulent discharge, eyelids stuck together, no significant preauricular lymphadenopathy.
• D. Herpes simplex keratitis: Usually unilateral with dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining.
questions.learning: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is an adenoviral conjunctivitis characterized by acute follicular conjunctivitis, preauricular lymphadenopathy, and subsequent corneal involvement (keratitis).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following quantitative methods is the best to study previous research studies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meta-analysis

The quantitative method which is the best to study previous research studies of a selected topic/research question is meta-analysis.

A systematic review is a process of collecting, reviewing, and presenting information from earlier research to answer a question. It is a qualitative technique. It may or may not involve a meta-analysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient presents to the emergency department after a car crash. On examination, his BP was 80/40mmHg and pulses were feeble, neck veins distended, and heart sounds were muffled. Which of the following changes will you expect in the jvp of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent Y descent

The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck vein suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade. The JVP finding most likely to be seen is absent y descent.

Cardiac tamponade is the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space. It results in the obstruction of the blood flow into the ventricles.

This manifests as Beck's triad which consists of the following:

* Distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return)

* Muffled heart sounds (fluid accumulation in the pericardial space)

* Hypotension

The physical examination findings in a patient with cardiac tamponade are:

* Tachycardia

* Hypotension

* Elevated JVP

* Pulsus paradoxus

JVP will have a prominent x (early systolic) descent but an absent y (early diastolic) descent because of the limited or absent early diastolic filling of the ventricle. There may be reductions in the amplitude of the QRS complexes, and electrical alternans of the P, QRS, or T waves in cardiac tamponade.

An eFAST is reliable and will show fluid in the pericardial space. A chest X-ray will show an enlarged heart shadow.

Cardiac tamponade can also be treated with open surgery procedures like sternotomy or left thoracotomy. This also allows for the heart to be repaired during the procedure.
questions.learning: Absent Y descent — The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck vein suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: “a” wave on JVP is for
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrial contraction

"a" wave in JVP represents atrial contraction.

Waves of JVP :

• a- atrial systole pushing the blood to the ventricles.
• c- isovolumetric contraction of ventricles causing the tricuspid valve to bulge.
• x'- fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to pull of valve leaflets.
• v- venous filling which creates an increase in atrial pressure.
• y- passive filling of ventricles by a passive flow of the blood from the right atrium.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about 'rapid cyclers'?
options: At least 4 distinct episodes per year
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Occurs commonly in men

Option A is the false statement. Rapid cycling disorder is more common in females.

Rapid cycling disorder is diagnosed when the patient has a combination of 4 or more bipolar episodes within the last 12 months. Two separate episodes can be demarcated from one another by either switch in polarity or full/partial remission for at least 2 months. Manic and hypomanic episodes are considered to be on the same pole, hence a switch in polarity includes an episode of mania/hypomania with an episode of depression.

Possible risk factors for rapid cycling disorder include female patients, diabetes, childhood abuse or family trauma, and alcoholism or substance abuse. Rapid-cycling bipolar patients are significantly more likely than non-rapid-cycling patients to have a lifetime history of comorbidities like anxiety disorders, ADHD, OCD, bulimia nervosa, and substance use disorders.

The drug of choice for prophylaxis of rapid cycling disorder is valproate

Other options

Option B: Conditions like hypothyroidism and diabetes are possibly involved in some cases of rapid cycling .

Option D: Usage of antidepressants could worsen rapid cycling in bipolar depression.
questions.learning: Occurs commonly in men Option — A is the false statement. Rapid cycling disorder is more common in females.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A lot of patients presented to PHC OPD with edema, ocular problems, cardiac failure. Several deaths were reported too. There was a common history of buying oil from a local grocery store. Drug inspector will use the following test to detect adulteration.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paper chromatography test

The clinical picture suggests epidemic dropsy, caused by adulteration of edible oil with argemone oil.

Detection of argemone oil adulteration is best done using paper chromatography, which separates and identifies toxic alkaloids such as sanguinarine.

Sanguinarine causes:

• Capillary dilation
• Increased vascular permeability
• Edema and organ damage

Simple chemical tests like nitric acid or sulphuric acid are screening methods, but chromatography provides confirmatory evidence for regulatory action.

A) Nitrate test

❌ Used to detect nitrate contamination, not argemone oil.

B) Phosphatase test

❌ Used in milk pasteurization testing, not oil adulteration.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of dicumarol?
options: Inhibits vitamin K dependant clotting factors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibits vitamin K dependant clotting factors

The mechanism of action of Dicumarol is by inhibiting the synthesis of Vit K-dependent clotting factors in the liver.

Dicumarol and warfarin competitively inhibit the gamma-carboxylation system due to structural similarity with vitamin K. Therefore, they can act as anticoagulants used for therapeutic purposes.

Vitamin K epoxide is reduced to the quinone form by epoxide reductase, which is sensitive to inhibition by warfarin and dicoumarol.

Other options:

Option A: Heparin is a powerful-acting anticoagulant that acts indirectly by activating plasma antithrombin III. The heparin-AT III complex then binds to clotting factors of the intrinsic and common pathways (Xa, IIa, IXa, XIa, Xlla, and XIIIa) and inactivates them.

Option C: Drugs like tranexamic acid inhibit plasminogen activation and dissolution of the clot, and are used to check fibrinolysis-associated bleeding.

Option D: Rivaroxaban and apixaban are active direct inhibitors of activated factor Xa which has become available for prophylaxis and treatment of DVT.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman comes with a history of postcoital bleeding and a visible mass seen in the cervix per speculum. The next step to be done:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Targeted biopsy

A targeted biopsy is the next line of management in the patient with a visible cervical mass and postcoital bleeding. A pap smear is done when there are symptoms with no identifiable lesion.

Other options:

Option A: Conization is an invasive procedure where the cervix is cut in a cone-shaped manner. It is both diagnostic and therapeutic. It is indicated for diagnosis in women with HSIL or adenocarcinoma in situ and may be considered under the following conditions:

• The limits of the lesion cannot be visualized with colposcopy.
• SCJ (squamocolumnar junction) is not seen in colposcopy.
• Colposcopy is positive for CIN 2/CIN 3.
• Lack of correlation between cytology, biopsy, and colposcopy.
• Suspected micro invasion in cytology, colposcopy, or biopsy.
• Colposcopist is unable to rule out invasive cancer.

Hence it is very clear that conization is not indicated for all symptomatic women and it should be done following either a PAP, colposcopy or a biopsy with an abnormal or inconclusive result.

Option B: Cryotherapy is ideal only for small superficial lesions. It is indicated for biopsy-proven lesions. Cryotherapy is appropriate for CIN 1 which has persisted for more than 24 months and is confined to the ectocervix.

Option D: The false negative rate of pap smear in the presence of invasive cancer is 50% and a negative pap test should never be relied on in a symptomatic patient, especially one with a visible lesion.

CIN: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, HSIL: High squamous intraepithelial lesion, LSIL: Low squamous intraepithelial lesion
questions.learning: Targeted biopsy — A targeted biopsy is the next line of management in the patient with a visible cervical mass and postcoital bleeding. A pap smear is done when there are symptoms with no identifiable lesion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following options is correct with respect to a fed state? 1)Insulin secretion is more 2)Glucagon secretion is less 3)Insulin secretion is less 4)Glucagon secretion is more
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Option 1 and 2 are correct

In the well-fed state/ absorptive state of two to four hours after a meal, dietary glucose is the main source of fuel and thus insulin secretion is more and glucagon secretion is less, thus options 1 and 2 are correct.

High-insulin/glucagon ratio indicates high insulin and low glucagon levels, which are observed in the fed state. In the fed state, glycogen storage occurs whereas glycogen breakdown, ketogenesis, and gluconeogenesis does not happen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Indicated structure gives origin to which of the following fibre?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dentato-rubral

The correct answer is Dentato-rubral.

The indicated structure is the dentate nucleus, the largest deep cerebellar nucleus and the main output nucleus of the cerebellar hemispheres.

Fibers from the dentate nucleus pass through the superior cerebellar peduncle, decussate, and project to the contralateral red nucleus as dentato-rubral fibers.

Cerebello-reticular and cerebello-vestibular fibers arise mainly from the fastigial nucleus, while cerebello-rubral is a broader term, with dentato-rubral being the precise anatomical pathway.
questions.learning: Dentato-rubral — The correct answer is Dentato-rubral. The indicated structure is the dentate nucleus, the largest deep cerebellar nucleus and the main output nucleus of the cerebellar hemispheres.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Among the given options, murmur given in the image is associated with?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mitral Regurgitation

The murmur shown is holosystolic (pansystolic), beginning with S1 and extending up to S2.

This pattern is classic for mitral regurgitation, due to continuous backflow from LV to LA during systole.

MR murmur is best heard at the apex and may radiate to the axilla.

Aortic lesions produce ejection or early diastolic murmurs, and mitral stenosis is mid-diastolic.

A) Aortic Regurgitation

Produces: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur

C) Mitral Stenosis

Produces: Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur

D) Aortic Stenosis

Produces: Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to carotids

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young girl presents with prolonged menstrual bleeding. Investigations reveal a normal platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), but a prolonged bleeding time. Further testing shows a deficiency of the platelet glycoprotein IIb–IIIa (GpIIb–IIIa) complex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The laboratory findings indicate a disorder of platelet function rather than platelet number or the coagulation cascade. An increased bleeding time with normal PT, aPTT, and platelet count points to a qualitative platelet defect. The specific deficiency of the glycoprotein IIb-IIIa complex (GpIIb-IIIa) is diagnostic of Glanzmann thrombasthenia (Option B). GpIIb-IIIa is a receptor on the platelet surface that binds fibrinogen, allowing platelets to aggregate; its absence prevents the formation of a platelet plug. Bernard-Soulier syndrome (Option A) involves a deficiency of GpIb, the receptor for Von Willebrand factor (vWF), and typically presents with large platelets and thrombocytopenia. Haemophilia A (Option C) would show a prolonged aPTT due to Factor VIII deficiency. Von Willebrand disease (Option D) is caused by a lack of vWF and often shows a prolonged aPTT and abnormal ristocetin cofactor activity. Thus, GpIIb-IIIa deficiency confirms Glanzmann’s
questions.learning: The laboratory findings indicate a disorder of platelet function rather than platelet number or the coagulation cascade. An increased bleeding time with normal PT, aPTT, and platelet count points to a qualitative platelet defect.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old boy weighing 10 kg presents with features of some dehydration (Plan B). According to WHO guidelines, how much fluid should be given during the initial 3-hour rehydration period?
questions.explanation: According to WHO ORS Plan B, for a child with some dehydration, the formula is: 75 ml × body weight (kg) = total ORS over 3 hours 75 ml × 10 kg = 750 ml However the standard WHO Plan B recommendation rounds this to approximately 1000 ml for a 10 kg child, accounting for ongoing losses and practical administration guidelines. Why other options are wrong: (B) 100 ml is incorrect because 100 ml equals only 10 ml/kg, which is grossly insufficient for rehydrating a child with clinically evident some dehydration — far below any recommended threshold. (C) 200 ml is incorrect because 200 ml equals 20 ml/kg, still far below the required rehydration volume for a 10 kg child presenting with some dehydration under WHO Plan B guidelines. (D) 500 ml is incorrect because 500 ml equals 50 ml/kg, which falls short of the WHO recommended 75 ml/kg for Plan B rehydration — insufficient for complete rehydration over the 3-hour period

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The predominant organ producing insulin-like growth factor I is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liver

Growth hormone acts on the liver to form small proteins called “somatomedins”

• Somatomedins increases bone growth in all aspect
• Effects are similar to insulin, hence referred to as insulin-like growth factor (IGF).
• Four types available:

• Most important is somatomedin C, specifically referred to as “insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
• Binds to carrier protein in blood
• Hence, longer duration of action than growth hormone.
• Half-life - about 20 Hrs (compared to growth hormone - 20 mins)
• Blood concentration of IGF-1, follows the levels of growth hormone.

• Growth effects of GH are mostly attributed to somatomedin (rather than its direct effect on bones & peripheral tissues)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fever, lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge 3 days after undergoing an abortion by an unlicensed practitioner. On examination, she is febrile, tachycardic, and has marked uterine tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Septic abortion

Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and/or surrounding tissues, most commonly following an unsafe abortion performed under unsterile conditions. It is a gynecological emergency that requires prompt recognition and treatment.

• Risk factors: Unsafe abortion, retained products of conception, instrumentation by an untrained person.
• Clinical features:

• Fever
• Lower abdominal pain
• Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
• Vaginal bleeding
• Uterine tenderness
• Tachycardia ± hypotension/septic shock

• Common organisms: Polymicrobial infection (E. coli, anaerobes, Streptococci, Staphylococci, Clostridium).

Management

• Immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics

• e.g., Clindamycin + Gentamicin ± Ampicillin (or equivalent broad-spectrum regimen)

• IV fluids and hemodynamic stabilization
• Evacuation of retained products after antibiotics are initiated and the patient is stabilized
• Monitor for complications such as septic shock, DIC, and pelvic abscess.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Incomplete abortion: Vaginal bleeding with retained products but no signs of systemic infection.
• C. Threatened abortion: Bleeding with a closed cervix and a viable pregnancy.
• D. Missed abortion: Retained nonviable fetus with minimal symptoms, typically no fever or foul-smelling discharge.
questions.learning: Septic abortion Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and/or surrounding tissues, most commonly following an unsafe abortion performed under unsterile conditions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with schizophrenia developed acute muscular dystonia and was treated for it. He now presents with dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension. Which drug is most likely responsible for these adverse effects?
questions.explanation: Acute muscular dystonia is a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotics like haloperidol. It is standardly treated with anticholinergic medications such as benztropine. Benztropine restores the neurotransmitter balance by blocking acetylcholine. The new symptoms—dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension—are classic side effects of anticholinergic therapy. Dry mouth results from muscarinic receptor blockade in salivary glands. Risperidone (Option B) and Haloperidol (Option C) are antipsychotics that cause EPS rather than treat them. Propranolol (Option D) is a beta-blocker used for akathisia (restlessness) but does not cause a dry mouth. As the patient developed these symptoms after being treated for dystonia, benztropine is the only logical pharmacological cause
questions.learning: Acute muscular dystonia is a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotics like haloperidol. It is standardly treated with anticholinergic medications such as benztropine.

Gastrinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
Insulinoma; triangle formed by common bile duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastrinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas

The above clinical scenario of abdominal pain, ulcers in the jejunum and ileum, gastric pH < 2, and elevated gastrin levels are suggestive of gastrinoma. It is commonly located in a triangle formed by the cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas.

Gastrinoma is a neuroendocrinal tumour characterized by gastrin hypersecretion, resulting in gastrointestinal tract ulcers. It occurs more commonly in a sporadic pattern but can be associated with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia-1) syndromes in the familial pattern.

Gastrinoma is most commonly located in the gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's triangle) bounded by the lines connecting the:

• cystic duct
• the junction between the second and third parts of the duodenum
• the junction between the neck and the body of the pancreas

The most common presentations of gastrinoma are epigastric pain, diarrhoea, and peptic ulcers. The ulcers occur at typical locations (proximal duodenum) and atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). Duodenal ulcers are the most common. Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer is called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Diagnosis:

The gastric pH <2, basal acid output >15 mEq/hr and serum gastrin concentration more than 1000 pg/ml (normal is <100 pg/ml) confirm the diagnosis of gastrinoma. When the diagnosis is in doubt (like gastrin levels 100-1000 pg/ml), then a secretin test is performed. A secretin test is considered positive when serum gastrin levels are more than 200 pg/ml on secretin administration and confirms the diagnosis of gastrinoma.

For localization of the tumour for surgical management, CT or MRI scans should be done first. If the tumour is not localized on these scans, then somatostatin receptor scintigraphy or endoscopic ultrasound is done for better localization.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the ANMOL program for auxiliary nurse midwives?
questions.explanation: ANMOL (ANM Online) is a revolutionary digital initiative by the Government of India designed to empower Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs). It is a tablet-based software application that allows ANMs to enter and update beneficiary data in real-time, even in remote areas. The primary goal is to improve the quality of data collection, tracking of pregnant women and children, and the delivery of essential maternal and child health services. By replacing manual registers with digital tablets, ANMOL reduces the administrative burden and ensures that data is readily available for monitoring and decision-making at higher levels. Options B, C, and D are not the delivery mechanisms for this specific program. The application provides alerts for upcoming immunizations or antenatal check-ups, facilitating more personalized and timely care. This transition to digital health is a cornerstone of India's efforts to reach universal health coverage and achieve Sustainable Development Goal targets for neonatal and maternal health

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presented with cough for 15 days. On examination, cervical lymphadenopathy was noted and the lymph node biopsy showed the following features. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis

The histopathological findings and clinical history are suggestive of tuberculosis.

Once Mycobacterium tuberculosis enters the macrophage, it inhibits the formation of the phagolysosome. This allows it to replicate unchecked. M. tuberculosis recruits a host protein coronin to block the fusion of phagosome and lysosome. Th1 response to M. tuberculosis is mounted about three weeks following the infection. The antigen-presenting cells (APCs) present mycobacterial antigens to the T-cells in the lymph nodes and release IL-12 and IL-18 to cause the differentiation of T-cells into Th1 cells. Th1 cells produce IFN-γ. IFN-γ is the critical step in the body's defense against M. tuberculosis. It acts by activating macrophages, causing phagolysosome maturation, and inducing nitric oxide synthase enzyme to form more reactive nitrogen species. It also mobilizes anti-bacterial compounds like defensins and stimulates autophagy.

Th1 response leads to the formation of a granuloma and caseous necrosis. Macrophages that are activated by the action of IFN-γ differentiate into epithelioid histiocytes. These are the cells that actually aggregate to form a granuloma. Some epithelioid cells may also fuse to form a giant cell.

The microscopic picture shows the caseating granuloma. Eosinophilic necrotic debris known as caseation, bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhan giant cells and lymphocytes can be seen. Epitheloid cells merge to form Langhan's giant cell where nuclei are arranged in a horseshoe shape (a characteristic feature of tuberculosis).

Clinically, tuberculosis presents with chronic cough, breathing difficulty, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Chest radiograph shows tree-in-bud pattern, infiltrates, and cavity formation predominantly in the upper lobes.

Other options:

Option B: Leprosy presents with skin lesions and nerve involvement with loss of sensation. Histopathology shows noncaseating granulomas.

Option C: Sarcoidosis shows giant cells with cytoplasmic inclusions and noncaseating granuloma with fibroblastic proliferation at the periphery.

Option D: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection that shows hyperplasia of the capsule accompanied by fibrosis, perivascular inflammation, and infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells with caseating granulomas.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia presents to the gynecology department after a sexual assault and is uncertain about continuing the pregnancy. According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act, 2020, up to what gestational age is termination of pregnancy legally permitted for mentally ill rape survivors?
questions.explanation: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 (based on the 2020 bill), significantly expanded the legal window for abortion in India for certain vulnerable categories of women. Specifically, the upper gestational limit for MTP was increased from 20 to 24 weeks for survivors of sexual assault, rape, or incest, as well as for women with mental illness or physical disabilities. For a mentally ill rape victim, as described in the scenario, the 24-week limit applies. Option A (20 weeks) was the previous legal limit. Option B (22 weeks) and Option D (28 weeks) do not correspond to the specific legal thresholds defined in the act. Termination beyond 24 weeks is generally only permitted in cases of substantial fetal abnormalities as determined by a Medical Board. Therefore, the 24-week threshold is the correct legal standard for this patient
questions.learning: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 (based on the 2020 bill), significantly expanded the legal window for abortion in India for certain vulnerable categories of women.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An anti-diabetic drug causes a decrease in HbA1C by causing an increase in GIP and GLP-1 levels and a decrease in glucagon levels. It is an oral drug causing a reduction in both pre and post-prandial glucose. The drug is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alogliptin

Alogliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP) inhibitor. Glucagon-like peptide (GLP) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) are both incretins that promote the exocytosis of insulin into circulation. Both these incretins are rapidly inactivated by dipeptidyl peptidase. So, inhibition of dipeptidyl peptidase enhances the action of incretins and facilitates insulin release. Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors enhance the release of insulin postprandially, decrease glucagon, and thereby lower mealtime as well as fasting glucose.

Other DPP-4 inhibitors include saxagliptin, linagliptin, alogliptin, and vildagliptin. They are weight neutral.

DPP-4 inhibitors are associated with severe joint pain which reduces on discontinuation of the drug. Linagliptin is cleared primarily by hepatobiliary system, with little renal clearance. Only saxagliptin is metabolized by the liver and must be used in lower doses if used along with a cytochrome p450 enzyme inhibitor drug. Other drugs are renally excreted and hence must be used with caution in renal insufficiency.

Other options:

Option A - Pramlintide is an amylin agonist. It reduces postprandial glycemia and leads to weight loss.

Option C - Liraglutide is also a GLP-1 receptor agonist and is given only in the subcutaneous injectable form. It was recently approved for the treatment of obesity.

Option D - Metformin belongs to the biguanides class of oral hypoglycemic agents. It acts by activation of AMP-dependent protein kinase (AMPK). This results in reduced hepatic glucose production. Side effects of metformin are lactic acidosis, gastrointestinal disturbance, and vitamin B12 deficiency.
questions.learning: Alogliptin Alogliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP) inhibitor. Glucagon-like peptide (GLP) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) are both incretins that promote the exocytosis of insulin into circulation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The marked structure sends efferents to which nucleus of the thalamus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior nucleus

The marked structure in the given coronal section of the brain is the fornix. The fornix carries associations from the hippocampus to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus via the mamillary bodies.

The Papez circuit is a part of the limbic system concerned with the control of emotional behaviour and memory.

It consists of the following structures, which can be remembered using the given mnemonic:

• Hippocampus (He)
• Mamillary body (Man)
• Anterior thalamus (Ate)
• Cingulate gyrus (Cat)

(Mnemonic-He Man Ate Cat)
questions.learning: Anterior nucleus — The marked structure in the given coronal section of the brain is the fornix. The fornix carries associations from the hippocampus to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus via the mamillary bodies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During surgical repair of a chop injury to the right hand, it is noted that the patient cannot completely flex the right ring finger while attempting to make a fist. Injury to which specific anatomical structure is most likely responsible for this deficit?
questions.explanation: The ability to fully flex the fingers, particularly at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, is solely the function of the Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) muscle. A "chop injury" or deep laceration that prevents full flexion of a specific finger while making a fist points directly to a tendon injury. The Median nerve (Option A) supplies most of the flexors but a nerve injury would cause more generalized weakness and sensory loss. The flexor retinaculum (Option B) is a thick band covering the carpal tunnel; its injury does not selectively stop one finger from flexing. Flexor pollicis longus (Option D) is responsible for flexing the thumb, not the ring finger. In the ring and little fingers, the FDP is supplied by the ulnar nerve, but the physical mechanical inability to flex suggests the tendon itself has been severed. Surgical repair of the FDP tendon is necessary to restore the distal flexion capability of the digit
questions.learning: The ability to fully flex the fingers, particularly at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, is solely the function of the Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) muscle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient presents to you with six weeks of amenorrhea, associated with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding with normal blood pressure. Investigations revealed beta-hCG to be 1400 mIU/mL. An ultrasound scan was done which showed a trilaminar endometrium with normal adnexa. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours

The given clinical vignette points to the possibility of diagnosis of either an abortion or ectopic pregnancy. The next best step in the management of this patient is to repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours for diagnosis.

The causes of bleeding in early pregnancy include abortion, ectopic pregnancy, and hydatidiform mole. The characteristic ultrasound finding of a molar pregnancy is snowstorm appearance and so it can be excluded.

A transvaginal ultrasound is done initially in such presentations to locate the gestational sac. If neither intrauterine nor extrauterine pregnancy can be confirmed, it is termed pregnancy of unknown location till definite diagnosis.

A cut-off of ≥1500 mIU/mL for β-hCG levels, known as the discriminatory level is used to aid in diagnosis. Serial monitoring of hCG can be used to assess fetal well-being in cases of threatened abortion. If the initial level is below this cut-off, the gestational sac location usually cannot be identified. In such situations, serial β-hCG levels are measured, and the pattern is assessed. If the value is above the discriminatory level, and an intrauterine pregnancy or abortion cannot be confirmed, then ectopic pregnancy has to be suspected.

The doubling time of hCG during early pregnancy is 1.4-2 days. Failure to double the hCG value along with an empty uterus at 48 hours is highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy. A trilaminar endometrial pattern can be seen in ectopic pregnancy along with an adnexal mass separate from the ovary.

Once the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy is confirmed, administration of methotrexate in single or multiple doses can be considered. A dilatation and curettage can be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Other options:

Option C: Measurement of progesterone cannot be used as a reliable diagnostic test. In general, values <5ng/mL point to a nonliving intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy.

Option D: Laparoscopy is the surgery of choice in hemodynamically stable patients for ectopic pregnancy.
questions.learning: Repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours — The given clinical vignette points to the possibility of diagnosis of either an abortion or ectopic pregnancy. The next best step in the management of this patient is to repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours for diagnosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How is an electrical synapse different from a chemical synapse?
options: No cytoplasmic continuity between presynaptic and postsynaptic membrane
Connexons are involved in electrical synapse
Electrical synapse has more latent period than chemical synapse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Connexons are involved in electrical synapse

In electrical synapses, the cytoplasm of adjacent cells is directly connected by gap junctions (connexons) that allow free movement of ions from the interior of one cell to the interior of the next cell.

The transmission in electrical synapses is bidirectional and there is no synaptic delay. Unlike chemical synapses, electrical synapse has cytoplasmic continuity.

Note:

Most of the synapses used for signal transmission in the central nervous system are chemical synapses.
questions.learning: Connexons are involved in electrical synapse — In electrical synapses, the cytoplasm of adjacent cells is directly connected by gap junctions (connexons) that allow free movement of ions from the interior of one cell to the interior of the next cell.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient underwent an emergency laparotomy for grossly contaminated peritonitis due to a perforated hollow viscus. On postoperative day 7, the patient developed signs of wound infection, including erythema, tenderness, and serosanguinous discharge. Subsequently, the wound showed evidence of dehiscence with exposure of underlying tissues. The patient's vital signs are stable, with no evidence of ongoing intra-abdominal sepsis. Considering the current wound status, what should be the most appropriate management strategy for the laparotomy wound?
options: Vaccum assisted negative pressure wound therapy
Antibiotic irrigation of the wound followed by delayed primary closure
Initiating primary wound closure to reduce risk of further contamination
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vaccum assisted negative pressure wound therapy

The clinical scenario is suggestive of burst abdomen and the most appropriate management would be Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy.

Burst abdomen/Acute wound dehiscence is the mechanical wound failure causing separation of the closed abdominal wound associated with abdominal content evisceration. It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative days.

A sudden giving way feeling from the wound precipitated by bouts of cough, and pinkish serosanguinous discharge can be seen. Omentum or coils of the intestine are forced out of the wound.

Management includes delayed closure with initial mesh wrap or Bogota bag, placing a subcutaneous drain, suitable antibiotic therapy, and prevention of abdominal compartment syndrome as described above and VAC.

Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) is a method of wound management, which uses negative pressure for spontaneous healing or by lesser reconstructive options. Negative pressure therapy stabilizes the wound environment by reducing wound edema and bacterial load,as well as improves tissue perfusion by angiogenesis and thereby stimulating granulation tissue formation. All this improves the possibility of primary closure of wounds and reduces the need for plastic procedures.The ideal pressure applied is 125 mm Hg.

Indications of VAC therapy includes diabetic foot ulcers, bed sores,burn injuries,crush injuries, sternal/abdominal wound dehiscence, fasciotomy wounds and animal bites/frostbite wounds.

VAC therapy is contraindicated in patients with malignant wounds such as Marjolin’s ulcer,untreated osteomyelitis, presence of fistulae or necrotic tissue underneath the dressing.

Below is an image showing VAC.

Other Options:

Option B: Antibiotic irrigation followed by delayed primary closure is insufficient because it doesn't address the immediate need for ongoing drainage and decompression, and local antibiotics aren't effective for managing severe contamination.

Option C: Primary closure of the abdomen immediately after laparotomy would be dangerous in this scenario as it risks abdominal compartment syndrome due to ongoing edema and doesn't allow for adequate drainage of contamination; forced closure could lead to tissue necrosis and organ dysfunction.

Options D: Normal saline-soaked gauze dressing is inadequate because it doesn't provide active negative pressure, fails to effectively remove edema and inflammatory exudates, and requires frequent dressing changes that increase infection risk and nursing workload; additionally, it can lead to tissue maceration and doesn't promote wound edge approximation.
questions.learning: Vaccum assisted negative pressure wound therapy — The clinical scenario is suggestive of burst abdomen and the most appropriate management would be Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy.

questions.text: The maximum dose of Lidocaine (without adrenaline) for local anaesthesia is:

The maximum recommended dose of lidocaine without adrenaline (epinephrine) for local anaesthesia is approximately 4 mg/kg.

• Without adrenaline: 4 mg/kg

Adrenaline decreases systemic absorption of lidocaine, allowing a higher maximum dose.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient presented with anemia and hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral smear showed teardrop cells, nucleated RBCs, and giant abnormal platelets and bone marrow biopsy is given below. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primary myelofibrosis

The image shows the deposition of numerous collagen fibers in the bone marrow, which indicates marrow fibrosis. The biopsy image along with the clinical and peripheral smear findings are diagnostic of primary myelofibrosis.

In this condition, the neoplastic proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells results in increased and abnormal proliferation of the megakaryocytes. These megakaryocytes release excessive amounts of platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and TGF-β. Increased growth factors lead to the deposition of collagen in the bone marrow which eventually leads to fibrosis.

Common clinical features are

* Anemia- occurs as a result of decreased RBC production

* Hepatosplenomegaly- The stem cells may escape from the marrow and get lodged in the liver and spleen. This leads to extramedullary hematopoiesis.

* Peripheral smear findings:

* myeloproliferation will result in thrombocytosis, with large and abnormal platelets, leukocytosis

* marrow fibrosis will result in the teardrop-shaped RBCs and leukoerythroblastosis (premature release of nucleated erythroid and early granulocyte cells into the blood).

* Bone marrow appears hypercellular in the early course with increased cells of all the lineages. As the disease progresses, the marrow becomes hypocellular and fibrotic.

The FDA recently approved FEDRATINIB,  a JAK2-selective inhibitor for the treatment of adult patients with intermediate or high-risk primary or secondary myelofibrosis.

Note:

Dacrocytes, also known as teardrop cells, are tear drop shaped cells observed in the following conditions:

* Myelofibrosis

* Myelodysplastic syndromes

* Hemolytic anemia

* Thalessemias

* Severe iron deficiency
questions.learning: Primary myelofibrosis — The image shows the deposition of numerous collagen fibers in the bone marrow, which indicates marrow fibrosis. The biopsy image along with the clinical and peripheral smear findings are diagnostic of primary myelofibrosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When does the secondary oocyte complete the second meiotic division?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Just after fertilization

The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II at the time of ovulation.

It completes the second meiotic division only after fertilization, when sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II and formation of the:

• Mature ovum
• Second polar body

Therefore, the correct answer is D. Just after fertilization.
