questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents with the development of seizures for which a CT-guided biopsy was done. The histopathology showed the presence of ‘psammoma bodies’. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meningioma

The clinical vignette and the histopathology showing a tumor with meningothelial whorls, syncytial cells with indistinct cell membranes, and psammoma bodies suggest the diagnosis of meningioma.

Meningioma: They are predominantly benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura, that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid.

* Meningiomas may be found along any of the external surfaces of the brain as well as within the ventricular system, where they arise from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus.

* Prior radiation therapy to the head and neck, typically is a risk factor.

* The most common cytogenetic abnormality is the loss of chromosome 22, especially the long arm (22q).

* Meningiomas are a common lesion in the setting of NF2 (multiple sites, especially in association with acoustic neuromas or glial tumors.

* The surface of the mass is usually encapsulated.

* They may also grow en plaque, in which the tumor spreads in a sheetlike fashion along the surface of the dura. This form is commonly associated with hyperostotic reactive changes in the adjacent bone.

* The lesions may contain numerous calcified psammoma bodies.

Histological subtypes:

* WHO Grade I – Menigothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcystic

* WHO Grade II- Clear cell, choroid, atypical

* Grade III – Papillary, rhabdoid, anaplastic

* Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade II/IV) - a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive local growth

* Anaplastic (malignant) meningioma (WHO grade III/IV) - highly aggressive tumor with the appearance of a high-grade sarcoma

* Immunoreactive for epithelial membrane antigen

* Keratin is restricted to lesions with the secretory pattern, and these tumors are also positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

* Moderate (3: 2) female predominance, usually solitary, but when present at multiple sites, the possibility of neurofibromatosis type 2 should be considered.

* Meningiomas often express progesterone receptors and may grow more rapidly during pregnancy.
questions.learning: Meningioma — The clinical vignette and the histopathology showing a tumor with meningothelial whorls, syncytial cells with indistinct cell membranes, and psammoma bodies suggest the diagnosis of meningioma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents to the ER with a history of RTA. On examination, GCS is 15/15, heart rate = 110/min, BP = 90/60 mmHg, and there is elevated JVP. The right chest is hyperresonant on percussion with decreased breath sounds. The left chest appears normal. But the patient is dyspneic and ecchymosis is noted over the chest wall. The abdomen was soft. The probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tension pneumothorax

The given clinical scenario of trauma with decreased breath sounds and a hyper-resonant note on percussion indicates pneumothorax. The presence of tachycardia, hypotension and elevated JVP is suggestive of tension pneumothorax.

Tension pneumothorax develops when there is a parietal or visceral pleural tear. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e. air enters the pleural space from the lung or chest wall during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration, leading to the collapse of the affected lung.

It is characterized by chest pain, tachypnoea, acute dyspnea, sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness), neck vein distention, tracheal deviation away from the side of injury, decreased chest movements on the affected side, hyper-resonance on percussion on the affected side and absent or decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed awaiting radiological confirmation.

Management includes:

• Immediate management: Needle decompression or needle thoracostomy with a wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line. In the pediatric age group, the needle thoracostomy location is at the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.
• Definitive management: Tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th intercostal space in the triangle of safety.

The triangle of safety is bounded anteriorly by the lateral border of the pectoralis major, posteriorly by latissmus dorsi and inferiorly by a horizontal line at the level of the nipple.

The X-ray below shows a left-sided tension pneumothorax. There is a large, well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side. The yellow arrows are pointing to the tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side.

Other options:

Options A:  Pericardial tamponade can mimic tension pneumothorax, but the absence of a tympanic note on percussion rules out its possibility. A patient with pericardial tamponade can present with hypotension, raised JVP, and muffled heart sounds (Beck’s triad), with normal breath sounds and no tracheal shift.

Option C: Dullness in percussion at the base of the left inferior angle of scapula in conjunction with tubular breath sounds (Ewart’s sign), chest pain that improves while sitting upright and worsens when lying down and pulsus paradoxus are indicative of pericardial effusion. Pericardial effusion develops into tamponade when the effusion leads to increased pressure, impairing ventricular filling and reducing cardiac output.

Option D: Massive hemothorax is the accumulation of >1500 ml of blood or one-third or more of the patient’s blood volume in the chest cavity. The patient will have collapsed neck veins, decreased breath sounds and a dull note on percussion.
questions.learning: Tension pneumothorax — The given clinical scenario of trauma with decreased breath sounds and a hyper-resonant note on percussion indicates pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All the following are properties of ventricular muscle fibers: 1. All or none law 2. Length-tension relation 3. Tetanus 4. Long refractory period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, and 4

All-or-None Law

• Cardiac muscle behaves as a functional syncytium
• Once threshold reached → entire ventricle contracts maximally
• No graded contraction like skeletal motor units

Length–Tension Relationship

• Preload ↑ → sarcomere length ↑ → force ↑
• Mechanism:

• Optimal actin-myosin overlap
• ↑ Ca²⁺ sensitivity of myofilaments

This is the Frank-Starling law: “The heart pumps what it receives”

Ventricular muscle behaves like a syncytium with unique electrical discipline.

It contracts as a unit, obeys Frank–Starling law, and absolutely refuses tetanus.

Cardiac action potential (with plateau)

↓

Prolonged Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels)

↓

Long absolute refractory period

↓

No re-excitation possible

↓

No summation → No tetanus

• Cardiac AP duration: \~200–300 ms
• Contraction duration: overlaps with refractory period

So:

• Second stimulus cannot trigger contraction
• Prevents sustained contraction (which would be fatal)

| Option | Property | Present in Ventricular Muscle? | Explanation

| ------ | -------- | ------------------------------ | -----------

| 1 | All-or-none law | ✅ YES | Entire myocardium contracts as a syncytium via gap junctions

| 2 | Length-tension relation | ✅ YES | Basis of Frank-Starling mechanism (↑ filling → ↑ force)

| 3 | Tetanus | ❌ NO | Prevented due to long refractory period

| 4 | Long refractory period | ✅ YES | Due to plateau phase (Ca²⁺ influx)
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 4 All-or-None Law • Cardiac muscle behaves as a functional syncytium • Once threshold reached → entire ventricle contracts maximally • No graded contraction like skeletal motor units Length–Tension Relationship • Preload ↑ → sarcomere length ↑ →…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme activity is measured to assess a deficiency of vitamin B₂ (riboflavin)?
questions.explanation: The activity of the enzyme erythrocyte glutathione reductase is the standard functional biomarker used to assess Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) status. This enzyme requires flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), which is derived from riboflavin, as an essential cofactor. In a state of deficiency, the enzyme's activity is significantly reduced; this can be measured by adding FAD to the assay and observing the degree of stimulation (the activity coefficient). Transketolase (Option A) is a thiamine-dependent enzyme used to assess Vitamin B1 status. Pyruvate dehydrogenase (Option B) and isocitrate dehydrogenase (Option D) are involved in central energy metabolism and utilize multiple cofactors, but they are not used as specific clinical diagnostic markers for isolated riboflavin deficiency in the same way. Therefore, measuring glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells is the definitive method for evaluating a patient for B2 deficiency
questions.learning: The activity of the enzyme erythrocyte glutathione reductase is the standard functional biomarker used to assess Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) status. This enzyme requires flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), which is derived from riboflavin, as an essential cofactor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), which enzyme deficiency is responsible for the condition?
questions.explanation: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare genetic disorders characterized by the total lack of T-cell function and impaired B-cell function. Approximately 15% of SCID cases follow an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern caused by a deficiency of the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). ADA is essential for the breakdown of purines; its absence leads to the accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine metabolites which are specifically lethal to developing lymphocytes. Ornithine transcarbamylase (Option A) is an enzyme in the urea cycle. Phosphomannose isomerase deficiency (Option B) leads to congenital disorders of glycosylation. HGPRT deficiency (Option D) results in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, characterized by gout and self-mutilation. ADA-SCID presents in early infancy with recurrent, severe opportunistic infections and failure to thrive. Because ADA is the hallmark enzyme deficiency associated with the autosomal recessive form of combined immunodeficiency, Option C is the correct answer
questions.learning: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare genetic disorders characterized by the total lack of T-cell function and impaired B-cell function.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following statements are true for descriptors of central tendency except:
options: Mode is affected by extreme values
Mean is affected by extreme values
Median is calculated by overall observation
Mode can be used as a qualitative data descriptor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mode is affected by extreme values

Mode is not affected by extreme values in a given set of data.

The mean of a given set of data is responsive to each and every value in the distribution. Thus, the mean is the measure of central tendency which is maximally affected by extreme values (option B). It is usually an inappropriate measure for describing skewed distributions. However, repeated samples from the same population will always tend to have similar means. Mean is able to resist fluctuations between different samples drawn from the same population better than mode or median.

To obtain the median of a given set of data, the values are first arranged in ascending or descending order of magnitude, and then the value of the middle observation is noted. Since the data has to be first arranged in order before the median can be determined, an overall observation is necessary for its calculation (option C).

Mode is the observed value in the frequency distribution that occurs with the greatest frequency. It is completely uninfluenced by extreme values in the distribution. The mode can be used to describe qualitative data (option D).
questions.learning: Mode is affected by extreme values Mode is not affected by extreme values in a given set of data. The mean of a given set of data is responsive to each and every value in the distribution.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The most important marker of male fertility in semen analysis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Morphology

Morphology of sperms is the most important marker of male fertility.

While sperm concentration and progressive motility have value for distinguishing infertile men, strict sperm morphology is the most important discriminating value compared toother parameters.
questions.learning: Morphology Morphology of sperms is the most important marker of male fertility. While sperm concentration and progressive motility have value for distinguishing infertile men, strict sperm morphology is the most important discriminating value compared…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis, palpable purpura, myalgia, and pulmonary hemorrhage was found to have p-ANCA positivity. Which of the following is the likely vasculitis in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microscopic polyangiitis

p-ANCA–positive pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with palpable purpura and pulmonary hemorrhage is characteristic of microscopic polyangiitis.

It is a non-granulomatous small-vessel vasculitis involving capillaries, venules, and arterioles.

Organ damage:

- Kidney → RPGN (crescentic GN)

- Lung → Pulmonary hemorrhage

- Skin → Purpura

| ANCA Type | Antigen | Disease Association

| --------- | ------- | -------------------

| p-ANCA /Microscopic polyangiitis | MPO (myeloperoxidase) | MPA, EGPA

| c-ANCA /Granulomatosis with polyangiitis | PR3 (proteinase-3) | GPA (Wegener)

| Feature | MPA | GPA | PAN

| ------- | --- | --- | ---

| Vessel size | Small | Small | Medium

| ANCA | p-ANCA (MPO) | c-ANCA (PR3) | Negative

| Granulomas | ❌ | ✔ | ❌

| Lung involvement | Hemorrhage | Nodules + cavitation | ❌

| Kidney | RPGN | RPGN | Mild

GPA is usually c-ANCA with granulomas, PAN spares lungs, and Behçet’s is not ANCA-associated.
questions.learning: Microscopic polyangiitis p-ANCA–positive pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with palpable purpura and pulmonary hemorrhage is characteristic of microscopic polyangiitis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with history of ischemic stroke was started on clopidogrel. However, she had another attack of stroke after 6 months. Which of the following is likely to be responsible for the failure of clopidogrel in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Downregulation of CYP2C19

Downregulation of CYP2C19 is responsible for the failure of clopidogrel in this patient.

Clopidogrel is a prodrug and its metabolic activation occurs in the liver. It is bioactivated by the CYP2C19 enzyme. If there is downregulation of this enzyme it will cause a decrease in the efficacy of clopidogrel and can lead to thrombotic events like stroke. Drugs that inhibit CYP2C19 can also decrease the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel. Proton-pump inhibitors may cause inhibition of CYP2C19 and when they are given in combination there would be a decrease in the efficacy of clopidogrel.

Therapeutic uses: Clopidogrel is used to reduce the rate of stroke and myocardial infarction. It also decreases the rate of deaths in patients with recent myocardial infarction or stroke. Other uses are acute coronary syndrome and peripheral arterial disease.

Adverse effects: Increased risk of bleeding especially when given with an anticoagulant or aspirin. Rarely thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura can occur.

CYP2C19: Common drugs that are metabolized include omeprazole, phenytoin, diazepam, and propanolol. Inducers of the CYP2C subfamily are rifampicin and carbamazepine. Omeprazole is an inhibitor.

Other options:

CYP2D6: Drugs metabolized include SSRIs,  tricyclic antidepressants, antiarrhythmic drugs, beta-blockers, and opiates. It is inhibited by quinidine and it will prevent the formation of morphine from codeine. Hence quinidine decreases the analgesic effect of codeine.

CYP1A1/2: It metabolizes few drugs like theophylline, paracetamol, caffeine and carbamazepine. It plays an important role in the activation of procarcinogens. Inducers are rifampicin, carbamazepine, polycyclic hydrocarbons, charbroiled meat, and cigarette smoke.

CYP2E1: It is involved in the oxidation of alcohol, halothane, and minor metabolism of other drugs. It is important to note that it is involved in the formation of hepatotoxic N-acetyl benzoquinone imine from paracetamol. Chronic alcoholism is responsible for the induction of this enzyme.
questions.learning: Downregulation of CYP2C19 Downregulation of CYP2C19 is responsible for the failure of clopidogrel in this patient. Clopidogrel is a prodrug and its metabolic activation occurs in the liver.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Craniopagus is defined as the fusion of ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Head only

Craniopagus is a type of conjoint twin where there is a fusion of the head or cranium.

Foramen magnum or the skull base never fuses in the case of craniopagus. They usually will have fused skulls and meninges. A shared cerebral cortex may occasionally be found.

Craniopagus has an incidence of 5%, and separation of the twins has a poor prognosis.

Dizygotic/fraternal twins result from the fertilization of two separate ova. Monozygotic/identical twins arise from the division of a single fertilized ovum. The outcome of the monozygotic twinning process depends on when division occurs.

Monozygotic types
Time of zygote division

Dichorionic diamniotic
<72 hours

Monochorionic diamniotic (more common)
4 to 8 days

Monochorionic monoamniotic
8 to 12 days

Conjoined twins
>12 days

Types of conjoined twins:

• Thoracopagus: united at the thorax
• Craniopagus: united at the head
• Cephalothoracopagus: fusion of both head and thorax
• Omphalopagous or xiphipagous: united anteriorly from the xiphoid to the umbilicus
• Parapagus: lateral fusion with two heads, sharing a single thorax, abdomen, and pelvis
• Ischiopagus: united at the pelvis
• Pygopagus: united in the sacral region
• Heteropagous: asymmetric forms

The image below shows the types of conjoined twins:
questions.learning: Head only Craniopagus is a type of conjoint twin where there is a fusion of the head or cranium. Foramen magnum or the skull base never fuses in the case of craniopagus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug can be used to treat both HIV and Hepatitis B?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir (available as TDF or TAF) is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that is highly effective against both the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and the Hepatitis B virus (HBV). It is a foundational component of modern antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV and is also considered a first-line treatment for chronic Hepatitis B due to its high potency and low risk of resistance. Lamivudine and Emtricitabine also cover both viruses, making them useful in co-infected patients. Dolutegravir (Option A) is a highly effective integrase inhibitor but only works against HIV. Zidovudine (Option C) is an older HIV medication with no activity against HBV. Ritonavir (Option D) is a protease inhibitor primarily used as a "booster" to increase the levels of other HIV drugs. In patients co-infected with HIV and HBV, it is essential to use a regimen that targets both viruses to prevent HBV "flares" if treatment is interrupted or the HBV develops resistance
questions.learning: Tenofovir (available as TDF or TAF) is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that is highly effective against both the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and the Hepatitis B virus (HBV).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young teenage boy with a history of drug abuse had been instilled with a shot of intravenous cocaine at a party. He is rushed to the emergency room by his friends. Some of the symptoms were diaphoresis, headache, and acute coronary spasm. Which of the following symptoms noted would go against the likely diagnosis of cocaine poisoning?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bradycardia

Cocaine intoxication presents with tachycardia and not bradycardia. Thus, the presence of bradycardia would go against the diagnosis of cocaine intoxication.

Cocaine is an alkaloid deliriant extracted from Erythroxylum coca.

Acute intoxication with cocaine leads to symptoms spanning 2 stages-

1. Stage of excitement/euphoria - associated with hypervigilance, anxiety, hyperactivity along with hyper-adrenergic signs of mydriasis, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, hyperthermia, and cardiac arrhythmias.
2. Stage of depression - associated with loss of reflexes, muscle paralysis, circulatory and respiratory failure, and coma.

Chronic intoxication is characterized by toxic delirium and tactile hallucination of bugs (cocaine bugs) or vermin crawling under the skin (formication).

Common complications include cerebrovascular accidents and myocardial ischemia.

Treatment includes intravenous diazepam for controlling seizures. For ventricular arrhythmias, propranolol may be given intravenously. If the patient has psychosis, haloperidol may be given. Treatment of chronic cocaine abuse requires psychiatric support.

Cocaine withdrawal is a triphasic syndrome that presents after the sudden stoppage of chronic cocaine use. The phases are as follows -

1. Crash phase (9 hours - 4 days): Anorexia, depression, excessive craving, hypersomnia, fatigue.
2. Normal mood, anxiety, and anhedonia (4 - 7 days)
3. Extinction phase (7 - 10 days): Absence of withdrawal symptoms but increased susceptibility to relapse.

Treatment for withdrawal includes bromocriptine and amantadine. They are useful in reducing cocaine craving.
questions.learning: Bradycardia Cocaine intoxication presents with tachycardia and not bradycardia. Thus, the presence of bradycardia would go against the diagnosis of cocaine intoxication.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is false regarding papillary thyroid cancer?
options: Most common age group is between 30- 50 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Calcitonin is the tumour marker

The wrong statement is option d. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma and not papillary carcinoma

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy with relatively good prognosis (option b) . It is more commonly seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50 (option a). Radiation exposure (option c) and a family history of thyroid malignancies are common etiologies. Genetic abnormalities in either the RET gene or the BRAF gene can be seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Clinical features include an asymptomatic thyroid swelling with cervical lymph node enlargement. In advanced disease, there may be features like hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.

An ultrasound scan accurately assesses the size and number of nodules, as well as categorizes the lesions as benign, indeterminate, or malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a diagnostic test, helpful in investigating an indeterminate or malignant lesion.

Histopathology shows the following features:

* Branching papillae

* Orphan Annie eye nuclei: optically clear nuclei with fine nuclear chromatin

* Pseudo inclusions: invaginations of the nuclear membrane

* Psammoma bodies: concentric calcifications in the core of the papillae.

Below is the histopathological image of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid with characteristic Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is known to spread via lymphatics, hence lymph node metastasis is commonly seen.

Treatment of Papillary thyroid carcinoma is as follows:

Total thyroidectomy is the treatment of choice. Routine central neck dissection is not recommended. Neck dissection is indicated in higher-risk situations, such as

* Tumor size > 4 cm (T3 stage) or gross extrathyroidal extension (T4 stage) or enlarged central lymph nodes - Total thyroidectomy + Central Neck Dissection

* Lateral Aberrant Thyroid - Total thyroidectomy + Modified Radical Neck Dissection + Central Neck Dissection

For occult papillary cancer (<1 cm tumor size, with no lymphatic, vascular or capsular invasion) - Lobectomy can be sufficient.

Radio-iodine ablation is undertaken when a whole-body iodine scan is positive after a total thyroidectomy for any differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary or follicular carcinoma).

The presence of any metastatic or residual thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy can be detected by observing the uptake of radio-iodine in the entire body. To achieve effective uptake of radio-iodine, TSH levels need to be greatly increased, for example, by withdrawing thyroxine after the surgery for 4-6 weeks.

A positive whole-body iodine scan after total thyroidectomy indicates that there is either a metastatic or residual disease present. These patients are treated with I131 for radio-iodine ablation.

A negative scan means there is no metastasis or residual thyroid tissue. They are followed up regularly with serum thyroglobulin, TSH and USG-neck.
questions.learning: Calcitonin is the tumour marker — The wrong statement is option d. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma and not papillary carcinoma Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy with relatively good prognosis (option b) .

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids is not formed after post-translational modification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Selenocysteine

Selenocysteine, the 21st amino acid, is formed by co-translational modification. It is coded by the UGA codon, which is normally a stop codon. The protein synthetic apparatus can identify a selenocysteine-encoding UGA by the presence of the selenocysteine insertion sequence (SECIS) in the untranslated region of mRNA.

Selenocysteine is an analog of cysteine and is synthesized from serine.

Selenocysteine is present at the active site of several human enzymes that catalyze redox reactions such as thioredoxin reductase, glutathione peroxidase, and deiodinase. Since Glutathione peroxidase contains selenocysteine and hence it is an antioxidant.

Impairments in human selenoproteins have been implicated in tumorigenesis and atherosclerosis and are associated with selenium deficiency cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease).
questions.learning: Selenocysteine Selenocysteine, the 21st amino acid, is formed by co-translational modification. It is coded by the UGA codon, which is normally a stop codon.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted to the ICU and is receiving oxygen at 2 L/min. Arterial blood gas analysis shows hypoventilation with a pH of 7.33 and a pCO₂ of 64 mmHg. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (PPV) should be given
Invasive positive pressure ventilation (PPV) should be given
Intubate and start on a ventilator
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD with acute respiratory acidosis (pH 7.33 and high ). For COPD patients with respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35), Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV), such as BiPAP, is the first-line intervention. NIPPV reduces the work of breathing, improves gas exchange, and significantly decreases the need for endotracheal intubation. Invasive ventilation (Option B and D) is reserved for patients who fail NIPPV or have contraindications like coma or severe hemodynamics. Increasing the oxygen flow rate (Option C) without providing ventilatory support can dangerously worsen hypercapnia in COPD patients by reducing their hypoxic respiratory drive. NIPPV should be initiated promptly while continuing medical therapies like bronchodilators and steroids. Successful management is indicated by an improvement in pH and a decrease in the within the first few hours
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD with acute respiratory acidosis (pH 7.33 and high ). For COPD patients with respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35), Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV), such as BiPAP, is the first-line…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. She is diagnosed with endometriosis and undergoes diagnostic laparoscopy, which reveals extensive pelvic adhesions, with the intestines adherent to the upper uterus and the ovaries fused together forming cystic masses. Following these findings, what should be the next appropriate step in her management?
options: Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge
questions.explanation: For a 30-year-old patient who wishes to conceive (infertility) but has extensive stage IV endometriosis, the goal of management is to restore normal pelvic anatomy and preserve fertility. The most appropriate subsequent course of action during laparoscopy is cystectomy of the ovarian endometriomas and extensive adhesiolysis (Option C). This procedure aims to free the ovaries and intestines and excise the cystic disease to improve the chances of spontaneous conception or success with assisted reproduction. LUNA (Option A) is an older procedure for pain that does not address fertility or adhesions. Gestrinone (Option B) is a medical therapy that suppresses the cycle but will not clear established adhesions or large cysts. Hysterectomy and oophorectomy (Option D) are "definitive" but radical treatments that would result in permanent surgical menopause and total loss of fertility, which is inappropriate for this young woman
questions.learning: For a 30-year-old patient who wishes to conceive (infertility) but has extensive stage IV endometriosis, the goal of management is to restore normal pelvic anatomy and preserve fertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the duration of abstinence post vasectomy?
questions.explanation: Post-vasectomy, a man is not considered sterile until all stored sperm in the reproductive tract are cleared. The standard medical advice is to use alternative contraception or practice abstinence for a duration of 3 months. This timeframe typically corresponds to roughly 20 ejaculations, which is the volume required to flush out remaining viable sperm. Confirmation of success must be obtained via a semen analysis showing zero sperm count before discontinuing protection. Options B (7 months), C (8 months), and D (5 months) are all significantly longer than the standard 12-week guideline. While individual clearance rates can vary, 3 months is the universally accepted clinical benchmark for initial follow-up testing. Relying on the procedure immediately after surgery can lead to unwanted pregnancy, making the 3-month buffer period critical for patient safety
questions.learning: Post-vasectomy, a man is not considered sterile until all stored sperm in the reproductive tract are cleared. The standard medical advice is to use alternative contraception or practice abstinence for a duration of 3 months.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with a 10-day history of severe knee pain and inflammation, along with dysuria. The patient also had diarrhea about a month ago, followed by malaise. Based on this clinical history, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of an asymmetric large joint arthritis (knee), urethritis (painful urination), and a preceding gastrointestinal infection (diarrhea 1 month ago) is pathognomonic for Reactive Arthritis (formerly Reiter’s syndrome) (Option A) . This is an HLA-B27 associated spondyloarthropathy where joints become inflamed as a sterile autoimmune response following a distant infection, often by Salmonella, Shigella, or Chlamydia. Enteropathic arthritis (Option B) is associated with active inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s/UC). Rheumatoid arthritis (Option C) is typically a symmetric, chronic polyarthritis of small joints. Psoriatic arthritis (Option D) involves skin lesions and dactylitis. Because the symptoms follow the classic "can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree" triad (though only eye/joint/urine are standard) and occur post-infection, Reactive Arthritis is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves NSAIDs and management of the trigger infection if still present
questions.learning: The combination of an asymmetric large joint arthritis (knee), urethritis (painful urination), and a preceding gastrointestinal infection (diarrhea 1 month ago) is pathognomonic for Reactive Arthritis (formerly Reiter’s syndrome) (Option A) .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most likely cause of irregular menstrual cycles in a 20-year-old woman, based on the ultrasound findings shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image displays an ovary with the characteristic "string of pearls" appearance—defined as 12 or more small follicles (2–9 mm in diameter) arranged peripherally around a dense echogenic stroma. This is the pathognomonic radiological finding for Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOD) or PCOS. Clinically, PCOD is the most common cause of irregular periods (oligomenorrhea) in young women. Obesity (Option B) and Hirsutism (Option C) are common features or comorbid conditions associated with PCOD, but they are not the primary underlying "cause" or the diagnosis itself based on the scan . Turner's syndrome (Option D) would show "streak ovaries" on ultrasound, indicating a total lack of follicles. The diagnosis of PCOS typically follows the Rotterdam criteria, requiring two of three features: polycystic ovaries on scan, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and ovulatory dysfunction. Thus, the visual of follicular carpeting confirms PCOD
questions.learning: The ultrasound image displays an ovary with the characteristic "string of pearls" appearance—defined as 12 or more small follicles (2–9 mm in diameter) arranged peripherally around a dense echogenic stroma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Least frequency of slow waves is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stomach

Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min).

The Basal electrical rhythm (BER) also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle. It is initiated by the interstitial cells of Cajal. The membrane potential fluctuates between -65mV and -45mV.

The BER is seen in all sites of gastrointestinal smooth muscle except in the esophagus and proximal stomach.

The rate of BER in various sites is as follows:

• Stomach: 4/min
• Duodenum: 12/min
• Distal ileum: 8/min
• Cecum: 2/min
• Sigmoid colon: 6/min

The BER does not cause contraction of the smooth muscle. However, when the BER is superimposed by the spike potentials, it increases muscle tension.

Acetylcholine causes an increase in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension. Epinephrine causes a decrease in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension.

Muscle contraction can occur only when the motor stimulus is provided during the depolarisation part of the BER.

Thus, BER does not cause muscle contraction by itself, but controls the rate and organization sites of the muscle contractions, as in coordination of the peristaltic activity and setting the rhythm of segmentation.
questions.learning: Stomach Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min). The Basal electrical rhythm (BER) also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A new drug is introduced into the market after which phase of the clinical trials?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phase III

A new drug is introduced into the market after phase III of the clinical trial.

Phase III of the clinical trial checks the efficacy and monitors the adverse reactions of a new drug and thus a new drug is introduced after this phase.

Phase II takes place over a short duration. During this period, the most prominent side effects are assessed. However, less common side effects might have gone undetected due to the shorter duration and smaller study group.

Phase III takes place over a longer duration and includes more population as compared to Phase II. Because these studies are larger and longer in duration, the results are more likely to show long-term or rare adverse effects. Hence, this phase is used to monitor adverse effects.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The bone marrow density along with the gestational age is plotted from two different studies. Which of the following is true for the relation between bone marrow density and gestational age?
options: Strength of correlation is same in A and B
Strength of the correlation is more in A than in B
Strength of the variation is more in B than A
Variation in variables is more with A than B
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strength of the correlation is more in A than in B

The strength of the correlation is more in graph A than in graph B.

Graphs A and B show a positive correlation between bone marrow density and gestational age.

In graph A: The data points in the scattergram are closer to the line of best fit, indicating a strong correlation.

In graph B: The data points are scattered farther away from the line of best fit, indicating a weak correlation.

Therefore, the strength of the correlation is more in graph A than B.
questions.learning: Strength of the correlation is more in — A than in B The strength of the correlation is more in graph A than in graph B. Graphs A and B show a positive correlation between bone marrow density and gestational age.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Given below is a USG taken at approximately 8 weeks of gestation. Which anomaly can be observed here?

USG - ultrasound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anencephaly

The given ultrasound image shows an open defect in the calvaria and skin. This is consistent with the diagnosis of anencephaly.

Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. It is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation.  Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly.

• Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, prominent orbits thereby resembling the face of a frog.
• Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

Neural-tube defects can be prevented with pre-conceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies.

The frog eye and showercap signs are shown below:

Other options:

Option B: Hydranencephaly: This condition involves the absence of cerebral hemispheres, replaced by fluid-filled sacs.

Option C: Meningocele: It involves herniation of the meninges through a defect in the skull or spinal column, forming a sac filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

The image below shows meningocele:

Option D: Encephalocele is caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone.

The image shows a newborn with encephalocele.
questions.learning: Anencephaly — The given ultrasound image shows an open defect in the calvaria and skin. This is consistent with the diagnosis of anencephaly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an intranuclear immuno-histochemistry marker for neuroendocrine tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. INSM

Most neuroendocrine markers are:

• Cytoplasmic (Chromogranin, Synaptophysin)
• Membranous (NCAM/CD56)

Only one stands out as NUCLEAR: INSM1 (Insulinoma-associated protein 1)

INSM (Insulinoma-associated protein 1) is a nuclear transcription factor and serves as an intranuclear immunohistochemistry marker for neuroendocrine tumors. Seen in:

• Small cell lung carcinoma
• Carcinoid tumors
• Neuroendocrine tumors (GI, pancreas, lung)

| A. Chromogranin | Secretory granule protein | Cytoplasmic (granular) | Classic NET marker | ❌ Not nuclear | More specific but less sensitive than synaptophysin

| B. NCAM (CD56) | Cell adhesion molecule | Membranous | Neuroendocrine tumors, NK cells | ❌ Not nuclear | Very sensitive but NOT specific

| C. Synaptophysin | Synaptic vesicle protein | Cytoplasmic (diffuse) | Most sensitive NET marker | ❌ Not nuclear | First marker to turn positive in NET

| D. INSM1 ✅ | Transcription factor | NUCLEAR | Neuroendocrine differentiation | ✔️ Matches question |

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of Rivaroxaban ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factor Xa inhibition

Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor. They represent a new class of oral anticoagulant drugs that do not require monitoring.

This group of drugs inhibit factor Xa in the final common pathway of clotting [conversion of Prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin (Factor IIa)]. They are given as fixed doses and have a rapid onset of action.

Oral direct factor Xa inhibitors are indicated in:

* Prevention of embolic stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation (without valvular heart disease)

* Venous thromboembolic disease (VTE)

* Postoperative thromboprophylaxis in patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty

Direct factor Xa inhibitors:

* Rivaroxaban

* Apixaban

* Edoxaban

* Betrixaban

Parenteral direct thrombin inhibitors:

* Bivalirudin

* Argatroban

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In patients with acute ischemic stroke, the ABCD² score is commonly used to predict the risk of stroke recurrence. Which of the following factors is NOT included in this stroke risk assessment tool?
questions.explanation: The ABCD2 score is a clinical tool used primarily to predict the short-term risk of a full stroke following a Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA). The components of the score are Age (60 years), Blood pressure (systolic 140 or diastolic 90 mmHg), Clinical features (unilateral weakness or speech impairment), Duration of symptoms (minutes), and Diabetes Mellitus. While a History of Stroke is a significant risk factor for future neurological events, it is notably absent from the standardized ABCD2 scoring criteria. Hypertension (Option B) is represented by the "B" in the acronym, Age (Option A) by "A", and Diabetes (Option D) by "D". The scoring helps clinicians decide on the urgency of hospital admission and the intensity of secondary prevention strategies. Scores ranging from 6 to 7 indicate a high risk of stroke within two days. Accurate application of this tool ensures that high-risk individuals receive timely intervention to prevent permanent neurological deficits and improve overall clinical outcomes

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with breathlessness and is diagnosed with a Pancoast tumor. Which of the following clinical features is least likely to be associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: A Pancoast tumor is an apical lung cancer that often invades the sympathetic chain, leading to Horner’s syndrome. Horner’s syndrome is characterized by a specific triad: miosis (constricted pupil), ptosis (drooping eyelid), and anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on the affected side. Enophthalmos (a recessed eye) is also frequently seen. Exophthalmos (Option D), which is the bulging or protrusion of the eyeball, is the opposite of enophthalmos and is typically associated with conditions like Graves' disease (thyroid eye disease) or orbital tumors, not sympathetic nerve damage. Anhidrosis (Option A) occurs specifically in preganglionic lesions like Pancoast tumors. Miosis (Option B) results from the loss of sympathetic innervation to the pupillary dilator muscle. Ptosis (Option C) occurs due to paralysis of the superior tarsal (Müller’s) muscle. Therefore, because exophthalmos represents a different pathological mechanism, it is not a finding associated with Pancoast tumor-induced Horner’s syndrome

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes uses molecular oxygen as a hydrogen acceptor to produce water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cytochrome C oxidase

Cytochrome C oxidase catalyzes the removal of hydrogen from a substrate using oxygen as a hydrogen acceptor and produces water as a reaction product.

Cytochrome C oxidase is a heme-containing enzyme present in many tissues. It is the terminal complex (complex IV) of the chain of respiratory carriers found in the inner mitochondrial membrane and transfers electrons from substrates to molecular oxygen, producing water as a reaction product. It can be inhibited by cyanide, hydrogen sulfide, and carbon monoxide.

Other options:

Option A: Catalase is a hemoprotein belonging to the enzyme class, oxidoreductases(Catalyze redox reactions). Peroxisomes are rich in catalases.

Option B: Superoxide dismutase protects aerobic organisms by removing the superoxide anion free radicals (O2-) generated during aerobic respiration.

Option D: Pyruvate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl CoA in the mitochondria. It is a multi-enzyme complex with 5 co-enzymes and 3 apo-enzymes. The co-enzymes of pyruvate dehydrogenase are thiamine pyrophosphate(TPP), co-enzyme A, FAD, NAD+, and lipoamide.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery runs in close relation to the region of the skull depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: The image identifies the Pterion, a critical anatomical landmark where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet. The anterior (frontal) branch of the middle meningeal artery (MMA) runs directly deep to the Pterion on the internal surface of the skull. This area is clinically significant because the skull is thin at the Pterion, making it vulnerable to fractures from lateral head trauma. A fracture here can rupture the MMA, leading to an epidural (extradural) hematoma, which typically presents with a "lucid interval" followed by rapid neurological deterioration. The anterior cerebral artery (Option A) is located deep in the longitudinal fissure between brain hemispheres. The internal carotid (Option B) enters the skull base far more medially. The deep temporal arteries (Option D) supply the temporalis muscle on the external surface of the skull. Rapid surgical intervention via a burr hole at the Pterion is often required to evacuate an MMA-related hematoma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male underwent a bilateral laparoscopic hernia repair for inguinal hernia. Postoperatively, he complained of pain in the right thigh. Which of the following nerve entrapment leads to this symptom?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is vulnerable during laparoscopic mesh fixation, causing meralgia paresthetica—burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh.

During laparoscopic repair:

• Mesh is fixed with tacks/staples near the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).
• The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve passes near this area under the inguinal ligament.

So it can easily get compressed or trapped.

❌A) Ilioinguinal nerve

Supplies:

• Upper medial thigh
• Root of penis / scrotum

Injury causes groin or scrotal pain, not lateral thigh pain.

Also more commonly injured in open hernia repair, not laparoscopic.

❌B) Iliohypogastric nerve

Supplies:

• Lower abdominal wall
• Suprapubic skin

Damage causes suprapubic pain, not thigh pain.

❌C) Femoral nerve

Injury causes:

• Weak knee extension
• Loss of patellar reflex
• Quadriceps weakness

The question only mentions pain So, unlikely.
questions.learning: Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh — The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is vulnerable during laparoscopic mesh fixation, causing meralgia paresthetica—burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old patient underwent a lumpectomy and was found to have low-grade DCIS with 2 mm clear margins. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radiotherapy

Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast malignancy in which malignant epithelial cells are confined to the ductal system without breaching the basement membrane. It is Stage 0 (TisN0M0) breast cancer. In a patient with:

• Low-grade DCIS
• Breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy)
• Clear surgical margins (≥2 mm)

The standard next step is adjuvant whole-breast radiotherapy, which significantly reduces the risk of ipsilateral local recurrence.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mastectomy: Reserved for multicentric/extensive DCIS, persistently positive margins, or when breast conservation is not feasible.
• B. BCT (Breast-Conserving Therapy): Lumpectomy has already been performed; breast-conserving therapy consists of lumpectomy + radiotherapy.
• D. Tamoxifen: May be offered in ER-positive DCIS after surgery ± radiotherapy to reduce recurrence but is not a substitute for radiotherapy.
questions.learning: Radiotherapy Ductal Carcinoma — In Situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast malignancy in which malignant epithelial cells are confined to the ductal system without breaching the basement membrane.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient who was diagnosed with prostate cancer is being investigated. The bone scan is reported as a super scan with increased uptake in the bones and reduced activity in the kidney and soft tissue. What is the reason for this super scan appearance?
options: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
Decreased uptake by adrenal glands and kidney
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis

The super scan appearance is due to increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis.

Diffuse osteoblastic metastatic diseases such as carcinoma breast and prostate carcinoma lead to a generalized increase in the skeletal uptake relative to soft tissue and absent or faint renal activity on a bone scan. This is known as a super scan. It may also be seen in generalized bone diseases such as hyperparathyroidism.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels may be useful to assist with the diagnosis and management.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Arrange the following steps of a Randomised controlled trial in sequential order: 1. Manipulation 2. Statistical analysis 3. Follow-up 4. Randomisation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4-1-3-2

A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) is the gold standard experimental study design used to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions such as drugs, vaccines, or preventive measures.

The essential features of an RCT are:

• Randomization
• Manipulation (intervention)
• Control group
• Follow-up

These components ensure minimal bias and strong causal inference.

In a Randomised Controlled Trial, participants are first allocated to groups by randomisation to minimize selection bias. This is followed by manipulation, where the intervention is applied to the experimental group.

Participants are then followed up to observe outcomes, and finally statistical analysis is performed to compare results between groups.

Limitations

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a schedule X drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ketamine

Ketamine is a schedule X drug.

According to The Drugs and Cosmetics Act-1945,

Schedule X drugs are those that have high abuse liability and are to be sold with a valid prescription only.

A prescription in duplicate, separate license requirement, meticulous storage, and dispensing records must be maintained by the chemist.

Option B: Thalidomide is a schedule H drug.

Option D: Colistin is a schedule P drug.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with mental retardation, bone pain, and inability to walk. On funduscopy examination, a cherry red spot is seen. There is no organomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates that the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease.

Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of β-hexosaminidase. It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, gradual loss of motor skills, and a macular cherry-red spot. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years.

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type.

Other options:

Options B - Niemann-Pick disease is an autosomal recessive inborn error of lipid metabolism. It results due to the deficiency of the sphingomyelinase enzyme. This results in the accumulation of sphingomyelin in the brain, lungs, liver, and spleen. The clinical features include a combination of hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, failure to thrive, severe psychomotor regression, interstitial lung disease, and a cherry-red spot in the macula.

Option C - Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) is an autosomal recessive condition that affects multiple organs. Presentation is usually at 6–24 months with corneal clouding, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and skeletal dysplasia. Glaucoma, retinal degeneration, and nasal discharge are the other features. The condition is generally fatal.

Option D - Gaucher disease is a glycolipid storage disorder that can present with hepatosplenomegaly, mental retardation, and erosion of long bones. It is caused by the deficiency of β-glucosidase. The Gaucher cell has a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic inclusions, which is a characteristic feature.
questions.learning: Tay-Sachs disease — The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates that the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a case of head injury, which patient would not require an immediate CT scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. One episode of vomiting

In head injury, the decision to obtain an immediate CT head is based on the presence of high-risk features that predict intracranial injury or need for neurosurgical intervention. CT is mandatory when any of the following are present:

• Post-traumatic seizure (especially in children) → suggests cortical irritation/bleed
• Suspected skull fracture (basal or depressed) → high risk of intracranial hemorrhage
• GCS < 13 or fall in GCS (eg, GCS 12 in RTA victim) → moderate/severe head injury requiring urgent imaging

In contrast, a single isolated episode of vomiting, with otherwise normal neurological examination and no additional high-risk features, does not by itself mandate immediate CT, since minor vomiting can occur after concussion. (Repeated vomiting or vomiting with other risk factors would require CT.) Therefore, the patient who would not require immediate CT is One episode of vomiting (Option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Detoxification of Xenobiotics for phase 1 reaction (Hydroxylation) require monooxygenase/cytochrome P-450 along with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NADPH

Phase I detoxification (functionalization reactions) of xenobiotics mainly involves oxidation reactions such as hydroxylation, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system present in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells.

In this system, NADPH acts as the reducing agent and provides electrons through NADPH–cytochrome P450 reductase, which allows molecular oxygen to be split, with one oxygen atom incorporated into the substrate (hydroxylation) and the other reduced to water.

Why other options are incorrect:

• NADH: Mainly involved in mitochondrial electron transport and not the primary reducing agent for cytochrome P450 reactions.
• FAD / FADH₂: These act as prosthetic groups in some enzymes but are not the direct electron donors for the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: According to Herrington classification, the decerebrate rigidity is characterized by all except ______
options: Rigidity occurs in all the muscles of the body
Increase in the rate of discharge of the ɣ efferent neuron
Increased excitability of the motor neuron pool
Decerebration produces no phenomenon akin to spinal shock
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rigidity occurs in all the muscles of the body

In decerebrate rigidity, there is rigidity in extensor muscles of all the four extremities (not all muscles of the body).

Decerebration

• Complete transection of the brain stem between the superior and inferior colliculi permits the brain stem pathways to function independently of their input from higher brain structures. This is called a mid-collicular decerebration.
• This lesion interrupts all input from the cortex (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts) and red nucleus (rubrospinal tract), primarily to distal muscles of the extremities.
• The excitatory and inhibitory reticulospinal pathways (primarily to postural extensor muscles) remain intact.
• The dominance of drive from ascending sensory pathways to the excitatory reticulospinal pathway leads to hyperactivity in extensor muscles in all four extremities which are called decerebrate rigidity.
• The excitatory input from the reticulospinal pathway activates γ-motor neurons which indirectly activate α-motor neurons (via Ia spindle afferent activity). This is called the gamma loop.

Option 4. Spinal shock is different from decebrate rigidity as it is a transient state that can occur immediately after a spinal cord injury. It is characterized by a temporary loss or depression of spinal reflexes below the level of the injury.
questions.learning: Rigidity occurs in all the muscles of the body — In decerebrate rigidity, there is rigidity in extensor muscles of all the four extremities (not all muscles of the body).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the given X-ray finding seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reflux esophagitis

The given image is a barium swallow X-ray showing a feline esophagus suggestive of reflux esophagitis.

The feline esophagus is also known as esophageal shiver. These folds are 1-2 mm thick and run horizontally around the entire circumference of the esophageal lumen. It is thought to be due to the contraction of the muscularis mucosae of the esophagus. This results in the shortening of the esophagus and the bunching up of the mucosa in the lumen.

The appearance is almost always associated with active gastroesophageal reflux. The findings are transient, seen following reflux and not during swallowing. The appearance is confined to the distal two-thirds of the thoracic esophagus.

It can also be seen in hiatus hernia and eosinophilic esophagitis. Here, the folds are permanent and associated with strictures.
questions.learning: Reflux esophagitis — The given image is a barium swallow X-ray showing a feline esophagus suggestive of reflux esophagitis. The feline esophagus is also known as esophageal shiver.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An old lady sustained a fall and developed a headache and neurological symptoms a few days later. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subdural hematoma

The given clinical scenario of an elderly suffering from headache and neurological symptoms following trauma is suggestive of subdural hematoma (SDH).

SDH (acute/chronic) is the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dural layers of the meninges. The source of the bleeding is usually from the rupture of bridging veins running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses. Elderly, alcoholics & patients on anticoagulation are at a higher risk of developing SDH, especially after head trauma including trivial incidents.

Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice.

Radiographic features of subdural hemorrhage are:

• Typically unilateral (85%).
• Crescent-like distribution (concavo-convex) around the periphery of the brain.
• Not limited by sutures (vs extradural hemorrhage which is limited by sutures)
• Hyperdense lesion on CT: Acute SDH
• Hypodense lesion on CT: Chronic SDH

The given image shows the hyperdense collection seen in acute SDH.

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

1. Thickness >1 cm
2. Midline shift >5 mm
3. Or GCS drop by two or more points from the time of injury to hospitalization.

Other options:

Option A: Multi-infarct dementia (MID) is a type of vascular dementia occuring due to multiple small infarcts leading to brain tissue injury. It commonly causes memory loss in the elderly.

Option B: Frontal lobe meningiomas are benign brain tumors that develop from the meninges. They cause personality changes that may be mistaken for depression.

Option C: Korsakoff syndrome is a memory disorder that results from vitamin B1 deficiency and is commonly seen in  alcoholics. These patients present with impairment in storing new memories, disorientation, and confabulation. Consciousness is preserved.
questions.learning: Subdural hematoma — The given clinical scenario of an elderly suffering from headache and neurological symptoms following trauma is suggestive of subdural hematoma (SDH).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the WHO-recommended SAFE strategy for the control of trachoma, what does the letter “S” represent?
questions.explanation: The SAFE strategy is the comprehensive, WHO-recommended public health approach for the global elimination of trachoma as a cause of blindness. The acronym stands for: Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics (specifically azithromycin) to treat active infection, Facial cleanliness to reduce transmission, and Environmental improvements such as access to water and sanitation. Therefore, the letter S specifically stands for Surgery. This surgical component is critical for individuals with advanced trachoma who have developed trichiasis (inward-turning eyelashes), which causes corneal scarring and blindness if left untreated. Options B (Symptom), C (Spectacles), and D (Symbol) are not part of the SAFE framework. Trachoma is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide. The success of the SAFE strategy depends on community-based implementation and universal coverage of these four pillars. Surgery remains the only effective way to prevent permanent vision loss in those who have already suffered from chronic, scarring conjunctival inflammation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a middle-aged man, an X-ray reveals multiple lytic bone lesions, leading to further evaluation with urine analysis. The test detects the presence of Bence Jones proteins. Among the immunoglobulins, which type is most commonly associated with this finding?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of a middle-aged patient with multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions on X-ray and Bence Jones proteins in the urine is classic for Multiple Myeloma. This is a plasma cell malignancy characterized by the production of monoclonal (M) proteins. In Multiple Myeloma, the most common immunoglobulin subtype secreted by the malignant plasma cells is IgG (found in approximately 50-60% of cases). IgA (Option A) is the second most common (about 20%). IgM (Option D) is associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia, which typically presents with hyperviscosity rather than lytic bone lesions. IgD (Option B) is extremely rare. Therefore, while several types of monoclonal proteins can be present, IgG is the immunoglobulin most frequently linked to the classic skeletal and renal manifestations of Multiple Myeloma. Bence Jones proteins themselves represent the excessive monoclonal light chains excreted by the kidneys
questions.learning: The clinical picture of a middle-aged patient with multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions on X-ray and Bence Jones proteins in the urine is classic for Multiple Myeloma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by a defect in which of the following platelet glycoproteins?
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS) is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in the GpIb/IX complex on the platelet surface. This complex serves as the primary receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF), mediating the essential step of platelet adhesion to the subendothelial matrix following vascular injury. When this step is impaired, patients develop a defective primary platelet plug. Characteristic findings include a prolonged bleeding time and "giant platelets" on a peripheral smear. Option A (GpIIb/IIIa) is defective in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which affects platelet aggregation. Option C (GpIa/IIa) binds collagen, and its defects are rare and mild. Option D (GpIV or CD36) is involved in scavenger functions. BSS is specifically distinguished by the failure of platelets to aggregate in response to ristocetin, a defect that is not corrected by adding normal plasma
questions.learning: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS) is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in the GpIb/IX complex on the platelet surface.

questions.text: Quadruple testing is done during:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 15-20 weeks

The quadruple screening test is ideally done in the second trimester, during 15-20 weeks of gestation. The most accurate values are seen during 16-18 weeks of gestation.

It is the measurement of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP), unconjugated estriol, hCG, and inhibin-A.

In Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) or Edward's syndrome (trisomy 18), quadruple-marker screenings do not provide any added benefit over first-trimester screenings. It is generally used as a stand-alone test if screening is done for the first time in the second trimester or if first-trimester screening is not available.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with hearing loss in the left ear and episodic pulsatile tinnitus. On examination, there was a mass in the middle ear behind the tympanic membrane. A CT performed is as shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glomus jugulare

The given clinical vignette of a woman with hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus and examination suggesting a mass behind the tympanic membrane and CT image showing a mass in the region of jugular foramen makes Glomus Jugulare the likely diagnosis.

Glomus tumors are the most common benign tumors of the middle ear. The tumors comprise paraganglionic cells and arise from glomus bodies which resemble carotid bodies. Glomus bodies are present in the dome of the jugular bulb and on the promontory along the course of the tympanic branch of the IX cranial nerve.

They are most commonly seen in females between the ages of 40-50 years. They are very slow-growing, thus it may take years before changes in symptoms are appreciated. It follows the rule of 10s - 10% are familial, 10% are multicentric, and 10% are functional (secrete catecholamines).

Depending on the area from which it arises, glomus tumors are classified into two types:

• Glomus jugulare, arising from the dome of the jugular bulb
• Glomus tympanicum, arising from the promontory of the middle ear

The presentation of glomus tumors is as follows:

• Intratympanic presentation

• Progressive hearing loss
• Pulsatile tinnitus is synchronous with pulse and can be stopped by carotid pressure
• Otoscopy: red reflex through the intact tympanic membrane
• Rising sign when a tumor arises from the floor of the middle ear
• Pulsation or Brown sign: when the ear canal pressure is raised with Siegel's speculum the tumor pulsates and blanches. This reverses when pressure is released.

• Polyp presentation

• Profuse bleeding
• Otorrhea if there is a secondary infection
• Red vascular polyp filling the meatus that bleeds easily

• Cranial nerve palsies

• Dysphagia and hoarseness with unilateral paralysis of the soft palate, and pharynx due to IX and X
• Vocal cord paralysis due to X
• Weakness of the trapezius and sternomastoid muscles XI
• Atrophy of half of the tongue XII

• Audible bruit over the mastoid

They can be diagnosed by CT scan, MRI, four-vessel angiography, brain perfusion and flow studies, embolization, and biopsy. It is treated by surgery, radiation, embolization, or a combination of them. Phlep sign is seen in a CT scan of the glomus jugulare tumor. It is erosion of the normal crest of bone between the carotid canal and jugular foramen.

The following image shows the rising sun sign in the case of glomus jugulare.

Other options:

Option A: Glomus tympanicum is a close differential to the jugular tumor, however, it commonly arises from the promontory of the middle ear rather than the jugular bulb and does not show the Phlep sign and it is also found in relation to the temporal bone on CT.

Option B: Giant cell reparative granuloma accounts for 1–7% of all benign lesions of the jaw. It often arises in the maxilla followed by the mandible and affects children and young adults. It is usually a slow-growing lesion. The fast-growing lesions are rare and despite the innocent histological appearance, have an aggressive behavior mimicking a malignant lesion. The following image shows the CT of the reparative granuloma of the maxilla showing the extension of tumor mass over the pterygoid plates and infratemporal fossa.

Option D: Acoustic neuromas are noncancerous, usually slow-growing tumors that form along the vestibulocochlear nerve. They arise from Schwann cells. Schwannomas can occur on any cranial or peripheral nerve in the body, but in the brain, acoustic neuromas are the most common schwannomas. The following image depicts the classical ice cream cone appearance of acoustic neuroma on MRI.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following procedure is shown in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior ethmoidal nerve block

The procedure shown in the given image is an anterior ethmoidal nerve block.

The anterior ethmoidal nerve supplies the roof of the nasal cavity. It is a branch of the nasociliary nerve which in turn is a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1). It is sometimes used in endonasal surgery.

Other options:

Option A: In nasolacrimal duct syringing, the puncta of the nasolacrimal duct near the medial canthus of the eye is probed using a lacrimal cannula. The below image shows lacrimal syringing.

Option C: Infraorbital nerve block causes anesthesia in the distribution of infraorbital nerve which includes lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, and upper teeth. It is most commonly done for dental procedures.

Option D: Trephination of the frontal sinus is a surgical procedure done for the drainage of pus in acute frontal sinusitis. In this procedure, the incision is made on the floor of the frontal sinus.
questions.learning: Anterior ethmoidal nerve block — The procedure shown in the given image is an anterior ethmoidal nerve block. The anterior ethmoidal nerve supplies the roof of the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following poisons cause bluish discoloration of the stomach mucosa on post mortem examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium amytal

In sodium amytal poisoning, the capsules stain the stomach mucosa and its contents, turquoise blue. Bluish discolouration of the stomach mucosa is also seen in copper sulphate poisoning.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following culture media is used to differentiate other E.coli species from E.coli O157: H7?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sorbitol MacConkey agar

E.coli O157: H7 can be differentiated from other E.coli species using sorbitol MacConkey agar.

There are more than 150 serotypes of Shiga toxin-producing E.Coli (STEC). Of these, O157:H7 is the most common type. Unlike most other E.Coli serotypes, the STEC O157:H7 does not use sorbitol and produces clear colonies on the Sorbitol MacConkey agar.

O157: H7 strains also are negative for β-glucuronidase using the substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-glucuronide (MUG) test. More than 90 per cent of other E.coli tests positive with this substrate.
questions.learning: Sorbitol MacConkey agar E.coli O157: H7 can be differentiated from other E.coli species using sorbitol MacConkey agar. There are more than 150 serotypes of Shiga toxin-producing E.Coli (STEC).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old unconscious female patient requires urgent neurosurgical treatment for hydrocephalus, but no relatives or attendants are available to provide identification or consent. In this situation, what should the doctor do?
options: Take consent by calling the relatives
questions.explanation: In medical ethics and law, the "Doctrine of Necessity" allows a physician to provide life-saving treatment to a patient who is unable to give consent due to an emergency condition (such as being unconscious). In this scenario, immediate neurosurgical intervention is necessary to prevent death or permanent disability from hydrocephalus. Therefore, the surgeon can and should "operate without consent". Waiting for relatives (Option B) or delaying for formal identification (Option A) would be a breach of the duty of care and could lead to medical negligence. Calling relatives (Option D) is ideal but should not delay the emergency procedure if they cannot be reached immediately. The doctor should document the situation clearly and seek a second opinion from another senior colleague if possible, but the priority is always to preserve life in an emergency where "implied consent" is assumed
questions.learning: In medical ethics and law, the "Doctrine of Necessity" allows a physician to provide life-saving treatment to a patient who is unable to give consent due to an emergency condition (such as being unconscious).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old multiparous woman presents with chronic lower back pain. The pain is non-radiating, worse with activity, and improves with rest. There are no neurological deficits. X-ray pelvis shows bilateral symmetric sclerosis of the iliac side of the sacroiliac joints, with joint spaces preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteitis condensans ilii

Osteitis Condensans iliiis a benign condition

• Seen mostly in multiparous women
• Causes triangular sclerosis on iliac side
• SI joint space remains normal
• No joint erosions ,No fusion

To rule out Ankylosing spondylitis:

• Causes erosions
• Causes joint space narrowing
• Eventually leads to joint fusion
• Pain is inflammatory
• Pain worse in morning, better with activity.
