questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A G2P1 delivered a preterm baby at 36 weeks. The baby was admitted in the NICU for a week and was given expressed breast milk. Unfortunately the baby did not survive. Which of the following drugs can be used to reduce the engorgement and pain of the lactating breasts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cabergoline

In the given scenario, the woman requires suppression of lactation, for which cabergoline is indicated.

In the postpartum period, prolactin promotes lactation. Dopamine(DA) is the primary regulator of prolactin secretion from the pituitary gland. DA released from the hypothalamus into the hypophyseal portal blood supply acts on lactotroph D2 receptors to decrease prolactin secretion. The DA agonists like bromocriptine and cabergoline are used in conditions requiring suppression of prolactin.

Cabergoline is an ergot derivative with a longer t1/2 (~65 h), higher affinity, and greater selectivity for the DA D2 receptor compared to bromocriptine. Cabergoline is the preferred drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia because of greater efficacy and lower adverse effects. Therapy is initiated at a dose of 0.25 mg twice a week or 0.5 mg once a week. Cabergoline induces remission in a significant number of patients with prolactinomas. At higher doses, cabergoline is used in some patients with acromegaly alone or in conjunction with somatostatin analogs.

Adverse Effects -

Compared to bromocriptine, cabergoline has a much lower tendency to induce nausea, although it still may cause hypotension and dizziness. Cabergoline has been linked to valvular heart disease, an effect proposed to reflect agonist activity at the serotonin 5HT2B receptor. However, this effect is seen primarily at the high doses used in patients being treated for Parkinson's disease and is not seen in the conventionally used doses (≤2 mg/week) for patients with prolactinomas.

Other options:

Option B - Sumatriptan is a 5HT1B/1D receptor agonist used in the treatment of acute attacks of migraine.

Option C - Chlorpromazine is a typical antipsychotic, which has D2 antagonistic activity. It is used in the treatment of schizophrenia, acute mania, and refractory nausea and vomiting. Hyperprolactinemia is an adverse effect associated with its use.

Option D - Pramipexole is a non-ergot alkaloid with a broader DA receptor agonist activity, with the highest affinity to D3 receptors. It is used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease and restless leg syndrome. It is not indicated for the treatment of breast engorgement.
questions.learning: Cabergoline — In the given scenario, the woman requires suppression of lactation, for which cabergoline is indicated. In the postpartum period, prolactin promotes lactation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought to the clinic with a two-week history of poor feeding and increased irritability. The family history is significant for tuberculosis, as the patient’s sister is currently receiving treatment for TB. In view of the clinical suspicion, a lumbar puncture is performed for further evaluation. Which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) finding would be most characteristic of the suspected condition?
options: Neutrophils, low sugar and low protein
Neutrophils, low sugar and high protein
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms (irritability, poor feeding) combined with a strong positive contact history of tuberculosis suggest tuberculous meningitis (TBM). The pathognomonic CSF profile for TBM is lymphocytosis (predominance of lymphocytes), markedly low sugar (hypoglycorrhachia), and very high protein. Acute bacterial meningitis would show a predominance of neutrophils (Options C and D) and low sugar. Viral meningitis typically shows lymphocytosis but with normal sugar levels. High sugar (Option B) is not characteristic of any infectious meningitis. TBM results from the rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space, leading to a chronic inflammatory response that thickens the basal meninges. This often results in cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus. Early diagnosis via LP is life-saving, as the mortality and long-term neurological morbidity associated with untreated TBM are extremely high
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms (irritability, poor feeding) combined with a strong positive contact history of tuberculosis suggest tuberculous meningitis (TBM).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which among the following statements is true regarding PNH?

PNH-Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
options: Anemia with heart failure is the most common cause of mortality
Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosis

Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosis and is the correct statement regarding PNH. It provides a sensitive means for detecting red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59.

Investigations in PNH include:

• Flow cytometry (gold standard) - deficiency of CD59 and CD55
• Ham test (acidified serum lysis) - lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH due to complement fixation
• Bone marrow biopsy -

• Hypercellularity with erythroid hyperplasia is seen in classical presentations
• Patients who develop pancytopenia will have hypocellular bone marrow

• Imaging - to evaluate venous thrombosis

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is due to acquired mutations in the phosphatidylinositol glycan A gene (PIGA), leading to a deficiency of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-linked proteins. Blood cells are deficient in three GPI-linked proteins that regulate complement activity making them susceptible to lysis or injury by complement. These are a decay-accelerating factor or CD55, membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis or CD59 (most important), and C8-binding protein.

Clinical features in paroxysmal intravascular hemolysis occur nocturnally in 25% of cases. Clinically, the patient would have hemolysis, pancytopenia, and a tendency for venous thrombosis. Intravascular hemolysis may be nocturnal and paroxysmal or chronic hemolysis without the dramatic hemoglobinuria. Some patients may complain of recurrent attacks of abdominal pain that may be related to thrombosis in abdominal veins.

Other options:

Option A: Thrombosis is the most common cause of death in persons with PNH and not anaemia with heart failure.

Option B: It is an acquired condition and not an inherited condition.

Option C: Sucrose lysis test is used for screening of PNH.
questions.learning: Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosis Flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosis and is the correct statement regarding PNH. It provides a sensitive means for detecting red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the organism in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucor

Microscopy showing broad, aseptate, ribbon-like hyphae with irregular branching is suggestive of mucor.

Mucormycosis/ Zygomycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of rhizopus (most prevalent), mucor, and absidia. The common clinical form is rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis in which there is an invasion of the blood vessels in the nasal cavity, eyes, and brain causing thrombosis, infarction, and necrosis. The blackish discoloration is due to arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis can be made by staining them with 10% potassium hydroxide and culture. On Sabouraud agar at 30-37°C, they appear as grey-white colonies with a thick cottony, fluffy surface. Under the microscope, they appear as irregularly branched broad hyphae with aerial sporangiophores which end in a sac containing spores called sporangium.

Other options:

Options A and C: Aspergillus and Talaromyces (previously known as Penicillium) both demonstrate septate hyphae with conidiophores.

Option D: Blastomyces is a dimorphic fungus that exists in the yeast form in body tissues and cultures maintained at 37°C and in the filamentous mold form in cultures at room temperature (25°C). In the yeast form, it shows thick-walled round yeast cells with single broad-based budding, giving a figure of 8 appearance.
questions.learning: Mucor Microscopy showing broad, aseptate, ribbon-like hyphae with irregular branching is suggestive of mucor. Mucormycosis/ Zygomycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of rhizopus (most prevalent), mucor, and absidia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy shows progressive loss of coordination over six months. Examination reveals a cauliflower-like mass in the left eye, leukocoria, and absence of the red reflex. Histopathology demonstrates Flexner– Wintersteiner rosettes. Which gene is implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation: The presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), an absent red reflex, and a cauliflower-like intraocular mass in a young child is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. The microscopic finding of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes—clusters of cuboidal or columnar cells arranged around a central lumen—is a pathognomonic histological feature of this tumor. Retinoblastoma is caused by a mutation in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 13q14. According to Knudson’s "two-hit" hypothesis, both alleles of the RB1 gene must be inactivated for the tumor to develop. The ATP7B gene (Option B) is associated with Wilson's disease, which causes Kayser-Fleischer rings. The rhodopsin gene (Option C) is linked to retinitis pigmentosa. The FBN1 gene (Option D) is mutated in Marfan syndrome, often causing ectopia lentis. Thus, given the classic clinical and histological findings, the RB1 gene mutation is the definitive genetic cause. Early diagnosis is vital to save the patient's life and, if possible, preserve vision and the eye
questions.learning: The presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), an absent red reflex, and a cauliflower-like intraocular mass in a young child is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Low serum thyroglobulin levels are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyrotoxicosis factitia

Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein produced exclusively by thyroid follicular cells and serves as a marker of endogenous thyroid hormone production. It is useful in differentiating the causes of thyrotoxicosis.

A. Thyrotoxicosis factitia ✓

• Caused by exogenous ingestion of thyroid hormone.
• Since the thyroid gland is suppressed and not actively producing hormone, serum thyroglobulin is low.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Subacute thyroiditis ✗: Destruction of thyroid follicles releases stored thyroglobulin, resulting in high serum thyroglobulin.
• C. Graves’ disease ✗: Increased thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion cause elevated thyroglobulin.
• D. Toxic multinodular goitre ✗: Autonomous thyroid nodules produce excess hormone, leading to increased thyroglobulin.
questions.learning: Thyrotoxicosis factitia Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein produced exclusively by thyroid follicular cells and serves as a marker of endogenous thyroid hormone production.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old male with chronic kidney disease undergoing chronic dialysis presents with worsening breathlessness. Examination reveals muffled heart sounds. Chest X-ray image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pericardial effusion

The patient has chronic kidney disease on dialysis, which is a risk factor for uremic pericarditis and pericardial effusion. The muffled heart sounds and the X-ray showing a markedly enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette (“water-bottle” appearance) support the diagnosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pneumothorax: Would show a hyperlucent hemithorax with absent peripheral lung markings.
• B. Pleural effusion: Produces blunting of the costophrenic angles and a meniscus, not a globular cardiac silhouette.
• D. Pulmonary embolism: Usually has a normal or nonspecific chest X-ray; it does not produce a “water-bottle” cardiac silhouette.
questions.learning: Pericardial effusion — The patient has chronic kidney disease on dialysis, which is a risk factor for uremic pericarditis and pericardial effusion. The muffled heart sounds and the X-ray showing a markedly enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with unilateral ptosis that worsens toward the evening. She is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. Which drug is considered the treatment of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fluctuating muscle weakness. The first-line drug of choice for the symptomatic management of myasthenia gravis is Pyridostigmine, a long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. By preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine, it increases its concentration at the motor endplate, facilitating improved muscle contraction. Prednisolone (Option B) and Cyclosporine (Option C) are immunosuppressants used if symptomatic therapy alone is insufficient. Plasma exchange (Option D) is reserved for severe myasthenic crises to rapidly remove antibodies. The hallmark of the disease is the diurnal variation (worsening as the day progresses/fatigue), which pyridostigmine effectively addresses by providing sustained relief of ptosis and weakness. Patients must be monitored for cholinergic side effects like salivation or abdominal cramps while on this medication
questions.learning: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fluctuating muscle weakness.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old man underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukemia 3 weeks ago. He now develops a generalized maculopapular skin rash starting on the palms and soles, profuse watery diarrhea, and rising serum bilirubin with jaundice. Biopsy of the skin shows individual keratinocyte necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration ("satellite cell necrosis"). Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism of this condition?
options: Recipient cytotoxic T cells attacking donor-derived hematopoietic stem cells
Donor-derived immunocompetent T lymphocytes recognizing recipient tissue as foreign and mounting an immune attack
Pre-formed recipient antibodies against donor ABO antigens causing immediate graft rejection
Reactivation of latent cytomegalovirus within donor-derived monocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Donor-derived immunocompetent T lymphocytes recognizing recipient tissue as foreign and mounting an immune attack

• This describes acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a classic complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation.
• It occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes, transferred along with the graft, recognize the immunologically distinct (and immunosuppressed) recipient's tissues as foreign and mount a cytotoxic immune response.
• The classic triad of organ involvement is skin (maculopapular rash, often starting on palms/soles, with characteristic satellite cell necrosis on histology), gastrointestinal tract (watery or bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain), and liver (cholestatic jaundice with elevated bilirubin).
• Option A (Recipient cytotoxic T cells attacking donor-derived hematopoietic stem cells) describes the reverse phenomenon (host-versus-graft, i.e., graft rejection).
• Option C (Pre-formed recipient antibodies against donor ABO antigens causing immediate graft rejection) describes a hyperacute transplant rejection mechanism (hemolytic, not GVHD).
• Option D (Reactivation of latent cytomegalovirus within donor-derived monocytes) describes an opportunistic infection unrelated to the core alloimmune mechanism of GVHD, though CMV reactivation can be a separate post-transplant complication.

Quick reference — Acute vs Chronic GVHD:

| Feature | Acute GVHD | Chronic GVHD

| ------- | ---------- | ------------

| Onset | Typically <100 days post-transplant | Typically >100 days post-transplant

| Classic organs | Skin, GI tract, liver | Skin, eyes, mouth, lungs, liver, joints — multisystem, sclerodermatous changes

| Histology | Apoptotic keratinocytes with satellite cell necrosis | Fibrosis, lichenoid/sclerotic changes resembling autoimmune connective tissue disease

| Mechanism | Donor T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity against host tissue | Dysregulated immune reconstitution with autoimmune-like features

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How much illumination is recommended by the Illuminating Engineering Society for the general office work?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 400 lux

Illumination is the amount of light falling on a surface and is measured in lux (lx). Adequate illumination improves visual performance, reduces eye strain, and enhances work efficiency. According to the Illuminating Engineering Society (IES), the recommended illumination for general office work is 400 lux.

• General office work: 400 lux
• Corridors and staircases: 100 lux
• Classrooms: 150–300 lux
• Drawing/design work: 700–1000 lux
• Operation theatre: 1000–10,000 lux (shadow-free lighting)
• Direct sunlight: Approximately 100,000 lux

Units of Light

• Luminous flux: Lumen (lm)
• Illumination: Lux (lx) = Lumen/m²
• Luminous intensity: Candela (cd)
questions.learning: 400 lux Illumination is the amount of light falling on a surface and is measured in lux (lx). Adequate illumination improves visual performance, reduces eye strain, and enhances work efficiency.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with a hypopigmented lesion on his back. On examination, there is a complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensation over the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hansen's disease

The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy/ Hansen's disease.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy has a long incubation period, usually ranging from 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

Ridley-Jopling classification of leprosy:

*

* Tuberculoid (TT)

* Borderline tubercular (BT)

* Borderline (BB)

* Borderline lepromatous (BL)

* Lepromatous (LL)

Indeterminate (IL)

One or a few hypopigmented or faintly erythematous, ill-defined to well-defined macular lesions with mild to moderate impairment of touch and/or thermal sensations. No thickening of peripheral nerves.

Borderline tuberculoid (BT)

Macular or plaque-type lesions numbering three to nine or more and asymmetrically located on any part of the body, with variable sizes and contours. Satellite lesions may be present. Loss of sensation is less intense than it is in TT lesions.

Several peripheral nerves are likely to be enlarged in an asymmetrical pattern, with sensory and motor deficits. Increased susceptibility to develop Type 1 leprosy reaction.

Tuberculoid (TT)
Well-defined, hypopigmented macule or as a raised, erythematous/brown/copper-colored plaque with a well-defined edge up to three in number.

Complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensations over the lesion.

Larger corresponding cutaneous nerves are thickened in a limited number of case

Mid-borderline (BB)

An unstable form of leprosy. Multiple plaque lesions and macular lesions; lesions are of various shapes and sizes, are bilateral, and usually occur in a more or less symmetrical. Minimal loss of sensation over the lesions.

Many nerves may be thickened, and this effect may be asymmetrical.

Borderline lepromatous (BL)

Numerous bilateral, round or oval, macular, diffusely infiltrated, erythematous, or hypopigmented lesions with moderately defined borders. Some loss of sensation may be detected, particularly over older lesions.

Widespread but asymmetrical thickening of peripheral nerves

Lepromatous (LL)

Innumerable bilateral, symmetrically distributed, diffusely indurated, erythematous, copper-colored, or skin-colored patches or plaques. There is no loss of sensation over these lesions.

Bilateral earlobe thickening and eyebrow loss occur. Coarse induration on the face gives rise to leonine facies.

Involvement of peripheral nerves occurs late and is bilateral and symmetrical, with sensory loss in a “glove-and-stocking” distribution.

Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy:

* Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.

* Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.

* Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load.
questions.learning: Hansen's disease — The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy/ Hansen's disease. Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30-year-old man develops auditory hallucinations and is unable to identify the source of the voices approximately seven hours after undergoing an appendectomy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A patient developing auditory hallucinations 7 hours post-surgery is classic presentation of postoperative delirium — an acute confusional state caused by physiological disturbance following surgery including anesthesia effects, hypoxia, electrolyte imbalance, or pain medications. Key features pointing to Delirium: 1. Acute onset after surgery 2. Hallucinations — perceptual disturbances 3. Postoperative setting — classic trigger 4. Unable to identify source — disorientation characteristic of delirium Why other options are wrong: (A) Delirium tremens is incorrect because delirium tremens occurs 48-72 hours after alcohol withdrawal — not 7 hours post-surgery. No history of alcohol dependence or withdrawal is mentioned here. (B) Acute transient psychotic disorder is incorrect because ATPD requires symptoms lasting at least 1 day with sudden onset psychosis — postoperative hallucinations have a clear organic physiological cause making delirium more appropriate diagnosis. (D) Alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect because alcoholic hallucinosis occurs in chronic alcoholics experiencing withdrawal, typically 12-24 hours after stopping alcohol — no alcoholism history is mentioned and surgical context clearly points to delirium
questions.learning: A patient developing auditory hallucinations 7 hours post-surgery is classic presentation of postoperative delirium — an acute confusional state caused by physiological disturbance following surgery including anesthesia effects, hypoxia, electrolyte…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with refractory hypertension and recurrent headaches. There is no history of diabetes or dyslipidemia. Renal function tests are normal. A CT angiogram of the renal arteries image shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fibromuscular dysplasia

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory disease-causing secondary hypertension in young women due to renal artery stenosis. Angiography classically shows a “string of beads” appearance caused by alternating areas of stenosis and aneurysmal dilatation in the renal artery.

It typically presents with refractory hypertension, normal renal function, and absence of atherosclerotic risk factors, and is treated with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty.

Why not other options:

A. Atherosclerosis: Elderly, proximal ostial stenosis, risk factors present.

B. Takayasu arteritis: Large-vessel disease with systemic features, not beaded renal artery.

D. PAN: Microaneurysms + systemic vasculitis signs.
questions.learning: Fibromuscular dysplasia Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory disease-causing secondary hypertension in young women due to renal artery stenosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old obese female presented with colicky pain in the right hypochondrium. On examination, her temperature is 100°F, her pulse rate is 94 bpm and her blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. There is scleral icterus and tenderness in right hypochondrium. Blood investigations show AST-22 IU/L, ALT-27 IU/L, S.bilirubin-5mg% and ALP- 200 mg%. What should be the initial investigation in this patient? ALP- Alkaline phosphatase, AST- Aspartate aminotransferase, ALT- Alanine aminotransferase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. USG

The symptoms of right hypochondrial pain, fever, scleral icterus, increased serum bilirubin, and ALP is suggestive of choledocholithiasis. The first investigation to be done in this case is a USG to look for biliary duct dilation and whether it is intra or extrahepatic. Once this is confirmed, ERCP can be done as it can remove the stone without operative intervention.

Clinical features of choledocholithiasis:

* Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, which may radiate to the back

* Biliary colic

* Vomiting

* Dyspepsia

* Flatulence

* Food intolerance particularly to fatty foods

* Altered bowel habits

* Jaundice.

Investigations:

Transabdominal ultrasound is the initial investigation to be done.

Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography is the best modality to view the proximal biliary tract while ERCP is used for distal biliary tract.

The most common indication for therapeutic ERCP is the relief of biliary obstruction due to gallstone disease and benign or malignant biliary strictures.  Pancreatic divisum can present with recurrent pancreatitis and ERCP can help diagnose this as well.

Pearl PF0601: Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

Diagnostic Evaluation of the Bile Ducts

* Hepatobiliary ultrasound: Initial procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary tract obstruction

* CT scan: Procedure of choice in investigating possible biliary obstruction if diagnostic limitations prevent HBUS

* MRCP: Useful modality for visualizing pancreatic and biliary ducts

* ERCP: Best visualisation of distal biliary tract

* Endoscopic sphincterotomy and stone removal can also be done

* PTC: Best visualisation of proximal biliary tract

* Indicated when ERCP is contraindicated or failed

* EUS: Most sensitive method to detect ampullary stones

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female presented in dermatology OPD with acne that is not resolving on oral isotretinoin and antibiotics therapy. Which of the following is the next best step among the following options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Evaluate for hyperandrogenism

Refractory acne in females (not responding to isotretinoin + antibiotics) → always evaluate for underlying hyperandrogenism.

o    Persistent, severe, or treatment-resistant acne often indicates hormonal etiology

o    Common causes:

§  PCOS (most common)

§  Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

§  Androgen-secreting tumors (rare)

• Clinical clues suggesting hyperandrogenism:

o    Irregular menstrual cycles

o    Hirsutism

o    Androgenic alopecia

o    Sudden onset or severe acne

• Next steps in evaluation:

o    Serum testosterone

o    DHEAS

o    LH/FSH ratio (PCOS)

• Management implication: Add hormonal therapy (OCPs, spironolactone) rather than escalating antibiotics/isotretinoin

Why not others:

• Dietary triggers → mild/moderate acne, not resistant severe acne
• Antibiotic resistance → already on isotretinoin (not primarily antibiotic-dependent)
• Drug triggers → consider, but less likely in classic persistent female acne

questions.text: A 35-year-old woman visits a Health and Wellness Centre for population-based screening under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD). Which of the following cancers is not included in routine screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colon cancer

Under NP-NCD, population-based screening includes:

• Hypertension
• Diabetes mellitus
• Oral cancer
• Breast cancer
• Cervical cancer

Colon cancer is not included in routine NP-NCD screening.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute loss of vision accompanied by pain on eye movement. Examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), a normal-appearing optic disc, and central scotoma on visual field testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The triad of sudden vision loss, pain on eye movements, and a central scotoma in a middle-aged patient is highly characteristic of optic neuritis. The presence of a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) confirms an optic nerve lesion. Crucially, the finding of an intact optic disc on fundoscopy points specifically to retrobulbar neuritis, where the inflammation occurs behind the globe, sparing the disc from visible edema. Optic nerve glioma (Option A) is a slow-growing tumor of childhood causing progressive, painless proptosis. Eale's disease (Option C) is a peripheral retinal vasculitis causing vitreous hemorrhage. Neuroretinitis (Option D) would show visible disc swelling accompanied by a macular star. Optic neuritis is frequently associated with Multiple Sclerosis. Therefore, because the symptoms localize to the nerve without disc changes, it is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The triad of sudden vision loss, pain on eye movements, and a central scotoma in a middle-aged patient is highly characteristic of optic neuritis. The presence of a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) confirms an optic nerve lesion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Functional residual capacity is:
options: Volume that remains after forced expiration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Expiratory reserve volume + residual volume

Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.

From the picture given below, (FRC = ERV + RV).

Lung Capacities:

The total lung capacity can be broken down into alternative capacities that help to define functioning lungs.

• The vital lung capacity refers to the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung or maximum inspiratory level.
• The inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level.
• The functional residual capacity represents the volume of the air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath.
questions.learning: Expiratory reserve volume + residual volume Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume. From the picture given below, (FRC = ERV + RV).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 48-year-old diabetic man presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and nasal polyps. CT of the paranasal sinuses is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Allergic fungal sinusitis

Allergic fungal sinusitis (AFS) is a non-invasive fungal sinus disease caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to fungal elements. The “double-density sign” on CT of the paranasal sinuses is a classic radiological feature and is highly suggestive of AFS.

Why not the other options?

• A. Invasive fungal sinusitis: Typically occurs in uncontrolled diabetics or immunocompromised patients with facial pain, black eschar, orbital involvement, and bone destruction rather than the double-density sign.
• C. Chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps: Polyps may be present, but the double-density sign is absent.
• D. Maxillary sinus carcinoma: Presents with unilateral symptoms and bone destruction but does not produce the double-density sign.
questions.learning: Allergic fungal sinusitis Allergic fungal sinusitis (AFS) is a non-invasive fungal sinus disease caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to fungal elements.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As a Medical Officer at a Primary Health Center planning a focus group discussion with antenatal mothers, what is the ideal number of participants to ensure effective interaction and meaningful engagement?
questions.explanation: A Focus Group Discussion (FGD) is a qualitative research and educational tool used to explore the attitudes and behaviors of a specific group. For an FGD to be effective, the group must be large enough to generate diverse viewpoints but small enough to allow every participant to speak and for the moderator to maintain control. The internationally recognized "ideal" number of participants for an FGD is 6 to 12 people. Option A (4-6) and Option B (3-5) are often too small, potentially leading to a lack of group dynamic or the conversation being dominated by a single individual. Option D (12-15) is typically too large, making it difficult for quieter members to participate and for the moderator to follow deep thematic threads. A group of 8 to 10 is often considered the "sweet spot" within the broader 6-12 range. This size fosters a comfortable, interactive environment where rich, qualitative data about health beliefs can be collected effectively

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In rural areas, one ASHA worker is assigned to a population of ___ people.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1000

In rural areas, a population of 1000 should have at least 1 ASHA.

An Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) does not procure ORS, contraceptives, IFA tablets, etc. from the CHC for her community.

An ASHA acts as a depot holder for these essential supplies, hence making them readily available to her community. These include Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORS), Iron Folic Acid tablets (IFA), chloroquine, Disposable Delivery Kits (DDK), Oral Pills & Condoms, etc.

General norm:

* Must be a woman - married/divorced/widow (age group 25-45 years)

* Must be a resident of that village

* Formal education of up to 10th standard

* At least 1 ASHA for a population of 1000.

Relaxations in the general norm:

* If no candidate is available with a qualification of 10th standard, the requirement can be relaxed to 8th standard.

* In tribal, hilly, and desert areas, the norm can be relaxed to 1 ASHA per habitation.

Note: The States have been given the flexibility to relax the population norms as well as the educational qualifications on a case-to-case basis, depending on the local conditions as far as her recruitment is concerned. However, these are exceptions and not the general norm.

Pearl PF0294: ASHA

ASHA is an Accredited Social Health Activist.

An ASHA must be a woman, a resident of the village, 25 to 45 years old and have a formal education till 10th standard preferably if they are in good numbers. This may be relaxed upto 8th standard only if no suitable person with this qualification is available. She is part of the primary health care at the village level.

National norm: In rural areas, a population of 1000 should have at least 1 ASHA, but in remote areas, one ASHA per habitation is the norm. In urban areas, 1 ASHA worker is assigned to a population of 1000-2500. This norm is also mandated by each state, differently, according to their requirements.

Responsibilities of ASHA:

* Health education and awareness

* Reproductive and child health and family planning

* Facilitate the access to health services

* Promotion of sanitation and household toilet construction

* Provision of primary medical care for minor ailments

* Provider of DOTS

* Depot holder of essentials like ORS, iron and folic acid tablets, condoms, disposable delivery kits, etc.

* Dispersal of health information on her community to higher centres

* Some responsibilities are integrated with Anganwadi workers and Auxiliary Nurse Midwife

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with fever and malaise for 1 week. On examination, a pansystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border. Echocardiography reveals a small vegetation (10 mm) on the tricuspid valve without regurgitation or abscess formation. There are no signs of heart failure, systemic embolization, or persistent bacteremia. Blood cultures are positive for Staphylococcus aureus. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intravenous antibiotics

The clinical scenario of a 27-year-old intravenous drug user presenting with fever, malaise, a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, and a small tricuspid valve vegetation (<10 mm) is highly suggestive of infective endocarditis (IE) affecting the tricuspid valve. Patients with IE and small vegetations without heart failure, systemic embolization, or persistent bacteremia should be managed initially with intravenous antibiotics as the first-line therapy.

Infective endocarditis is an infection of the endothelium of the heart, which can be caused by bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms.  Acute IE rapidly damages the cardiac structures and spreads to extracardiac sites, frequently involving a highly virulent organism (e.g., S. aureus) attacking a previously normal valve.

Patients with infective endocarditis can have cardiac or non-cardiac manifestations.

Cardiac manifestations of IE:

* Presence of new regurgitant murmurs

* Congestive heart failure due to valve dysfunction

* Perivalvular abscesses and intracardiac fistulae- This is caused due to the extension of infection beyond the valves and into the adjacent myocardial tissue

* Conduction system defects- due to the damage of the interventricular septum by the abscess.

* Embolization of coronary arteries

Noncardiac manifestations of IE are:

* Arterial emboli- causing pain of ischemia of the organs

* Osler's nodes -are painful, red, nodular lesions usually located in the pads of the fingers and toes

* Roth's spots- retinal hemorrhages with a pale center

* Janeway lesions- In contrast to Osler's nodes, these are faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles. They occur as a result of septic embolization and are commonly associated with staphylococcal IE.

* Splenic abscess

* Cerebral abscess

* Immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis

* Positivity for rheumatoid factor

* Petechiae on oral and conjunctival mucosa

* Splinter subungual hemorrhages-painless, dark red lines in the nailbed.

* Mycotic aneurysms

* Splenomegaly

Treatment for infective endocarditis involves antibiotic therapy initiated immediately upon a definitive diagnosis. The duration of antibiotics is usually a total of 4 to 6 weeks. High serum bactericidal levels are necessary to eradicate organisms in inaccessible avascular vegetations.  Early surgical treatment is usually reserved for cases with paravalvular extension, abscess, severe valve dysfunction, or persistent bacteremia despite optimal antimicrobial therapy.

For cases with severe complications, like intractable heart failure, large vegetations, valvular destruction or persistent infection, surgical intervention is required.

Other options:

Option A and D: Immediate surgical intervention or tricuspid valve replacement is not recommended unless there are complications such as large vegetations, valve dysfunction, abscess formation, or persistent infection despite appropriate antibiotic therapy.

Option C: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in IE, due to risk of intracranial hemorrhage after septic emboli.

Pearl PF2203: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Pathologic criteria

* Clinical criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when:

* Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR

* If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy.

Pearl PF2204: Microbial Etiology of Infective Endocarditis

Streptococcus viridians

Other causes include enterococci and the so-called HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella), all commensals in the oral cavity, gram-negative bacilli and fungi.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presents with fever and neck stiffness for 11 days. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose (50 mg/dL), and markedly elevated protein levels (3000 mg/dL), with a negative Gram stain. Chest X-ray reveals upper lobe involvement with enlarged hilar lymph nodes. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of subacute fever, neck stiffness (meningeal irritation), and classic CSF findings points strongly toward Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM). TBM typically presents with a "lymphocytic" pleocytosis, significantly elevated protein levels (often much higher than in bacterial or viral types), and decreased glucose levels. The negative Gram stain further supports a non-bacterial etiology. Most importantly, the chest X-ray showing upper lobe involvement and hilar lymphadenopathy is highly suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis as the primary source. Bacterial meningitis (Option B) usually presents more acutely with a neutrophilic pleocytosis and a positive Gram stain. Fungal meningitis (Option C) can have similar CSF findings but is less likely in the presence of classic pulmonary TB signs on X-ray. Viral meningitis (Option D) typically has normal glucose levels and much lower protein levels. Given the 11-day subacute course and the pulmonary findings, Tuberculous Meningitis is the definitive diagnosis, requiring immediate initiation of anti-tubercular therapy and corticosteroids to prevent neurological sequelae
questions.learning: The clinical triad of subacute fever, neck stiffness (meningeal irritation), and classic CSF findings points strongly toward Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He has a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute and a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg. On clinical examination, hyper-resonance is noted on the left side of the chest, and the chest X-ray (shown) reveals corresponding findings. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 2nd ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS
questions.explanation: The patient presents with trauma, hypotension (shock), respiratory distress, and hyper-resonance, which is the classic triad for a Tension Pneumothorax. This is a clinical emergency where air is trapped in the pleural space, shifting the mediastinum and compressing the heart. According to updated ATLS guidelines, the immediate decompression site for an adult is "wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space" (ICS) at the mid-axillary line, immediately "followed by an intercostal drain" (chest tube) at the same level. The 2nd ICS (Option A) was the older recommended site but is now preferred only for children. Aspiration of fluid (Option C) is for pleural effusion, not air. Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening condition that must be diagnosed and treated clinically before waiting for an X-ray if the patient is unstable
questions.learning: The patient presents with trauma, hypotension (shock), respiratory distress, and hyper-resonance, which is the classic triad for a Tension Pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following is seen in freshwater drowning?

A. Haemodilution
B. Hypokalemia
C. Hyponatremia
D. Arrhythmia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A,C,D

In cases of freshwater drowning, hyperkalemia is seen due to hemolysis of swollen RBCs and not hypokalemia.

Freshwater is hypotonic to plasma and is rapidly absorbed from the alveoli and into the RBCs. The RBCs finally swell up and lyse resulting in the release of intracellular potassium causing hyperkalemia. Increased intravascular blood volume combined with hyperkalemia causes arrhythmia.

Seawater is hypertonic to plasma and causing a shift of fluid from the blood to alveoli causing pulmonary edema. There is a net decrease in blood volume causing a fall in blood pressure.

The table below summarises the cause of death in different types of drowning.

Type of drowning
Cause of death

Freshwater drowning

Seawater drowning

Disruption of surfactant

Dry drowning

Laryngeal spasm/Vagal inhibition

Post immersion Syndrome / Secondary drowning

• Cerebral anoxia
• Pneumonia
• Pulmonary edema
• Chemical pneumonitis
• Metabolic acidosis
questions.learning: A,C,D — In cases of freshwater drowning, hyperkalemia is seen due to hemolysis of swollen RBCs and not hypokalemia. Freshwater is hypotonic to plasma and is rapidly absorbed from the alveoli and into the RBCs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following pancreatic hormones: 1. Insulin 2. Islet amyloid polypeptide (Amylin) 3. Glucagon 4. Somatostatin Which of the above is/are secreted by beta cells of the pancreatic islets?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

The β-cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin and islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin), which work together to regulate postprandial glucose levels. Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, while amylin slows gastric emptying, suppresses glucagon secretion, and promotes satiety.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Insulin✅: Secreted by β-cells; lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis.
• 2. Islet amyloid polypeptide (Amylin)✅: Co-secreted with insulin by β-cells; delays gastric emptying and suppresses postprandial glucagon release.

Incorrect options:

• 3. Glucagon❌: Secreted by α-cells, not β-cells.
• 4. Somatostatin❌: Secreted by δ-cells, where it inhibits the release of both insulin and glucagon.
questions.learning: 1 and 2 The β-cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin and islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin), which work together to regulate postprandial glucose levels.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the most common cause for hospital admission after day care surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Postoperative nausea and vomiting

Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is the most common cause of unanticipated hospital admission following daycare surgery.

The two most common complications of daycare surgery are PONV and postoperative pain. PONV refers to the presentation of symptoms in the postoperative care unit or within 24 hours of the procedure. Pain is usually managed preoperatively and postoperatively with the administration of analgesics. While it is a common complication, postoperative pain is not the most common cause of unanticipated hospital admission. Opioid medications which are commonly used to treat postoperative pain present with side effects such as nausea and vomiting which may aggravate PONV.

The occurrence of PONV can be based on the following factors, patient, choice of anesthetic agent, and the procedure. The risk factors are:

• Patient: Women (higher incidence in pregnancy), history of PONV or motion sickness, nonsmokers, younger age (incidence decreases as the age increases).
• Anesthetic agent: General anesthesia, inhalational agents (isoflurane, sevoflurane), nitrous oxide, longer duration of anesthesia, preoperative opioid administration.
• Procedure: Laparoscopic procedures, lithotripsy, gynecologic procedures, adenotonsillectomy, strabismus surgery.

The drugs used in the prophylaxis and treatment of PONV include ondansetron, dexamethasone, and transdermal scopolamine.
questions.learning: Postoperative nausea and vomiting Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is the most common cause of unanticipated hospital admission following daycare surgery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following regimen is commonly used in the treatment of retinoblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vincristine, carboplatin and etoposide

Chemotherapy commonly used is a three-drug regimen containing vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide.
questions.learning: Vincristine, carboplatin and etoposide Chemotherapy commonly used is a three-drug regimen containing vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 15-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea and signs of virilization. She has prepubertal development of breasts and pubic hair and is tanner stage 2. She has a blind-ended vagina and clitoromegaly. She has normal male testosterone levels. Her genotype is 46XY. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5 alpha reductase deficiency

The clinical scenario points towards the diagnosis of 5 alpha-reductase deficiency.

The 5 alpha-reductase enzyme converts testosterone into a more potent form of the male sex hormone called dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Testosterone is required for the development of male internal genitalia, whereas DHT has a role in the development of male external genitalia. At puberty, testosterone is responsible for aggressive psychosexual behavior, deepening of the voice, increased muscle mass, and initiating spermatogenesis.

In 5 alpha reductase deficiency, there is a failure of conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. As testosterone levels are normal there is a normal development of Wolffian ducts and thus male internal genitalia are normal. However, some cases may have a blind-ending vagina.

As levels of DHT are low the child will have a female-looking external genitalia at birth. These children tend to be raised as females till puberty, by which they start exhibiting virilization which is caused by testosterone. Hence clitoromegaly is seen. There is a lack of breast development as testosterone is not converted to estrogen. Pubic hair is scanty as its development depends on both testosterone and dihydrotestosterone.

Investigations reveal an increase in the ratio of testosterone to DHT after hCG administration.

If the child wants to be raised as a female, then the testes have to be removed before the child attains puberty and virilization of the child. Estrogen therapy that is appropriate for inducing and maintaining feminization should be started at the time of usual pubertal maturation or immediately after gonadectomy is performed in an adult. Surgical correction in the form of vaginoplasty is performed. If the child is raised as a male corrective procedure include hypospadias correction, correction of chordee, and reconstruction of the urethra.

Other options

Option B: 17 alpha-hydroxylase deficiency results in decreased production of testosterone by adrenal glands. However, there will be normal testosterone production from the testes. Hence depending on the testosterone and dihydrotestosterone levels the child may have female-looking external genitalia or ambiguous genitalia at birth. 17 alpha-hydroxylase deficiency also results in a decrease in 17-OH progesterone levels and cortisol levels. Hence there is an increase in ACTH due to the loss of negative feedback which increases aldosterone. Due to an increase in aldosterone, the child will have hypertension and hypokalemia.

Option C: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder in which the androgen receptors are absent, scanty, or fail to respond to testosterone. Hence there will be no signs of virilization. The serum testosterone levels will be elevated. There will be normal breast development as testosterone is converted to estrogen.

Option D: Swyer syndrome results from a mutation in the SRY gene on the Y chromosome. This results in dysgenetic gonads. There is no production of AMH and testosterone and hence there is development of female internal and external genitalia. There will be no signs of virilization.
questions.learning: 5 alpha reductase deficiency The clinical scenario points towards the diagnosis of 5 alpha-reductase deficiency. The 5 alpha-reductase enzyme converts testosterone into a more potent form of the male sex hormone called dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the figure shown below, mechanism of action of valproate is best represented by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

The diagram represents GABA synthesis, metabolism, and receptor modulation:

• Glutamate → GABA via GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase)
• GABA degradation via GABA transaminase
• Synaptic GABA acts on GABA-A receptor
• Modulators:

• Benzodiazepines → increase frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening
• Barbiturates → increase duration of opening

Why option A is correct (Valproate)

Valproate mechanism:

• Inhibits GABA transaminase → ↓ GABA degradation
• → ↑ GABA levels in synapse

In the figure:

• Label A is positioned at GABA degradation pathway
• Blocking this step = exact mechanism of valproate

Why others are wrong

• B → Likely represents GABA reuptake inhibition (e.g., tiagabine)
• C → Likely presynaptic modulation
• D → GABA-A receptor modulation (benzodiazepines/barbiturates)

| Drug | Mechanism | Site of Action | GABA Effect

| ---- | --------- | -------------- | -----------

| Tiagabine | Blocks reuptake (GAT-1) | Synaptic cleft | ↑ GABA

| Vigabatrin | Inhibits breakdown | Intracellular | ↑ GABA

| Valproate | Mixed (↑ synthesis, ↓ breakdown) | Multiple | ↑ GABA

| Felbamate | NMDA antagonist | Postsynaptic | ↓ Glutamate

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl presents with a history of low-grade fever, weight loss, abdominal pain and amenorrhoea for six months. On examination, a pelvic mass is felt on the left side and signs of ascites are positive. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis with tubo-ovarian mass

The given clinical scenario with abdominal pain, amenorrhoea, pelvic mass and ascites is suggestive of genital tuberculosis.

Genital tuberculosis:

It is caused by M. tuberculosis and almost always occurs secondary to primary infection elsewhere in the extragenital states. The sites and frequency of involvement are as follows:

• Fallopian tubes (90-100%)
• Endometrium (50-60%)
• Ovaries (20-30%)
• Cervix (5-15%)
• Vulva and vagina (< 1%)

Presentation is variable and it can be asymptomatic in 10-20% of cases, infertility, menstrual irregularities, abdominal pain and mass, vaginal discharge, fistula formation, ectopic pregnancy and ascites. The mass is made up of rolled-up omentum that is adherent to the uterus and adnexa.

Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weakness, anorexia or night sweats may be present.

Investigations:

• CBC, ESR and Mantoux test
• Hysterosalpingography shows a lead-pipe appearance of the fallopian tube, calcification of the tube, beading and variation in the filling, cornual block, jagged fluffiness of tubal outline and tobacco pouch appearance of hydrosalpinx and pyosalpinx.
• Laparoscopy establishes the diagnosis of genital TB. It shows tuberculous lesions and perihepatic adhesions (if present).

Differential diagnosis:

• Ovarian cyst, broad ligament cyst or encysted fluid
• Pelvic inflammatory disease
• Ectopic pregnancy
• Carcinoma cervix
• Elephantiasis of the vulva
• Pregnancy
• Puberty menorrhagia and postmenopausal bleeding
• Fungal infection and sarcoidosis

Management:

It is treated with anti-tubercular therapy for 6 months (DOT strategy):

First 2 months

Next 4 months

• Isoniazid 15 mg/ kg body weight
• Rifampicin 450-600 mg
• Pyrazinamide 30 mg/body weight
• Ethambutol 30 mg/ kg body weight

3 times a week.

• Isoniazid 15 mg/kg body weight
• Rifampicin 450-600 mg

3 times a week

Indications and contraindications for surgery:

Indications
Contraindications

• Unresponsiveness of the disease in spite of adequate antitubercular chemotherapy.
• Tubercular pyosalpinx, ovarian abscess or pyometra.
• Persistent menorrhagia and/or chronic pelvic pain causing deteriorating health status

• Presence of active tuberculosis in extragenital site
• Favorable response to antimicrobial therapy with the diminishing size of the pelvic mass
• The accidental discovery of tubercular tubo-ovarian mass on laparotomy in a young patient.

Types of surgery include vulvectomy (if vulval hypertrophy is present), removal of the adnexal mass, drainage of pyometra and fistula repair.

TAH+BSO is rarely required nowadays. Tuboplasty is contraindicated.

Option B: Ovarian tumors usually don't affect menstrual cycles. Though virilizing tumors can cause amenorrhoea, other features of virilization such as hirsutism, flattening of breasts, and enlargement of the clitoris are generally present.

Option C: Though ectopic pregnancy may be suspected here, the tube is likely to rupture with exacerbation of pain, bleeding, and peritonitis before six months of gestation. Additionally, the absence of vaginal bleeding/spotting, and the presence of weight loss makes the diagnosis unlikely.

Option D: Submucous fibroid is associated with menorrhagia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which physiological adaptation does not happen at high altitudes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory acidosis

The physiological adaptation that does not happen at high altitudes is respiratory acidosis. Respiratory alkalosis is the physiological adaptation seen at high altitudes due to hyperventilation. It is a method of acclimatization. Compensatory mechanisms that are carried out to increase altitude tolerance are called acclimatization.

Following are the physiological changes that occur during acclimatization:

• Hyperventilation leads to respiratory alkalosis and shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left (and shifts to right after aclimitization).
• Increased erythropoietin secretion, leading to an increase in circulating red blood cells
• Increased number of mitochondria
• Increased myoglobin to facilitate the movement of O2 into the tissues.
• Increased tissue cytochrome oxidase
• Increased sympathetic tone
• Renal suppression of carbonic anhydrase and excretion of dilute alkaline urine brings the pH of the blood to normal.
• Decreased maximal exercise capacity (by ~1% for every 100 meters gained above 1500 meters)

Other options:

Option A- In response to the high altitude hypoxia, pulmonary vasoconstriction occurs due to which blood flow is distributed where it is most effective, leading to distribution of blood flow to the pulmonary areas in proportion to their alveolar O2 pressures.

Option B- Polycythemia - Erythropoietin secretion increases on the ascent to high altitude which results in polycythemia

Option D- Hypoxia - Total barometric pressure decreases as altitude increases, resulting in decreased Po2 (partial pressure of oxygen) leading to hypoxic hypoxia.
questions.learning: Respiratory acidosis — The physiological adaptation that does not happen at high altitudes is respiratory acidosis. Respiratory alkalosis is the physiological adaptation seen at high altitudes due to hyperventilation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Carhart's notch is seen in _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Otosclerosis

Carhart's notch is seen in otosclerosis. Carhart's notch is a dip at 2000 Hz in Bone Conduction, seen in pure tone audiometry.

Pure Tone Audiometry in Otosclerosis:

• Air conduction is poor & worse for lower frequencies.
• Large A-B gap
• Bone conduction is normal.
• In some cases, there is a dip in the bone conduction curve.
• It is different at different frequencies but is maximum at 2000 Hz and is called Carhart’s notch.

Note: Boiler’s notch is a similar dip in the BC and AC curve but at 4000 Hz, as seen in noise-induced hearing loss.
questions.learning: Otosclerosis Carhart's notch is seen in otosclerosis. Carhart's notch is a dip at 2000 Hz in Bone Conduction, seen in pure tone audiometry.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency room following a bike accident. Examination reveals the right upper limb in abduction and external rotation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior Dislocation of the Shoulder

The upper limb in abduction and external rotation and radiograph are both suggestive of anterior dislocation of the shoulder.

The AP view radiograph shows the disturbed articulation between the humeral head and glenoid fossa. The humeral head is seen below and medial to the glenoid socket. This suggests anterior dislocation of the shoulder joint. In young adults, the common cause for anterior dislocation is athletic injuries, while in older adults, falls are a more common cause.

Anterior dislocation is the most common among shoulder dislocations. It occurs due to a fall on the hands. The head of the humerus is driven forwards and tears the capsule resulting in an avulsion in the glenoid labrum (Bankart lesion). Sometimes, the posterolateral part of the head of the humerus is crushed resulting in the Hill-Sachs lesion.

The clinical features include severe pain and the patient usually supports his dislocated arm with the opposite arm. On examination, the arm is usually abducted, externally rotated and the lateral outline of the shoulder may be straightened and sometimes a prominent acromion process or a bulge below the clavicle may be appreciated.

The anteroposterior radiograph shows the humeral head lying below and medial to the glenoid socket. It may also show the Bankart lesion and the Hill-Sachs lesion.

Other Options:

Option A: Luxatio erecta is also known as inferior dislocation of shoulder. This is caused due to severe hyperabduction. The radiograph shows that the head of the humerus is present below the glenoid and the shaft is in an abducted position.

Option B:  Light bulb sign is seen on AP radiographs in the posterior dislocation shoulder. In posterior dislocation of the shoulder, the humerus rotates internally. This causes changes to the normal radiographic contour of the head of the humerus. The humerus appears similar to a lightbulb in AP views.

Pearl PF2105: Tests for anterior shoulder dislocation

Bryant’s test: Anterior axillary fold is at a lower level on the dislocated side.

Dugas test: The patient is made to place the hand on the opposite shoulder. The examiner then applies gentle pressure on the flexed elbow to make it touch the chest. In shoulder dislocation, the elbow cannot be made to touch the chest.

Hamilton ruler test: In a normal shoulder, a ruler (scale) placed on the lateral side of the arm will not touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion at the same time.

In anterior shoulder dislocation, the ruler will simultaneously touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion.

Callway Test: The vertical circumference of the axilla is increased on the dislocated side as compared to the normal side.

Pearl PF1173: Methods of reduction of shoulder dislocation

Kocher's technique - TEAM (Traction → External Rotation → Adduction → Medial Rotation)

Hippocratic method- Surgeon applies a firm and steady pull on the semi-abducted arm by keeping his foot on the axilla against the chest wall. The foot is used as the fulcrum.

Stimson's gravity technique: Patient is left prone and weight is attached to the elbow or wrist on the affected side. Gravity stretches the muscle and reduction occurs in 15-20 minutes.
questions.learning: Anterior Dislocation of the Shoulder — The upper limb in abduction and external rotation and radiograph are both suggestive of anterior dislocation of the shoulder.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman presents to the emergency department with blood pressure of 220/120 mmHg, along with headache, seizure, and blurred vision. Which intravenous antihypertensive is preferred for managing hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: This pregnant patient presents with severe hypertension (220/120 mm Hg) accompanied by headache, seizures, and visual disturbances, which is diagnostic of eclampsia with hypertensive emergency. Immediate blood pressure control is essential to prevent catastrophic complications such as intracerebral hemorrhage, placental abruption, and maternal death. IV labetalol is the preferred first-line intravenous antihypertensive for acute management of severe hypertension in pregnancy. It has a rapid onset, effectively lowers blood pressure, and has a good safety profile for both mother and fetus due to its combined α- and β-adrenergic blocking action. Why the other options are less suitable: IV hydralazine (Option C): An accepted alternative, but it is associated with more maternal side effects such as tachycardia, headache, and flushing, and less predictable BP control. IV nitroglycerine (Option B): Mainly used for acute pulmonary edema or refractory cases, not first-line for eclampsia. IV sodium nitroprusside (Option D): Avoided in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity, especially with prolonged use. Important note: While BP control is crucial, magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure control and prevention in eclampsia. Both therapies must be instituted promptly as part of comprehensive management
questions.learning: This pregnant patient presents with severe hypertension (220/120 mm Hg) accompanied by headache, seizures, and visual disturbances, which is diagnostic of eclampsia with hypertensive emergency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Determine the histological image shown below
questions.explanation: The histological image displays transitional epithelium (urothelium), which is specialized to line the urinary tract (ureters and bladder). Its hallmark feature is the presence of several layers of cells where the surface cells are large and dome-shaped (often called "umbrella cells"). These cells have the unique ability to flatten and stretch when the bladder is full and return to their dome shape when it is empty. Stratified squamous epithelium (Option D) would show flat, scale-like cells on the surface. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium (Option A) consists of a single layer of cells of varying heights that appears layered. Non-keratinized squamous epithelium (Option B) lines moist surfaces like the esophagus and lacks the characteristic "dome" cells. The elasticity of transitional epithelium is vital for accommodating the fluctuating volumes of urine. Identifying the "umbrella" surface cells is the definitive histological task for diagnosing this specific tissue type on medical examinations

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During the first trimester of pregnancy, propylthiouracil (PTU) is considered the safer medication for managing hyperthyroidism, as it has a lower risk of teratogenic effects compared to methimazole.
questions.explanation: Managing hyperthyroidism during pregnancy requires a careful balance between maternal health and fetal safety. During the first trimester, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the preferred and safer medication of choice (Option A). PTU is favored because it is more highly protein-bound and crosses the placenta less readily than other options, and it is less associated with major congenital malformations. In contrast, Methimazole (Option B) and its prodrug Carbimazole (Option C) are associated with a higher risk of "methimazole embryopathy," including defects like aplasia cutis and choanal or esophageal atresia when used in early pregnancy. Radioactive iodine (Option D) is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy as it can destroy the fetal thyroid gland and is potentially teratogenic. Many clinicians switch patients from Methimazole to PTU during the first trimester and then back to Methimazole for the remainder of the pregnancy to avoid PTU-induced maternal hepatotoxicity
questions.learning: Managing hyperthyroidism during pregnancy requires a careful balance between maternal health and fetal safety. During the first trimester, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the preferred and safer medication of choice (Option A).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the best screening investigation for metabolic disorders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tandem mass spectrometry

Tandem mass spectrometry (MS) is the technique of choice for screening neonates for inherited metabolic diseases.

Tandem MS employs the equivalent of two mass spectrometers linked in series (MS-MS or MS2). It can be used to screen blood samples from newborns for the presence and concentrations of amino acids, fatty acids, and other metabolites.

Abnormalities in metabolite levels indicate inherited metabolic diseases, such as phenylketonuria, ethylmalonic encephalopathy, and glutaric acidemia type 1.
questions.learning: Tandem mass spectrometry Tandem mass spectrometry (MS) is the technique of choice for screening neonates for inherited metabolic diseases. Tandem MS employs the equivalent of two mass spectrometers linked in series (MS-MS or MS2).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea for three days, following consumption of raw fish. He is otherwise stable, and physical examination is unremarkable. Stool analysis shows no pus, and culture grows on Wagatsuma agar. Which causative agent is most likely responsible for his illness?
questions.explanation: The history of consuming raw fish followed by diarrhea and abdominal pain is highly suggestive of Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection. This halophilic organism is a leading cause of seafood-borne gastroenteritis. The definitive laboratory clue is the growth on Wagatsuma agar, which is used to detect the Kanagawa phenomenon (hemolysis), a marker of virulent strains. Vibrio cholerae (Option A) causes profuse "rice-water" diarrhea and characteristically grows yellow colonies on TCBS agar. Salmonella typhi (Option B) presents with high-grade fever (step-ladder pattern) and bradycardia rather than acute raw-fish-linked diarrhea. Shigella sonnei (Option C) typically causes inflammatory diarrhea with pus and blood in the stool. V. parahaemolyticus gastroenteritis is usually self-limiting, requiring only oral rehydration therapy. It is common in coastal regions where raw or undercooked shellfish and fish are consumed. Prevention focuses on proper cooking and avoiding cross-contamination of seafood products
questions.learning: The history of consuming raw fish followed by diarrhea and abdominal pain is highly suggestive of Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection. This halophilic organism is a leading cause of seafood-borne gastroenteritis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The man present with a case of cervical rib has tingling sensation and paresthesia on the medial side of arm. Which of the marked structure is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C

A cervical rib can compress the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1), producing thoracic outlet syndrome. Clinical features of lower trunk compression:

• Paresthesia and tingling on the medial side of the arm and forearm
• Weakness of intrinsic hand muscles
• Possible ulnar nerve distribution symptoms

The lower trunk (C8–T1) lies close to the first rib and cervical rib, making it vulnerable to compression.

Structures affected: Nerves derived from C8–T1, especially:

o    Ulnar nerve

o    Medial cutaneous nerve of arm

o    Medial cutaneous nerve of forearm

In the diagram, the marked structure C corresponds to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with recurrent lung infections and sinusitis is diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis. Which channel defect is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloride channel

Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which encodes a ATP-gated chloride ion channel present in the apical membranes of the epithelial cells. It regulates the flow of ions across epithelial membranes of sweat glands, respiratory airways, pancreatic ducts, etc. The defect leads to high salt concentrations in sweat and viscous luminal secretions in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include:

* Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps (Option A).

* Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus (Option C), and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis (Option D).

* Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels.

* Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females.

* Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease.

Diagnostic tests:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

1. Presence of

* Clinical symptoms affecting at least one system (respiratory, genitourinary or gastrointestinal) or

* Positive screen during neonatal screening or

* A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

* Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on different days or

* Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or

* Increased nasal potential difference.

Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.
questions.learning: Chloride channel Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which encodes a ATP-gated chloride ion channel present in the apical membranes of the epithelial cells.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The best way to manage the wound shown in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cleaning and dressing

The given image shows a superficial injury to the skin, an abrasion. Cleaning and dressing is the appropriate management of an abrasion.

Wound cleaning is the removal of bacteria and particles to decrease the chances of infection. It includes the “TIME” acronym:

• T - Tissue : Assessment and debridement of non-viable tissue or foreign material
• I - Inflammation/Infection : Assess the etiology of each wound
• M - Moisture Balance : Assess the etiology of wound exudate
• E - Edge of the wound : Assess the edge and surrounding skin

Wound irrigation or toilet is washing the wound with normal saline.

Wound debridement is performed using a surgical blade or fine scissors to remove any devitalized, nonviable tissue or any embedded foreign body (option B).

Skin grafting is required only in situations of wonuds with larger areas soft tissue loss (options C and D).
questions.learning: Cleaning and dressing — The given image shows a superficial injury to the skin, an abrasion. Cleaning and dressing is the appropriate management of an abrasion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin, when infused in supraphysiological doses, causes macular edema and macular cysts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B3

Macular cysts and edema may develop in patients due to the infusion of supraphysiological doses of vitamin B3 (niacin toxicity).

The toxic effects of niacin include:

• Flushing associated with skin dryness, itching, paresthesia, and headache is seen. These effects may be seen with even a low dose of 30mg/day. Pre-medication with aspirin alleviates these symptoms as these symptoms are mediated by prostaglandins.
• Macular edema and macular cysts
• Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
• Hepatic toxicity presents as jaundice with elevated AST and ALT levels.
• Fulminant hepatitis requiring liver transplantation.
• Glucose intolerance
• Hyperuricemia

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the most widespread calculation of Stillbirth Rate, the numerator is defined as foetal deaths weighing over ‘X’ gram at birth, during the year. Which one of the following is the correct value for ‘X’?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1000

The Stillbirth Rate (SBR) is an important indicator of maternal and perinatal health. In the traditional and most widely used definition (Park’s PSM), a stillbirth is defined as the birth of a dead fetus weighing 1000 g or more (or after 28 weeks of gestation) during a given year.

Stillbirth Rate = (Number of stillbirths ≥1000 g ÷ Total births [Live births + Stillbirths]) × 1000

Hence, the correct value of ‘X’ is 1000 g.
