questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: The Gold Standard for diagnosis of Celiac disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic small bowel biopsy

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). While serologic tests are useful for screening, the gold standard for diagnosis is an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with multiple duodenal (small bowel) biopsies, which confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating characteristic mucosal changes.

Characteristic histopathological findings:

• Villous atrophy
• Crypt hyperplasia
• Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh classification)

Key points:

• Best initial screening test: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA) antibody (along with total serum IgA).
• Gold standard: Endoscopic duodenal biopsy.
• Treatment: Lifelong gluten-free diet.
questions.learning: Endoscopic small bowel biopsy Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents to the outpatient department with primary amenorrhea and recurrent cyclical pain. On perineal examination, a bulging mass is seen protruding at the vaginal opening. What is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
options: Transverse septum in the proximal vagina
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of primary amenorrhea (absence of periods), cyclical pelvic pain, and a visible vaginal protrusion is pathognomonic for an imperforate hymen . The protrusion is a bulging, often bluish membrane caused by hematocolpos (the accumulation of menstrual blood trapped behind the hymen). A transverse vaginal septum (Option A) would also cause obstructive amenorrhea and cyclical pain, but the obstruction is typically higher up and would not present as a protrusion at the introitus. Complete vaginal atresia (Option B) involves a lack of the vaginal canal, meaning no protrusion would be visible. Cervical agenesis (Option D) would present with amenorrhea and pain due to hematometra, but without the vaginal bulge. The classic visual sign of a tense, bulging membrane between the labia in an adolescent girl confirms the diagnosis. Treatment involves a cruciate incision to drain the accumulated blood and create a permanent opening
questions.learning: The clinical triad of primary amenorrhea (absence of periods), cyclical pelvic pain, and a visible vaginal protrusion is pathognomonic for an imperforate hymen .

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which clinical situations is it essential to perform serial measurements of serum beta‑hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) levels?
options: Pregnancy associated with Neural tube defects
questions.explanation: Serial monitoring of serum beta-hCG is the absolute standard of care for the follow-up of a molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease) . After surgical evacuation, hCG levels must be measured weekly until they become undetectable to ensure that no trophoblastic tissue remains. Persistent or rising levels indicate the development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (e.g., choriocarcinoma), which requires chemotherapy. In Down syndrome (Option A), hCG is measured as part of a one-time "quadruple screen," not for serial monitoring. Neural tube defects (Option B) are screened via alpha-fetoprotein. Rh-negative pregnancy (Option D) is managed by monitoring maternal antibody titers, not hCG. Therefore, because hCG is the definitive tumor marker for molar disease progression, its serial measurement is critical for patient survival and the detection of malignancy. Patients are typically advised to avoid pregnancy until hCG levels have remained normal for six months

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with lacy white lesions involving the oral cavity and genital region, along with an abnormal forward extension of the proximal nail fold onto the nail bed. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lichen planus (LP) is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the skin, mucous membranes, and nails. The "lacy lesions" in the mouth are known as Wickham striae, a hallmark of oral LP. Genital involvement is also common. The "extension of the proximal nail fold onto the nail bed" describes a "dorsal pterygium," which is a classic and highly characteristic nail finding in lichen planus caused by scarring of the nail matrix. Psoriasis (Option B) typically presents with nail pitting, oil spots, and onycholysis, not pterygium. Pityriasis rosea (Option C) presents with a herald patch and a "Christmas tree" distribution of lesions, usually sparing the nails and mouth. Pityriasis rubra pilaris (Option A) involves follicular papules and orange-red plaques. The skin lesions of LP are classically described as the "6 Ps": planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques. Diagnosis is usually clinical but can be confirmed by biopsy showing a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate
questions.learning: Lichen planus (LP) is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the skin, mucous membranes, and nails. The "lacy lesions" in the mouth are known as Wickham striae, a hallmark of oral LP.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman with a fibroid uterus develops severe acute pain abdomen at 28 weeks of gestation. There is no history of fever and the WBC count is 8000 cells/mL. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Torsion of fibroid

The given scenario of severe acute abdominal pain without fever/leucocytosis in a pregnant woman with a fibroid is suggestive of fibroid torsion.

The incidence of fibroid in pregnancy is about 1 in 1,000. Due to increased vascularity in pregnancy, the fibroid increases in size and becomes softer. The torsion is seen in the subserous pedunculated fibroid where the venous return is blocked at its site of attachment in the uterus. This leads to severe acute abdominal pain. Due to the complication being more local than systemic, fever or leucocytosis are generally not seen.

A transvaginal ultrasonogram is immediately done to detect the position and size of the fibroid, which is followed by laparotomic myomectomy as a part of emergency surgical management.

Other options:

Option A: Red degeneration of fibroid is seen commonly in the second half of pregnancy or puerperium. It is due to a hemorrhagic infarction of the tissue and typically presents as acute focal abdominal pain with fever and leucocytosis. Treatment is usually conservative with bed rest, analgesics, and sedatives.

Option B: Preterm labor is where the labor starts before 37 completed weeks. It is characterized by true labor pain. The abdominal pain is slowly increasing in intensity and duration and is also accompanied by show (expulsion of the cervical mucus plug). There are intervals between episodes of contractions where the patient doesn't complain of abdominal pain.
questions.learning: Torsion of fibroid — The given scenario of severe acute abdominal pain without fever/leucocytosis in a pregnant woman with a fibroid is suggestive of fibroid torsion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: As a junior resident monitoring a patient on mechanical ventilation, arterial blood gas analysis reveals hypoventilation with respiratory acidosis. Which modification in the ventilator settings would be most effective in correcting this abnormality?
questions.explanation: Respiratory acidosis in a ventilated patient results from alveolar hypoventilation, which causes retention of carbon dioxide (CO₂). Correction requires increasing minute ventilation to enhance CO₂ clearance. Minute ventilation equals tidal volume × respiratory rate; therefore, increasing the respiratory rate is the most direct way to “wash out” excess CO₂. Decreasing FiO₂ (Option A) reduces oxygenation without correcting CO₂ retention. Increasing PEEP (Option C) improves oxygenation by preventing alveolar collapse but does not directly treat hypercapnia. Increasing plateau pressure (Option D) is unsafe due to the risk of barotrauma and ventilator-induced lung injury. Hence, raising the respiratory rate is the standard intervention for ventilation-induced respiratory acidosis
questions.learning: Respiratory acidosis in a ventilated patient results from alveolar hypoventilation, which causes retention of carbon dioxide (CO₂). Correction requires increasing minute ventilation to enhance CO₂ clearance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study, an investigator compares the mean blood pressure values (along with their standard deviations) between two independent groups. Which statistical test is most appropriate to determine whether the difference between the two means is statistically significant?
questions.explanation: The study involves comparing the means of two independent groups with continuous data (blood pressure). The unpaired (independent samples) t-test is the standard parametric test for this purpose. A paired t-test (Option A) is used only for matched pairs or before-and-after measurements within the same group. The chi-square test (Option C) is used to determine associations between categorical variables, not to compare means. ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) (Option D) is used when comparing the means of more than two independent groups. Since the investigator is specifically assessing the difference between exactly two separate, independent sets of mean values, the unpaired t-test is the most appropriate statistical choice
questions.learning: The study involves comparing the means of two independent groups with continuous data (blood pressure). The unpaired (independent samples) t-test is the standard parametric test for this purpose.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the given organism?
questions.explanation: The provided image (located at the top of Page 9) displays characteristic large, smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia arranged in clusters, which are diagnostic features of Epidermophyton floccosum. A key distinguishing feature of this genus is the absence of microconidia, which separates it from other common dermatophytes. This fungus is a frequent cause of tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and tinea unguium. Microsporum gypseum (A) produces thin-walled, ellipsoidal macroconidia with up to six cells. Microsporum audouinii (B) typically shows very rare conidia and is known for pectinate hyphae. The genus Trichophyton (D) is characterized by abundant microconidia and rare, smooth, pencil-shaped macroconidia. Because the visual evidence specifically highlights the "beaver-tail" or club-shaped morphology and lacks smaller spores, the identification is definitively Epidermophyton. Morphology of dermatophytes is a high-yield topic for FMGE, and correctly differentiating between these three main genera based on microscopic conidial structure is essential for clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The provided image (located at the top of Page 9) displays characteristic large, smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia arranged in clusters, which are diagnostic features of Epidermophyton floccosum.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with a long-standing history of diabetes is found to have cataract formation. Which metabolic by-product is mainly responsible for the development of cataracts in this condition?
questions.explanation: In patients with chronic diabetes, high blood glucose levels overwhelm the normal glycolytic pathway, leading to increased activity of the enzyme aldose reductase. This enzyme converts glucose into sorbitol via the polyol pathway. Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol that is poorly metabolized and slowly converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase in the lens. Consequently, sorbitol accumulates within the lens fibers. Because it is highly hygroscopic (osmotically active), it draws water into the lens, causing cellular swelling, oxidative stress, and the aggregation of crystallin proteins. This structural disruption results in the characteristic "snowflake" cataract of diabetes. Galactitol (Option B) is a similar osmotic product but is responsible for cataracts in patients with galactosemia, not diabetes. Fructose (Option D) is the end product of this pathway but does not cause osmotic damage. Thus, sorbitol is the primary metabolic culprit in diabetic cataractogenesis
questions.learning: In patients with chronic diabetes, high blood glucose levels overwhelm the normal glycolytic pathway, leading to increased activity of the enzyme aldose reductase.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young woman presents with ptosis that shows diurnal variation. CT scan of the chest reveals an anterior mediastinal mass consistent with a thymic tumor. Which receptor is most likely affected in this condition?
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels at the NMJ
questions.explanation: The combination of diurnal ptosis (weakness that worsens during the day and improves with rest) and a thymic mass is highly characteristic of Myasthenia Gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies target and destroy the nicotinic acetylcholine (ACh) receptors on the post-synaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). The thymus gland plays a critical role in the pathogenesis, with roughly 15% of MG patients having a thymoma. Presynaptic ACh receptors (Option A) are not the target in MG. Voltage-gated calcium channels (Option C) are targeted in Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome, which is often associated with small cell lung cancer rather than thymoma. Acetylcholinesterase (Option D) is the enzyme that breaks down ACh; while it is inhibited by drugs used to treat MG, it is not the target of the disease's autoantibodies. Thus, the post-synaptic ACh receptor is the site of the defect
questions.learning: The combination of diurnal ptosis (weakness that worsens during the day and improves with rest) and a thymic mass is highly characteristic of Myasthenia Gravis (MG).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with curd-like white vaginal discharge. On examination, petechiae appear when the discharge is removed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A thick, white, "curd-like" (or cottage-cheese-like) vaginal discharge is the hallmark of Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (yeast infection). The discharge is characteristically adherent to the vaginal walls; when it is forcibly removed or scraped away during examination, the underlying mucosa often appears inflamed and may show small, pinpoint hemorrhages known as petechiae. Trichomoniasis (Option B) involves a frothy, yellow-green discharge. Gardnerella vaginalis (Option C, Bacterial Vaginosis) features a thin, greyish discharge with a fishy odor. Gonorrhea (Option D) presents with a mucopurulent cervical discharge. Candidiasis is most commonly caused by Candida albicans and is triggered by factors such as antibiotic use, pregnancy, or uncontrolled diabetes. The associated pruritus is usually intense. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding budding yeast or pseudohyphae on a KOH mount. Treatment involves topical or oral antifungal agents like fluconazole or clotrimazole. The curd-like consistency and the petechiae upon removal are the key diagnostic anchors

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with Crohn’s disease presents with diffuse abdominal pain, and examination reveals rigidity and guarding, indicating peritoneal irritation. Imaging confirms an ileal perforation. What is the next step in management?
options: Antibiotics and NPO (nil per os, nothing by mouth)
questions.explanation: The patient presents with ileal perforation, a life-threatening surgical emergency characterized by generalized peritonitis (rigidity and guarding) . In the context of Crohn's disease, a perforation mandates urgent surgical exploration to control the source of contamination. Because the tissue is typically inflamed and friable in Crohn’s, primary repair is often unsafe, making the creation of an ileostomy (Option C) the standard of care for fecal diversion and patient stabilization. Antibiotics and NPO (Option A) are supportive measures but cannot resolve a mechanical perforation. Upper GI endoscopy (Option B) is strictly contraindicated in a suspected or confirmed perforation due to the risk of worsening the pneumoperitoneum. While a CT (Option D) might have been used for diagnosis, once the perforation is already confirmed by imaging, the clinical priority shifts entirely to immediate surgery. Therefore, operative intervention is the definitive life-saving next step

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are characteristic features of Turner syndrome, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prominent occiput

Turner syndrome (45,X) shows classic somatic features like webbed neck, shield chest with wide-spaced nipples, and short 4th metacarpal due to SHOX gene haploinsufficiency.

Classic Phenotype

• Short stature
• Webbed neck
• Shield chest
• Wide spaced nipples
• Streak ovaries → primary amenorrhea

Skeletal abnormalities and lymphatic dysgenesis are characteristic.

Prominent occiput is not a recognized feature of Turner syndrome and is more associated with certain craniofacial anomalies in other syndromes.

A. Prominent occiput- Incorrect statement

• Not a feature of Turner syndrome
• Seen more in:

• Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
• Some neural tube defects

B. Short 4th metacarpal

• Gives knuckle dimpling when making a fist
• Also seen in:

• Pseudohypoparathyroidism

C. Webbed neck

• Due to cystic hygroma in fetal life
• Leaves behind lateral neck folds

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines has not been introduced to the immunization programme in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Influenza

Influenza vaccine (Flu shot) has not been introduced to the National Immunization Programme in India.

The Influenza vaccine provides protection against viral flu caused by the influenza virus.

Note: Bacterial Hemophilus influenzae type-b (Hib) vaccine is different from the viral influenza (Flu) vaccine. HiB is a part of the pentavalent vaccine.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: When asked about her age, a woman states that she is 39 years old and explains this by saying she is married to an older man and has two children aged 15 and 18 years. Which psychiatric disorder does this presentation suggest?
questions.explanation: Circumstantial speech is a thought disorder where the patient provides excessive, unnecessary, and tedious details before eventually reaching the point or answering the original question. In this case, the woman was asked her age but detailed her marriage and children first, although she did ultimately answer "39 years old". Derailment (Option A) involves a loosening of associations where speech shifts randomly between unrelated topics without any logical connection. Flight of ideas (Option C), often seen in mania, is characterized by rapid, pressured shifting between topics, often with only superficial associations. Tangentiality (Option D) is similar to circumstantiality, but the key difference is that the patient never actually returns to answer the original question. Recognizing these patterns is essential for accurate psychiatric diagnosis and mental status examinations. Circumstantiality is frequently seen in individuals with personality disorders or organic brain syndromes
questions.learning: Circumstantial speech is a thought disorder where the patient provides excessive, unnecessary, and tedious details before eventually reaching the point or answering the original question.

questions.text: The image below shows the insertion of transversus abdominis muscle. Identify the conjoint tendon:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C

The structure marked C is the conjoint tendon.

The conjoint tendon is formed from the lower fibres of internal oblique and the lower part of the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis. It is attached to the pubic crest and extends to a variable extent along the pectineal line.

Transversus Abdominis muscle

Origin: internal surface of 7th -12th costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, connective tissue deep to lateral third of inguinal ligament.

Insertion: Linea Alba with aponeurosis of internal oblique, pubic crest, and pecten pubis via the conjoint tendon.

A: Lumbar fascia
B: Transversus Abdominis
D: Inguinal Ligament

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for balance and equilibrium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Semicircular canal

The semicircular canals that are a part of the bony labyrinth are responsible for balance and equilibrium.

The semicircular canals are three loop-shaped structures filled with endolymph fluid and lined with hair cells that detect angular acceleration in three planes (horizontal, vertical, and oblique).

When the head moves, the fluid inside these canals shifts, causing the hair cells to bend. This bending generates nerve impulses that are transmitted to the brain via the vestibular nerve, informing the brain about the direction and speed of head movement. This mechanism is essential for maintaining posture, coordinating eye movements, and ensuring balance.

Other options:

Option A: The vestibule, which includes the utricle and saccule, also contributes to balance by detecting linear acceleration and the position of the head relative to gravity. However, the semicircular canals are primarily responsible for detecting rotational movements, making them key to the sensation of balance and equilibrium.

Option C: The organ of Corti is the sense organ of hearing and is situated on the basilar membrane of the cochlear duct. It detects sound vibrations and converts them into electrical signals for the auditory nerve. It is involved in hearing, not balance or equilibrium.

Option D: The cochlea is a spiral-shaped organ responsible for converting sound waves into electrical signals. It contains hair cells that detect sound vibrations and transmit them as nerve impulses to the auditory nerve, allowing us to perceive sound.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use and smoking presents with repeated episodes of vomiting and sudden, sharp epigastric pain. The symptoms began shortly after heavy alcohol intake. He is now febrile and tachycardic. Bedside imaging reveals the presence of free air under the diaphragm. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with recurrent vomiting and sudden sharp epigastric pain, along with a history of chronic alcohol consumption and smoking, which are strong risk factors for peptic ulcer disease (PUD). The X-ray shows a key diagnostic feature: free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). This indicates perforation of a hollow viscus, most commonly due to a perforated peptic ulcer. When an ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the stomach or duodenal wall, air escapes into the peritoneal cavity, producing this classic radiological sign. Clinically, perforation presents with: 1. Sudden severe epigastric pain (“stabbing”) 2. Vomiting 3. Signs of peritonitis (guarding, rigidity) 4. Possible fever and tachycardia Why other options are incorrect: 1. Tension pneumothorax → Chest findings, not abdominal free air 2. Boerhaave syndrome → Esophageal rupture, shows mediastinal air 3. Mallory-Weiss tear → Causes bleeding, not perforation
questions.learning: The patient presents with recurrent vomiting and sudden sharp epigastric pain, along with a history of chronic alcohol consumption and smoking, which are strong risk factors for peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

questions.text: The confusion assessment test is used in:

Correct answer: C. Delirium

The confusion assessment test is used in the detection of delirium.

Delirium is reported to occur in a wide range of mechanically ventilated ICU patients and can be detected by the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)-ICU or the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist.

These tools are used to ask patients to answer simple questions and perform simple tasks and can be used readily at the bedside.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Dialysis will prevent all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peripheral neuropathy

Dialysis does not prevent peripheral neuropathy. Complications like seizures, metabolic acidosis, and uremic pericarditis can be prevented by dialysis.

Peripheral neuropathy is postulated to be caused due to middle molecules (50-200kDa). Conventionally used dialysis membranes have pore sizes that prevent larger particles (such as middle molecules) from passing through them.

Suggested methods for the removal of middle molecules include:

• High flux dialysis
• Protein adsorptive membranes
• High-cutoff membranes

Aggressive removal of middle molecules or larger low-molecular-weight proteins (LMWPs) has been a growing concern since it causes massive albumin leakage.

β2-microglobulin (B2M),α1-microglobulin (A1M) and albumin leakage during a dialysis session are useful parameters for assessing middle-molecule removal.

Renal transplantation is the best treatment option available for peripheral neuropathy in diabetes.
questions.learning: Peripheral neuropathy Dialysis does not prevent peripheral neuropathy. Complications like seizures, metabolic acidosis, and uremic pericarditis can be prevented by dialysis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with severe maxillofacial trauma following a road traffic accident, which airway management technique is most appropriate as the initial step?
questions.explanation: In severe maxillofacial trauma, the airway is often compromised due to bleeding, edema, fractured bones, and distorted anatomy. In such situations, tracheostomy is the safest and most appropriate initial airway management, as it bypasses the upper airway entirely. This avoids the risk of failed intubation and prevents further injury. It provides a definitive airway quickly, especially when conventional routes are difficult or dangerous. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Orotracheal intubation: Although usually first-line, it may be difficult or impossible here due to distorted anatomy and can worsen injuries or dislodge clots. (C) Nasotracheal intubation:Contraindicated in maxillofacial trauma, especially with possible basilar skull fracture, as the tube may enter the cranial cavity. (D) Oxygen therapy: Provides only supportive care and does not secure the airway, which is critical in severe trauma

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was admitted to the hospital for prolapsing rectal mass and painless rectal bleeding. Histopathological examination reveals enlarged and inflamed glands filled with mucin. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hamartoma

The given features are suggestive of a juvenile polyp, which are a type of hamartomatous polyp. They are benign growths that are composed of a disorganized mixture of different types of tissues.

Juvenile polyps are malformations of epithelium and lamina propria commonly located in the rectum. It is seen in children <5 years of age. The typical presentation is painless rectal bleeding. Sometimes, there may be a proliferating rectal mass.

The disease may be sporadic or syndromic.

• Sporadic juvenile polyp occurs as a single mass and is called a retention polyp.
• Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterized by multiple hamartomatous polyps, which may be premalignant.

Morphologically, both of these types are indistinguishable.

• Gross appearance: They appear as pedunculated, smooth reddish lesions, and with cystic spaces.
• Microscopic appearance: The cysts appear as dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris.

Adenoma: Adenomas are benign tumors that arise from glandular tissue. While they may present with rectal bleeding, they are not commonly seen in young children and are not typically pedunculated like juvenile polyps.

Choristoma: Choristomas are non-neoplastic masses that arise from heterotopic tissue, i.e., tissues found in abnormal locations. They are not associated with juvenile polyps.
questions.learning: Hamartoma — The given features are suggestive of a juvenile polyp, which are a type of hamartomatous polyp. They are benign growths that are composed of a disorganized mixture of different types of tissues.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3 months old baby was brought with photophobia and lacrimation. Which of the following cannot be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction

Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO) is least likely to cause watering and photophobia.

Nasolacrimal duct obstruction is the most common disease of the lacrimal system. It usually presents in the first few weeks or months of life as excessive tearing and ocular discharge. It mostly occurs due to incomplete canalization of the duct.

Congenital NLDO mainly results in persistent tearing and sometimes a discharge from the eyes but not photophobia, as the light sensitivity is not directly related to this condition.

Typically, diagnosis is established through a combination of patient history and physical examination. In cases where symptoms are intermittent, the presence of an obstruction can be confirmed using the fluorescein dye disappearance test.

The initial treatment involves performing nasolacrimal massage, typically 2-3 times daily, along with cleansing the eyelids using warm water and applying topical antibiotics. If it does not resolve after massaging by the age of 6 to 10 months, lacrimal duct probing is done.

If probing fails, other treatment options include intubation with silastic tubing with or without balloon dilatation of the nasolacrimal duct and dacryocystorhinostomy.

Other options:

Option A: Congenital entropion: This is a condition where the eyelid is turned inward, causing the eyelashes to rub against the cornea. This can lead to irritation, photophobia, and excessive tearing (lacrimation).

Option B: Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is caused by impaired aqueous outflow due to a maldeveloped anterior chamber angle. Clinically, the child presents with lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm.

Option C: Congenital distichiasis: This is a condition where an extra row of eyelashes grows from the meibomian glands on the eyelid margin. These extra lashes can irritate the cornea, leading to photophobia and tearing.
questions.learning: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO) is least likely to cause watering and photophobia. Nasolacrimal duct obstruction is the most common disease of the lacrimal system.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At which of the following centers are the records of eligible couples maintained?
questions.explanation: The Sub-centre is the peripheral-most unit of the Indian healthcare system, serving a population of 3,000 to 5,000. It is the designated primary site where the records of all "eligible couples" (those where the wife is in the reproductive age of 15–49) are meticulously maintained in the Eligible Couple Register. This task is primarily performed by the Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) or Female Health Worker. While the Primary Health Centre (PHC, Option A) supervises the sub-centres and maintains aggregate data, the primary source and repository of individual couple data is at the sub-centre level. Community Health Centres (CHC, Option B) and District Hospitals (Option D) are higher-level referral facilities that do not maintain these localized community family records. The maintenance of this register is critical for planning family welfare services, tracking contraceptive use, and ensuring the delivery of maternal and child health interventions. It serves as the foundation for the "eligible couple" surveillance system in the national family planning program

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What embryological defect is responsible for the developmental abnormalities shown in the given image?
options: Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of posterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of complete neural tube
Failure in closure of caudal neuropore of neural tube
questions.explanation: The provided image illustrates anencephaly, a lethal neural tube defect characterized by the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp. This condition results from the failure of the anterior (cranial) neuropore to close during the fourth week of embryological development, typically around day 25. When this closure fails, the developing forebrain is exposed to amniotic fluid and subsequently degenerates. Failure of the posterior or caudal neuropore (Option B and D) results in various forms of spina bifida, which affect the spinal column rather than the cranium. Complete failure of neural tube closure (Option C) leads to craniorachischisis, where both the brain and the entire spinal cord are exposed. Anencephaly is frequently associated with maternal folic acid deficiency and can be detected prenatally through elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels. Because the defect is specifically localized to the cranial vault, the anterior neuropore failure is the definitive cause
questions.learning: The provided image illustrates anencephaly, a lethal neural tube defect characterized by the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A child presented with itchy plaques over the neck, the bilateral popliteal and cubital fossa. What could be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atopic dermatitis

The given clinical history of itchy plaques over the neck, cubital fossa and popliteal fossa suggests the diagnosis of ‘atopic dermatitis’.

Atopic dermatitis is the cutaneous expression of the atopic state, characterised by a family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis or eczema.

The etiology is only partially defined, but there is a clear genetic predisposition. A characteristic defect is impaired epidermal barrier. In many patients a mutation in gene encoding filaggrin (a structural protein in the stratum corneum) is responsible. The lesions are distributed in the flexural aspects.(as shown in the image).

Patients may display many immunoregulatory abnormalities, including increased IgE synthesis, increased serum IgE levels, delayed type hypersensitivity reactions.

The cardinal symptom is itching, along with rash.

Atopic Eczema can be divided into 3 phases: Infantile, Childhood, and Adult phases.

Infantile phase: The lesions of Atopic Eczema most frequently start on the face but may occur anywhere on the skin surface. Often, the napkin area is relatively spared.

• When the child begins to crawl, the exposed surfaces, especially the extensor aspect of the knees and elbows are most involved.
• The lesions consist of erythema and discrete or confluent oedematous papules. The papules are intensely itchy and may become exudative and crusted as a result of rubbing.
• Secondary infection and lymphadenopathy are common.

Childhood Phase: From 18 to 24 months onwards, the sites most characteristically involved are the elbow and knee flexures, a mixture of erythema, crusting, excoriation, hyper‐ and hypopigmentation, and warty lichenification may be seen depending on the skin type on the sides of the neck, wrists, and ankles.

• The sides of the neck may show a striking reticulate pigmentation, sometimes referred to as atopic dirty neck.
• The erythematous and oedematous papules tend to be replaced by lichenification.

Adult Phase: The picture is essentially similar to that in later childhood, with lichenification, especially of the flexures and hands.

Other options:

B) Dermatitis herpetiformis:

• Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely pruritic, skin condition associated with gluten‐sensitive enteropathy.
• It typically appears in the 4th decade, and the patients present with itching and rash, most typically over the extensor surfaces of the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp.
• They may also have symptoms associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathies, like bloating, diarrhea and other gastrointestinal complaints.
• On examination, multiple erythematous papules and vesicles can be seen over the extensor aspects. They appear symmetrical and heal without scarring. The oral cavity may show mucosal abnormalities and enamel pits.

C) Pemphigus vegetans:

It is a rare form of the bullous disorder that presents with large, moist, verrucous, vegetating plaques studded with pustules on the groin, axillae and flexural surfaces.

D) Psoriasis:

• Plaque psoriasis is the most common type of psoriasis and is seen in 80-90% of patients.
• The peak on occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.
• The lesions are red, scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.
• They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.
• They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.

questions.text: Which of the following crystalloid infusions, when given in large quantities, is likely to cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NS

Large-volume infusion of normal saline (0.9% NaCl) delivers excess chloride relative to sodium. Large-volume normal saline → ↑Cl⁻ → ↓HCO₃⁻ → hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (normal anion gap)

This increases plasma chloride, causing bicarbonate dilution and a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.

| NS (0.9%) | High Cl⁻ | Causes acidosis

| Ringer Lactate | Lactate → HCO₃⁻ | Alkalinizing

| D5W | Free water | Neutral

| DNS | Dextrose + NS | Mild acidosis possible but less prominent

Ringer lactate is balanced, D5W is free water, and DNS does not cause significant hyperchloremia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with a history of repeated sinopulmonary infections caused by encapsulated organisms. Which of the following is most likely to be deficient in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgG2

Deficiency of IgG2 results in recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated organisms.

IgG is the only maternal immunoglobulin that is normally transported across the placenta and provides natural passive immunity to the newborn. IgG1 is the antibody maximally transported across the placenta, whereas IgG2 has the least transplacental movement.

Deficiencies of other IgG:

• IgG1- bacterial infections (diphtheria, tetanus)(Option A)
• IgG3- viral infections (Option C)
• IgG4- parasitic infections (Option D)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Which of the following tests can be used if otoacoustic emissions is absent for screening?

1. Pure tone audiometry
2. Tympanometry
3. Free field audiometry
4. Speech audiometry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 4

Among the given options, tympanometry (Test 2) and speech audiometry (Test 4) are used in cases where otoacoustic emission (OAE) is absent for screening.

Otoacoustic emissions are sounds produced by the outer hair cells of cochlea. These sounds then travel in the reverse direction from the outer hair — basilar membrane and perilymph of cochlea— oval window — ossicles and tympanic membrane (middle ear) — ear canal (external ear).

Hence in the absence of OAE, pathologies of the middle and external ear should be ruled out before making a definitive diagnosis of cochlear pathology.

Tympanometry is an objective test that can be performed in patients with absent OAE to rule out any middle ear pathologies. Speech audiometry is a subjective test that can be performed in these patients to confirm if the hearing loss is due to cochlear or retro cochlear pathology (neural hearing loss).

Impedance Audiometry also known as Tympanometry is an objective test that is based on the principle that when the sound strikes the tympanic membrane, certain amount of sound is absorbed, while the rest is reflected So a stiffer tympano-ossicular system would reflect greater sound than a compliant one. By marking the compliance of tympano-ossicular system against various pressure changes, different types of tympanograms are obtained which are diagnostic of various middle ear pathologies.

In speech audiometry, the patient’s ability to hear and understand speech is measured. The speech reception threshold (SRT) is the lowest intensity of sound at which 50% of the words are repeated correctly by the patient. Speech discrimination scores test the capacity of the patient to understand speech. Hence, speech audiometry is a subjective test.

The rollover phenomenon is diagnostic of retrochochlear pathologies. Here, the phonetically balanced word score falls with an increase in speech intensity above a particular level due to nerve fatigue. The graph in cochlear disorders will rather show a plateau after a certain level unlike the fall seen in the rollover phenomenon.

A better objective test that could be used to diagnose retro-cochlear pathologies is brainstem auditory evoked response audiometry (BERA). It is a noninvasive test that can find any pathologies of central auditory pathways through the VIIIth nerve to pons and midbrain.

Other options:

1. Pure tone audiometry (Test 1) is a test that measures the threshold of hearing by air and bone conduction and thus the degree and type of hearing loss. Pure tone audiometry is a subjective test for hearing and is not employed in cases where OAE is absent when better objective tests such as tympanometry are available.

3. Free field audiometry (Test 3), a part of behavior observational audiometry is used in the age group where children start localizing sounds when an auditory signal is presented. This test is not useful in this case as the possibility of hearing loss is already established with absent OAE.
questions.learning: 2 and 4 Among the given options, tympanometry (Test 2) and speech audiometry (Test 4) are used in cases where otoacoustic emission (OAE) is absent for screening.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40 year old male patient presented with pain and hearing loss after trauma to his right ear. Otoscopy reveals the presence of blood clots along with irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane. What is the next step in management in this case?
options: Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics

In this case, the presence of blood clots and irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane suggests traumatic injury to the ear. The initial management involves keeping the ear dry to prevent infection and further damage.

When a patient presents with pain and hearing loss after trauma to the ear, it's important to manage the condition appropriately. Systemic analgesics can be prescribed to alleviate pain.

Other options:

* It's important to avoid introducing any foreign substances into the ear canal, such as ear drops or irrigation, as this can exacerbate the injury and increase the risk of infection.

* Aspirating and performing audiometry may be considered later in the management process, once the acute phase has resolved and the extent of damage needs further evaluation.

* Giving gentamicin and levofloxacin or other antibiotics is not indicated at this stage unless there are signs of infection, as prophylactic antibiotic use is generally not recommended due to the risk of promoting antibiotic resistance.
questions.learning: Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics — In this case, the presence of blood clots and irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane suggests traumatic injury to the ear.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who underwent Nissen's fundoplication was seen in the ward during evening rounds. He is asymptomatic at present with stable vitals. What is the next line of management for this patient?
options: Nasogastric tube to prevent gas bloat syndrome
Insert chest tube to prevent pneumothorax
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Monitor vitals

The patient is asymptomatic, therefore no further action needs to be taken other than monitoring his vitals.

The most common complication of Nissen’s fundoplication is gas-bloat syndrome.

Fundoplication is a procedure in which the fundus of the stomach is wrapped around the lower end of the esophagus. After this procedure, most patients are unable to belch gas from the stomach into the esophagus. This causes increased gas in the stomach resulting in bloating sensation, abdominal discomfort, and flatulence. This is known as gas bloat syndrome and occurs more commonly with Nissen total fundoplication.

Other options:

During the early postoperative period, patients who report persistent nausea and demonstrate inadequate intake of a liquid diet should undergo abdominal radiography. If significant gastric distention is identified, a nasogastric tube can safely be placed to decompress the stomach for 24 hours.

Pneumothorax is the most common complication that occurs intraoperatively. Chest tube needs to be inserted if pneumothorax takes place, which is not seen in this case.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the labelled structure in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Midbrain

The labeled structure is the midbrain.

The midbrain develops from the midbrain vesicle, the cavity of which becomes much reduced to form the cerebral aqueduct or aqueduct of Sylvius.

The midbrain:

* Is of small size and is completely surrounded by cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space

* Has a cavity called the cerebral aqueduct, which opens above into the third ventricle

* Is located in the posterior cranial fossa

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with ear wax and was subjected to syringing to remove the wax. She developed a syncopal episode while doing the procedure when the tip of the syringe touched the ear canal. Which of the nerves is responsible for this episode of syncope?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arnold's nerve

The posterior wall of the external auditory canal is supplied by the auricular branch of the Vagus (Arnold's nerve). When this nerve is stimulated, a vasovagal response is initiated which results in the syncopal episode.

When the vagus nerve is stimulated, a parasympathetic response occurs leading to braycardia and decreased blood flow into the brain which causes syncope.

Nerve supply of External auditory canal:

* Anterior wall and roof- the auriculotemporal branch of mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3) (Option A).

* Posterior wall and floor - the auricular branch of Vagus (Arnold's nerve). Cough response while cleaning the ear canal is mediated by the vagus which also supplies the larynx.

* Posterior wall also receives sensory supply by the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.learning: Arnold's nerve — The posterior wall of the external auditory canal is supplied by the auricular branch of the Vagus (Arnold's nerve). When this nerve is stimulated, a vasovagal response is initiated which results in the syncopal episode.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: When does the anterior fontanelle close?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 12-24 months

The anterior fontanelle ideally closes between 18-24 months. However, the closest answer in the given options is 12–24 months of age.

Fontanelle of the skull:

* The anterior fontanelle is present between the two frontal and two parietal bones. It closes at around 18-24 months. The junction is marked by bregma where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet.

* The posterior fontanelle is present between the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid suture and closes at around 2-3 months of birth.

* The sphenoid fontanelle corresponds to the pterion and also closes at around 2-3 months of birth.

* The mastoid fontanelle closes around at the end of the first year.
questions.learning: 12-24 months The anterior fontanelle ideally closes between 18-24 months. However, the closest answer in the given options is 12–24 months of age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate is noted to have bilious vomiting at 6 hours of life with abdominal distention. An X-ray is ordered (see image). The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Duodenal atresia

The neonate presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension within hours of birth. The X-ray shows the classic “double-bubble sign” due to air in the stomach an d proximal duodenum with absence of distal intestinal gas.

Why not other options?

• A. Pyloric stenosis: Causes non-bilious projectile vomiting, usually at 2–8 weeks of age. X-ray does not show the double-bubble sign.
• B. Esophageal atresia: Presents with excessive salivation, choking and respiratory distress; X-ray shows a dilated proximal esophageal pouch.
• C. Duodenal atresia: Correct. Presents early with bilious vomiting and shows the double-bubble sign.
• D. Hirschsprung’s disease: Presents mainly with delayed passage of meconium, abdominal distension and intestinal obstruction; double-bubble sign is not typical.
questions.learning: Duodenal atresia — The neonate presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension within hours of birth. The X-ray shows the classic “double-bubble sign” due to air in the stomach an d proximal duodenum with absence of distal intestinal gas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female came to OPD with complaints of backache. On examination, Schober test was positive and her eyes and nose were hyperpigmented. Probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ochronosis

Given X-ray shows intervertebral disc calcification and hyperpigmentation of nose and eyes are present. Both features are indicative of ochronosis as diagnosis.

• Ochronosis also known as alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder.
• It is due to deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase leading to accumulation of homogentisic acid.

• Clinical features: Triad of

• Homogentisic aciduria (urine turns dark color on standing due to oxidation or alkalinisation)
• Eumelanin like pigmentation of skin, sclera, cartilages etc.
• Degenerative chronic arthropathies especially of spine, hip, knees.

Option a: Hypoparathyroidism doesn't explain hyperpigmentation and other clinical features of hypoparathyroidism aren't mentioned.

Option b: Fluorosis - dental symptoms are not mentioned and osteoporosis will be marked in case of fluorosis. Also, hyperpigmentation is not a typical feature of fluorosis.

Option d: Ankylosing spondylitis – females are unlikely to be affected and it doesn’t explain hyperpigmentation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What should be the minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4 weeks

The minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines is 4 weeks.

This is because decreasing the interval between two doses may interfere with the antibody response and protection. Thus, live vaccines can either be given on the same day according to the schedule or 4 weeks apart.

Note: In Park 27th ed. the minimum interval between two live vaccines is given as 3 weeks. However, several other standard sources including CDC and UNDP suggested an interval of 4 weeks. When both are given in options, it is recommended to mark 4 weeks as the correct answer.
questions.learning: 4 weeks The minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines is 4 weeks. This is because decreasing the interval between two doses may interfere with the antibody response and protection.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following statements about gap junctions are true except:
options: They are composed of connexin proteins arranged into connexons
They allow direct passage of ions and small molecules (<1 kDa) between adjacent cells
They are present in cardiac muscle and are responsible for electrical coupling at intercalated discs
They require ATP hydrolysis to actively transport molecules between cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. They require ATP hydrolysis to actively transport molecules between cells

• Gap junctions are channels of passive, non-ATP-dependent diffusion — they allow direct intercellular passage of ions, second messengers, and small molecules (generally <1 kDa) down their electrochemical or concentration gradients, without requiring energy expenditure.
• Each gap junction channel is formed by the alignment of two connexons (hemichannels), each composed of six connexin subunits, from adjacent cells.
• They are essential for electrical coupling and synchronized contraction in cardiac muscle (at intercalated discs) and smooth muscle, as well as in other tissues like the lens, liver, and neurons (electrical synapses).
• The statement that they require ATP hydrolysis for transport is false — this describes active transport mechanisms (e.g., ATPase pumps), not gap junction-mediated diffusion.

Quick reference — Gap Junction Essentials:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Structural protein | Connexin (6 connexins → 1 connexon/hemichannel; 2 connexons → 1 complete channel)

| Transport mechanism | Passive diffusion (no ATP required)

| Size limit | Permits molecules <1 kDa (ions, cAMP, IP3, small metabolites)

| Key locations | Cardiac muscle (intercalated discs), smooth muscle, lens fibers, hepatocytes, neurons (electrical synapses), beta cells of pancreas

| Functional role | Electrical coupling, metabolic coupling, synchronized contraction

| Regulation | Closed by ↑intracellular Ca²⁺, ↓pH (acidosis); important in limiting injury spread after cell damage

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the term used to describe an extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Distichiasis

The extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line is called distichiasis.

Distichiasis can occur due to congenital or acquired causes. These lashes may irritate the cornea. Management is by lid splitting with cryotherapy to the base of the hair follicles.

Other options:

Option A: Trichiasis is inward misdirection of cilia, with the normal position of the lid margin.

Option C: Tylosis is the thickening of the tarsal plate.

Option D: Madarosis is the loss of eyelashes or eyebrows.
questions.learning: Distichiasis — The extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line is called distichiasis. Distichiasis can occur due to congenital or acquired causes.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery is maintained on anesthesia with halothane. During the procedure, the patient suddenly developed hyperthermia and muscle rigidity. Which of the following drugs is most likely implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Suxamethonium

The given clinical scenario of a patient being operated under halothane, developing hyperthermia and muscle rigidity is suggestive of an episode of malignant hyperthermia. The drug most likely implicating/causing this condition is suxamethonium (succinylcholine).

Suxamethonium is a peripherally acting depolarizing muscle relaxant, commonly administered during the induction of anesthesia to relax muscles of the jaw, neck, and airway and thereby facilitate laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation.

Malignant hyperthermia is a rare genetic hypermetabolic muscle disease. It occurs due to mutation of the gene for the ryanodine receptor (Ryr 1), located on chromosome 19. Ryr 1 is an ion channel responsible for calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

The symptoms develop when the patient is exposed to inhaled anesthetics (halothane in this case) or suxamethonium/succinylcholine.

The mutated Ryr 1 leads to a sudden release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of the skeletal muscle. This uncontrolled increase in intracellular calcium removes the inhibition of troponin, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, which in turn, leads to an increase in adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) activity. This results in an uncontrolled hypermetabolic state with increased oxygen consumption and CO2 production, producing severe lactic acidosis and hyperthermia.

The key clinical features are:

• Succinylcholine-induced masseter muscle rigidity (causing trismus) or generalized muscle rigidity
• Tachycardia
• Hypercarbia ( increased CO2 production) and reduced oxygen saturation
• Hyperthermia ( rise of 1° Celsius can occur every 5 minutes)
• Arrhythmia
• Hypertension
• Myoglobinuria and myoglobinemia indicating muscle damage
• Metabolic derangements like hyperkalemia and mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis

Treatment is to discontinue the triggering agents i.e; inhaled anesthetics and succinylcholine followed by administration of 100% oxygen. Metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia need to be corrected. Hyperthermia must be controlled by cooling the patient.

Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice. It is given at a dose of 2.5 mg/ kg intravenously and can be repeated every 5-10 minutes till the attack subsides.

Other options:

D-curare or D-tubocurarine (option A), cis-atracurium (option C), and rocuronium (option D) are non-depolarizing muscle relaxants and are not implicated in malignant hyperthermia.
questions.learning: Suxamethonium — The given clinical scenario of a patient being operated under halothane, developing hyperthermia and muscle rigidity is suggestive of an episode of malignant hyperthermia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a case of drowning, the following organism was isolated from the internal organs. What is true regarding this organism?
options: Outer wall contains silica and chlorophyll
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Outer wall contains silica and chlorophyll

The organism shown is a diatom, which is important in diagnosis of drowning.

• Diatoms are unicellular algae, not bacteria
• They possess:

• Silica-containing cell wall (frustule)
• Chlorophyll for photosynthesis

• Have a characteristic symmetrical, glass-like appearance

In drowning: --> Water containing diatoms enters lungs → bloodstream → deposited in organs (bone marrow, liver, brain)

Presence of diatoms in internal organs supports antemortem drowning

Why not other options:

• Unicellular bacteria: Incorrect → diatoms are algae
• Not acid resistant: Silica wall makes them acid resistant
• Only in bone marrow: Found in multiple organs, not restricted

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which unit is used to express the strength of the magnetic field?
questions.explanation: The "Tesla" (T) is the international unit used to measure the strength of a magnetic field. In clinical practice, most MRI scanners operate at magnetic field strengths of 1.5T or 3.0T. Higher field strengths generally provide a better signal-to-noise ratio, allowing for higher-resolution images and faster scan times. Hounsfield Units (Option B) are used in "CT scans" to represent tissue density (radio-density). Kilohertz (Option C) is a unit of frequency used in signal processing and radio waves. Hg or Mercury (Option D) is a unit used to measure "pressure," such as blood pressure or intracranial pressure. Understanding the strength of an MRI magnet is essential for safety protocols, as higher Tesla magnets create stronger attractive forces on ferromagnetic objects and can interact more intensely with implanted medical devices. The safety zone surrounding an MRI scanner is strictly maintained to prevent accidents related to this powerful magnetic field
questions.learning: The "Tesla" (T) is the international unit used to measure the strength of a magnetic field. In clinical practice, most MRI scanners operate at magnetic field strengths of 1.5T or 3.0T.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the basic model of a nuclear family life cycle, consider the following phases: 1. Contraction 2. Dissolution 3. Extension 4. Formation Which one of the following best represents the correct sequence of phases in a normal nuclear family?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4 → 3 → 1 → 2

The family life cycle describes the predictable stages through which a nuclear family progresses from its formation to its eventual dissolution. Understanding these stages helps in planning appropriate maternal, child, and geriatric health services.

The normal sequence of phases in a nuclear family is: Formation → Extension → Contraction → Dissolution

• Formation: Begins with marriage and establishment of a new family.
• Extension: Family expands with the birth and upbringing of children.
• Contraction: Children become independent, leave home, marry, and start their own families (“empty nest” phase).
• Dissolution: Ends with the death of one or both spouses, marking the end of the family unit.
questions.learning: 4 → 3 → 1 → 2 The family life cycle describes the predictable stages through which a nuclear family progresses from its formation to its eventual dissolution.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Interpret the following graph.
options: Normal, negatively skewed, positively skewed, skewed with outliers
Normal, positively skewed, negatively skewed, normal with outliers
Normal, negatively skewed, positively skewed, normal with outliers
Skewed with outliers, positively skewed, negatively skewed, normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Normal, positively skewed, negatively skewed, normal with outliers

The graph shown is of a boxplot, and option B represents the correct answer. 1 is normal, 2 is positively skewed, 3 is negatively skewed, and 4 is normal with an outlier.

A boxplot is a method for graphically depicting groups of numerical data through their quartiles. Box plots may also have lines extending vertically from the boxes (whiskers) indicating variability outside the upper and lower quartiles, hence the terms box-and-whisker plot.

It shows the five-number summary of a set of data including,

• Minimum score
• First (lower) quartile
• Median
• Third (upper) quartile and
• Maximum score

In the box plot, a simple box extends from the 25th percentile (lower limit of the box) to the 75th percentile (upper limit of the box) and the line through the box indicates the median value (50th percentile).

The top and bottom ends of the whiskers are the highest and lowest value of that group excluding outliers

Interpreting the box plot:

• When the median is in the middle of the box, and the whiskers are about the same on both sides of the box i.e when each quartile is of the same length, then the distribution is symmetric or normal (as shown in box plot-1).
• When the median is closer to the bottom of the box, and if the whisker is shorter on the lower end of the box, then the distribution is positively skewed (skewed right as shown in boxplot-2).
• When the median is closer to the top of the box, and if the whisker is shorter on the upper end of the box, then the distribution is negatively skewed (skewed left as shown in boxplot-3).
• Small circles or unfilled dots are drawn on the chart to indicate where suspected outliers lie. Filled circles are used for known outliers (as shown in boxplot-4 ).
questions.learning: Normal, positively skewed, negatively skewed, normal with outliers The graph shown is of a boxplot, and option B represents the correct answer. 1 is normal, 2 is positively skewed, 3 is negatively skewed, and 4 is normal with an outlier.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Conjunctival xerosis is due to the deficiency of which of the following vitamin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A

Xerophthalmia includes conjunctival xerosis (dryness) with Bitot’s spots (white patches of keratinized epithelium appearing on the sclera), corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia (softening of the cornea) that leads to corneal scarring and ultimately, blindness.

According to WHO grading, the order of progression is as follows:

* XN: Night blindness

* X1A: Conjunctival xerosis

* X1B: Bitot's spot (It is a triangular, silvery-white, foamy patch on the bulbar conjunctiva which is usually bilateral. The most common site is temporal.)

* X2: Corneal xerosis

* X3A: Keratomalacia affecting less than 1/3rd of the corneal surface

* X3B: Keratomalacia affecting greater than 1/3rd of the corneal surface

* XS: Corneal scar

* XF: Xerophthalmic fundus

Other options:

* Option A: Vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

* Option C: Vitamin B1/thiamine deficiency leads to Beriberi(wet or dry beriberi) and Wernicke encephalopathy

* Option D: Vitamin B3/niacin deficiency leads to pellagra, which is characterized by dementia, dermatitis, and diarrhea.

Pearl PF1761: Vitamin-A supplementation & treatment of Vitamin-A deficiency

Vitamin A supplementation

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which plasmodium species affects the brain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Falciparum

The Plasmodium species that primarily affects the brain is Plasmodium falciparum. It causes severe forms of malaria, including cerebral malaria, which can lead to several neurological complications.

Cerebral malaria is diagnosed in the case of P. falciparum parasitemia with altered consciousness. Common features include seizures and hypoglycemia. Retinal haemorrhages, neurological findings like hemiplegia, absent or exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and a positive Babinski sign can also be seen.

All patients with severe malaria should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the structure in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blastocyst

The arrow is pointing at Blastocyst.

Around the 4th/5th day of development, the morula becomes the blastocyst. Fluid passes into the morula from the uterine cavity and converts it to a blastocyst with a fluid-filled cavity called blastocoele. This fluid partially separates the cells of the inner cell mass from the outer cell mass.

Cell masses in the blastocyst:

* The outer cell mass is called the trophoblast and forms a major part of the placenta

* The inner cell mass is called the embryoblast and forms the embryo proper

The blastocyst normally implants in the functional layer of the uterine endometrium.

Timeline of implantation:

* 3-4 days after fertilization: The morula (12-16 cells) enters the uterus.

* 4th day after fertilization: The advanced morula reaches the uterine lumen.

* 4-5 days after fertilization: The early blastocyst stage is seen.

* 6-7 days after fertilization: The blastocyst implants in the uterus. Implantation corresponds to 20-22 days of the menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A teacher demonstrated the steps of handwashing to her students. Students also performed the same activity later at school and at home. What is the type of learning in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Psychomotor

The type of learning seen in this case is psychomotor learning.

The psychomotor domain includes learning by observation, physical movements, and the usage of motor skill areas of the brain. The development of these skills requires practice, depending upon the complexity of the task. It is measured based on speed, precision, distance, and procedures in execution.

The three domains in learning are the cognitive, psychomotor, and affective domains. They are described as follows.

Cognitive learning includes the domain of knowledge. Bloom's taxonomy described six levels of cognitive skills. This was revised to include types of knowledge and cognitive processes. The cognitive processes include remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating. Eg. Solving multiple-choice questions in the NEET PG entrance exam involves the usage of the cognitive domain.

Psychomotor learning includes the domain of skills. It includes imitation, manipulation, precision, articulation, and naturalization. Eg. Learning how to insert an IV cannula by observing the residents and nurses during the internship involves the usage of the psychomotor domain.

Affective learning includes the domain of attitude and values. It includes receiving, responding, valuing, organizing, and characterization by value. Eg. Communicating with patients with empathy, responding to their concerns, and interacting with the relatives of patients involves the usage of the affective domain.

Integration of all these three methods in teaching and learning methodology leads to a better understanding of the subject.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Windkessel effect is shown by all except ____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radial artery

Windkessel effect is shown by all except the radial artery.

The windkessel effect is seen in the large elastic arteries like the aorta, carotid, and renal artery. The elasticity or windkessel effect is the exclusive property of large and elastic vessels. These vessels when stretched undergo elastic recoil.

The aorta is stretched during systole. This expansion causes temporary storage of blood, allowing more blood to enter the aorta. This buffer stock of blood is released during diastole, to maintain organ perfusion even during diastole.

The image given below shows the windkessel effect seen in the aorta.

Several methods can be used to evaluate the elastic properties of the aortic Windkessel in living humans. One simple approach is to measure the pulse wave velocity along the aorta, where a higher velocity indicates increased stiffness and elastic resistance. Alternative methods involve assessing the ratio between pulse pressure and changes in aortic volume (delta P/delta V). These methods can be noninvasively performed using ultrasound or tomographic techniques.
